s: “Circumcision is a matter of the heart. It is in the spirit, not in the letter.” Romans 2:29.

1. An excellent man once made a sad remark. He said that anyone who now preaches the most essential duties of Christianity runs a risk. A large part of his hearers may think of him as “a preacher of new teachings.”

Most people still claim to follow the Christian religion, but the way they live has drained away its real substance. Some truths show how the Spirit of Christ differs from the spirit of the world. As soon as anyone puts forward one of these truths, they cry out, “You are telling us strange things. We want to know what these things mean.” Yet he is only preaching to them “Jesus and the resurrection,” and what necessarily follows from it: If Christ has risen, then you must die to the world and live completely for God.

2. This is a hard saying for the natural man. He is alive to the world and dead to God. He will not easily be persuaded to accept it as God’s truth. He will accept it only if it is explained in such a way that it has no use or meaning left.

He “does not accept the” words “of the Spirit of God” when they are taken in their plain and obvious meaning. “They are foolishness to him. And” indeed “he cannot understand them, because they are understood only in a spiritual way.” They can be perceived only by a spiritual sense, and in him that sense has never yet been awakened. Because he lacks it, he rejects as idle human fancies the very things that are both the wisdom and the power of God.

3. “Circumcision is a matter of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter.” In other words, the mark of a true follower of Christ, of someone God has accepted, is not outward circumcision, or baptism, or any other outward form. It is a right state of soul, a mind and spirit made new in the image of the One who created it. This is one of those important truths that can only be understood in a spiritual way.
The Apostle himself hints at this in his next words: “That person’s praise does not come from people, but from God.”
It is as if he said: “Whoever you are, you follow your great Master in this way. But do not expect the world—the people who do not follow him—to say, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant!’
Understand that the world thinks the circumcision of the heart, the seal of your calling, is foolishness.
Be content to wait for your praise until the day when your Lord appears.
On that day you will receive praise from God, in the great gathering of people and angels.”
First, I plan to look closely at what this circumcision of the heart is. Second, I will mention some thoughts that naturally come from this study.
I. 1. First, then, I will look at what the circumcision of the heart is that will receive God’s praise.

In general, we can say that it is a settled condition of the soul, which the sacred writings call holiness. It directly means being cleansed from sin, “from everything that makes flesh and spirit unclean.” As a result, it also means having the same virtues that were in Christ Jesus. It means being so “made new in the spirit of our mind” that we are “perfect as our Father in heaven is perfect.”
2. To be more specific: circumcision of the heart includes humility, faith, hope, and love.

Humility is a right view of ourselves. It cleans our minds of proud ideas about our own perfection, and of thinking too highly of our own abilities and achievements. These ideas are the natural fruit of a corrupted nature.
Humility completely cuts off the empty thought, “I am rich and wise, and I need nothing.” It convinces us that by nature we are wretched, poor, miserable, blind, and naked.

It convinces us that even at our best we are, in ourselves, nothing but sin and emptiness. Confusion, ignorance, and error rule our understanding. Unreasonable, earthly, sensual, and devilish passions have taken over control of our will. In a word, no part of our soul is healthy, and all the foundations of our nature are out of place.

3. At the same time we are convinced that we cannot help ourselves by our own power. Without the Spirit of God, we can do nothing but add sin to sin. He alone works in us by his almighty power, so that we either want to do what is good or actually do it. Without the supernatural help of his Spirit, we cannot even think a good thought. That is as impossible for us as creating ourselves, or making our whole souls new in righteousness and true holiness.

4. Once we have formed this right view of how sinful and helpless our nature is, one result is sure. We stop caring about the “honor that comes from people.” That honor is usually given for some good quality people suppose we have.
Someone who knows himself does not want or value praise that he knows he does not deserve.
So it is “a very small thing to him to be judged by people.”

He compares what the world has said for or against him with what he feels in his own heart. So he has every reason to think that the world, like the god of this world, has been “a liar from the beginning.”

And what about those who are not of the world? If it were God’s will, he would like them to see him as someone who wants to be found a faithful manager of his Lord’s goods. Perhaps that would help him be more useful to his fellow servants. Since that is his only reason for wanting their approval, he does not depend on it at all. For he is sure that whatever God wants done, God will never lack people to do it. God can raise up servants even from these stones to do what pleases him.
5. This is the humble mind that people learn from Christ when they follow his example and walk in his steps.

They come to know their disease, and more and more they are cleansed from one part of it: pride and vanity. This knowledge makes them willing and ready to accept the second thing that circumcision of the heart includes. That is faith, which alone can make them whole. It is the one medicine given under heaven to heal their sickness.
6. Faith is the best guide for the blind, the surest light for those in darkness, and the most perfect teacher for the foolish.

But it must be a faith that is “mighty through God for pulling down strongholds.” It must overturn all the prejudices of corrupt reason, all the false sayings that people honor, all evil customs and habits, and all the “wisdom of the world that is foolishness to God.” It must be a faith that “throws down imaginations,” reasonings, “and every proud thing that sets itself up against the knowledge of God, and takes every thought captive to obey Christ.”
7. “Everything is possible for the one who” believes in this way.

“The eyes of his understanding have been opened,” and he sees what his calling is. It is to glorify God in his body and in his spirit, because God bought him at such a high price. Both now belong to God, because God redeemed them as well as created them.
He feels “the exceeding greatness of this power.” God raised Christ from the dead, and in the same way he is able to “make us alive when we were dead in sin, by his Spirit who lives in us.”

“This is the victory that overcomes the world: our faith.” This faith is not only a firm agreement with everything God has revealed in Scripture. That includes especially these important truths: “Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.” “He carried our sins in his own body on the tree.” “He is the sacrifice that pays for our sins, and not only for ours, but also for the sins of the whole world.” But this faith is also the revealing of Christ in our hearts. It is a God-given evidence or conviction of his love, his free, undeserved love for me, a sinner. It is a sure confidence in his forgiving mercy, produced in us by the Holy Spirit. Through this confidence every true believer is able to testify: “I know that my Redeemer lives.” I have an “Advocate with the Father.” “Jesus Christ the righteous” is my Lord and “the sacrifice for my sins.” I know he has “loved me and given himself for me.” He has made peace between God and me, even me. And I “have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.”

8. A faith like this will always clearly show the power of the One who gives it. He sets his children free from the yoke of sin and “cleans their consciences from dead works.” He makes them so strong that they no longer have to obey sin and its desires. Instead of offering the parts of their body to sin “as tools for doing wrong,” they now “offer themselves” completely “to God, as people who have come back from death to life.”
9. Those who are born of God through faith in this way also have strong comfort through hope.
This is the next thing that circumcision of the heart includes: the witness of their own spirit together with the Spirit, who testifies in their hearts that they are God’s children.

In fact, it is the same Spirit who gives them a clear and cheerful confidence that their heart is upright before God. He gives them a firm assurance that, through his grace, they are now doing what pleases him. They are now on the path that leads to life, and by God’s mercy they will stay on it to the end.
It is he who gives them a living expectation of receiving every good thing from God’s hand. He gives them a joyful hope of the crown of glory that is kept in heaven for them.
This hope is an anchor. It keeps a Christian steady among the waves of this troubled world. It keeps him from crashing on either of two deadly rocks: presumption or despair.
He is not discouraged by a false idea that his Lord is harsh. Nor does he look down on the riches of his goodness.

He does not think the difficulties of the race ahead of him are too great for his strength to overcome. But he also does not expect them to be so small that they will give way before he has used all his strength.

He already has experience in the Christian battle. It assures him that his “work is not wasted” if he does “whatever his hand finds to do with all his might.” That same experience keeps him from the empty idea that he can gain anything in any other way. No virtue can be shown and no praise won by weak hearts and feeble hands. It can only be done by those who follow the same path as the great Apostle to the Gentiles. “I run,” he says, “but not without a clear aim. I fight, but not like someone beating the air. I keep my body down and bring it under control. Otherwise, after I have preached to others, I myself might be rejected.”
10. With this same discipline every good soldier of Christ must train himself to endure hardship.
Made firm and strong by it, he will be able to give up not only the works of darkness, but also every appetite and every desire that is not subject to God’s law.
For as St. John says, “Everyone who has this hope makes himself pure, just as he is pure.”

Every day he makes it his care to clean the deepest corners of his soul. He does this by God’s grace in Christ and through the blood of the covenant. He cleans out the lusts that once possessed and polluted it: impurity, envy, malice, and anger. He clears away every passion and attitude that is of the flesh, whether it springs from his inborn corruption or feeds it. He knows well that his very body is God’s temple, and so he must let nothing common or unclean into it. He knows that holiness always suits the house where the Spirit of holiness kindly chooses to live.

11. But whoever you are, you still lack one thing. You have joined a lively hope to deep humility and steady faith, and in this way you have largely cleansed your heart from the pollution you were born with.
If you want to be perfect, add love to all these. Add love, and you have the circumcision of the heart. “Love fulfills the law; it is the goal of the commandment.”
Very excellent things are said about love. It is the essence, the spirit, and the life of every virtue.
It is not only the first and great commandment. It is all the commandments in one.
“Whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovable,” or honorable, “if there is any virtue, if there is anything worthy of praise”—all of it is included in this one word: love.
In love there is perfection, glory, and happiness.
This is the royal law of heaven and earth: “You are to love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.”
12. This does not forbid us to love anything besides God. It means that we also love our brother.
Nor does it forbid us (as some have strangely imagined) to enjoy anything except God.

To think that would mean that God, the Fountain of holiness, is directly the author of sin. For he has joined pleasure, in a way that cannot be separated, to the use of the created things we need to sustain the life he has given us.
So this can never be what his command means.
Our blessed Lord and his apostles tell us what it really means. They say it so often and so plainly that it cannot be misunderstood.

They all agree with one voice about what these statements truly mean: “The Lord your God is one Lord.” “You shall have no other gods but me.” “You shall love the Lord your God with all your strength.” “You shall hold on to him.” “Your soul’s desire shall be for his name.” They mean nothing other than this: the one perfect Good shall be your one final goal.
You must desire one thing for its own sake: to enjoy the One who is All in All.
You must set one happiness before your souls: union with the One who made them. That means having “fellowship with the Father and the Son” and being joined to the Lord in one Spirit.
You are to follow one purpose to the end of time: enjoying God, now and in eternity.
Desire other things only as far as they lead to this.
Love created things only as they lead you to the Creator.
But in every step you take, let this be the glorious point where your view ends.
Let every feeling, thought, word, and action be placed under this goal.
Whatever you desire or fear, whatever you seek or avoid, whatever you think, say, or do—let it all aim at your happiness in God. He is the only Goal as well as the Source of your being.
13. Have no goal, no final goal, except God.
This is what our Lord says: “Only one thing is needed.” And if your eye is fixed only on this one thing, “your whole body will be full of light.”
This is what St. Paul says: “I do this one thing: I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling in Christ Jesus.”
This is what St. James says: “Wash your hands, you sinners, and make your hearts pure, you who are double-minded.”
This is what St. John says: “Do not love the world or the things in the world.
For everything in the world—the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life—does not come from the Father, but from the world.”

Think of seeking happiness in any of these things. It may be the desire of the flesh, which pleasantly stirs the outward senses. It may be the desire of the eye, which delights the imagination with what is new, great, or beautiful. Or it may be the pride of life: show, grandeur, and power, or what usually comes with them, applause and admiration. Seeking happiness in these things “does not come from the Father.” It neither comes from the Father of spirits nor is approved by him. It comes “from the world.” It is the clear mark of those who refuse to let him rule over them.
II. 1. So I have looked closely at what the circumcision of the heart is that will receive God’s praise.
Second, I will mention some thoughts that naturally come from this study. They give a plain rule by which every person can judge whether he belongs to the world or to God.

First, it is clear from what has been said that no one has a right to God’s praise unless his heart is circumcised by humility. He must be little, lowly, and vile in his own eyes. He must be deeply convinced of the inborn “corruption of his nature,” “by which he has gone very far from original righteousness.” He is inclined to all evil and turned away from all good; he is corrupt and detestable. He has a “fleshly mind that is an enemy of God. It is not subject to God’s law, and in fact it cannot be.” He must feel constantly, deep in his soul, that without the Spirit of God resting on him, he cannot think, desire, say, or do anything good or pleasing in God’s sight.

I say again: no one has a right to God’s praise until he feels his need of God. And not until he seeks the “honor that comes from God alone.” He must neither desire nor pursue the honor that comes from people, except only as far as it leads to this.

2. Another truth naturally follows from what has been said. No one will receive the honor that comes from God unless his heart is circumcised by faith, a “faith that is God’s own work.” He must refuse to be led any longer by his senses, appetites, or passions. He must not even be led by natural reason, that blind leader of the blind which the world idolizes. Instead he lives and walks by faith. He takes every step as one “seeking him who is invisible.” He “does not look at the things that are seen, which are temporary, but at the things that are not seen, which are eternal.” He governs all his desires, plans, and thoughts, all his actions and conduct, as one who has entered behind the veil, where Jesus sits at the right hand of God.

3. Some people spend much of their time and effort laying another foundation. It would be good if they knew this faith better. They base religion on the eternal fitness of things, on the inner excellence of virtue, and on the beauty of the actions that come from it. They also base it on what they call the reasons of good and evil, and on how beings relate to each other.
These explanations of the basis of Christian duty either agree with Scripture or they do not.
If they agree, why confuse well-meaning people and draw them away from the more important matters of the law with a cloud of terms? These terms explain the simplest truths until they become obscure.

If they do not agree, then these people should consider who the author of this new teaching is. Is he likely to be an angel from heaven who preaches a gospel different from that of Christ Jesus? Even if he were, God, not we, has already pronounced his sentence: “Let him be cursed.”

4. Our gospel knows no other foundation for good works than faith, and no other foundation for faith than Christ. So it clearly tells us something. We are not his disciples if we deny that he is the Author of both our faith and our works. Nor are we his disciples if we deny that his Spirit inspires them and makes them perfect.
“Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.”

Only he can give life to those who are dead to God. Only he can breathe into them the breath of Christian life. He goes before them, walks with them, and follows them with his grace, so that their good desires lead to good results.
And “all who are led by the Spirit of God in this way are sons of God.”
This is God’s short and plain description of true religion and virtue. And “no one can lay any other foundation.”

5. Third, we can learn from what has been said that no one is truly “led by the Spirit” unless “the Spirit bears witness with his spirit that he is a child of God.” He must see the prize and the crown before him, and “rejoice in hope of the glory of God.”
So those who have taught that we should not think of our own happiness when we serve God are badly mistaken!

No! God often and clearly teaches us to “look to the reward.” He teaches us to weigh our hard work against the “joy set before us,” and these “light troubles” against that “far greater weight of glory.”

Yes, we are “strangers to the covenant of promise” and “without God in the world” until God, “in his abundant mercy, has given us new birth into a living hope of an inheritance that cannot decay, is not defiled, and does not fade away.”

6. But if this is true, it is high time for certain people to be honest with their own souls. They are far from finding in themselves this joyful assurance that they meet the terms of that covenant and will receive its promises. In fact, they argue with the covenant itself and speak evil of its terms. They complain that the terms are too strict, and that no one ever did or ever will live up to them.

What is this but accusing God of being a hard Master, who demands more from his servants than he enables them to do? It is as if he mocked the helpless works of his hands by binding them to do the impossible. It is as if he commanded them to overcome when neither their own strength nor grace was enough for them.
7. These blasphemers might almost convince people at the opposite extreme that they are not guilty. Those people hope to keep God’s commands without making any effort at all.

What a vain hope! A child of Adam expects to see the kingdom of Christ and of God without striving and struggling first “to enter through the narrow gate.” He was “conceived and born in sin,” and his “inner parts are very wicked.” Yet he thinks he can be “made pure as his Lord is pure” without walking in his steps and “taking up his cross daily.” He thinks so without “cutting off his right hand” and “plucking out his right eye and throwing it away.” He dreams of getting rid of his old opinions, passions, and attitudes, and of being “made holy through and through in spirit, soul, and body”—without a constant, continuing life of self-denial in everything!

8. What less than this can we conclude from the words of St. Paul quoted above? For Christ’s sake he lived “in weaknesses, in insults, in needs, in persecutions, in troubles.” He was full of “signs, and wonders, and mighty works.” He had been “caught up to the third heaven.” Yet, as a recent writer strongly puts it, he believed that without this constant self-denial all his virtues would be unsafe, and even his salvation would be in danger.

“I run,” he says, “but not without a clear aim. I fight, but not like someone beating the air.” With these words he plainly teaches us that whoever does not run like this, and does not deny himself daily like this, is running without a clear aim. He fights as uselessly as someone who “beats the air.”

9. Lastly, we can conclude from what has been said that a person whose heart is not circumcised by love talks just as uselessly about “fighting the fight of faith.” He hopes just as vainly to win the crown that never decays.

Love cuts off the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eye, and the pride of life. It engages the whole person, body, soul, and spirit, in the eager pursuit of that one goal. Love is so essential to a child of God that without it, anyone who lives is counted as dead in God’s sight.
“If I speak with the tongues of people and of angels, but do not have love, I am like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so that I can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.”
Even more, “if I give all I own to feed the poor, and give my body to be burned, but do not have love, it does me no good.”
10. So here is the sum of the perfect law. This is the true circumcision of the heart.
Let the spirit return to God who gave it, with all its affections following after it.
“Let all the rivers flow back again to the place they came from.
He did not want other sacrifices from us. But he has chosen the living sacrifice of the heart.
Let it be offered up to God continually through Christ, in flames of holy love.
And let no created thing be allowed to share it with him. For he is a jealous God.
He will not share his throne with anyone else. He will reign without a rival.
Let no plan and no desire be allowed there unless its final goal is God.

This is the way those children of God once walked. Though they are dead, they still speak to us.” “Do not desire to live except to praise his name. Let all your thoughts, words, and actions lead to his glory.
Set your heart firmly on him, and on other things only as they are in him and come from him.
Let your soul be so completely filled with love for him that you love nothing except for his sake.”
“Have a pure intention of heart. Keep his glory steadily in view in everything you do.”
“Fix your eyes on the blessed hope of your calling, and make everything in the world serve it.”

For then, and only then, do we have that “mind in us which was also in Christ Jesus.” That is when, in every movement of our heart, in every word of our tongue, and in every work of our hands, we “pursue nothing except in relation to him, and under what pleases him.” It is when we, too, neither think, nor speak, nor act to do our “own will, but the will of him who sent us.” It is when, “whether we eat or drink, or whatever we do, we do it all for the glory of God.”
“Even if I give away everything I own to feed the poor, and even if I give my body to be burned, but I do not have love, it does me no good at all.”
1 Corinthians 13:3.
I have good reason to fear that one day this will be said about most of you who are here: this Bible passage did you no good, just like all the others you heard before.

Some of you may not be serious enough to listen to it. Some who listen will not believe it. Some who believe it will still find it a hard teaching, so they will forget it as fast as they can. And a few will accept it gladly for a while. But some of them have no roots of humility or self-denial. So when persecution comes because of the word, they will fall away rather than suffer for it.

Some people do listen to it, believe it and remember it. They even take it so deeply into their hearts that it puts down roots, survives the heat of temptation and starts to bear fruit. Yet even among these, not all will bear fruit that fully ripens.
The worries or pleasures of this world, and the desire for other things (which they may not have felt until then), will grow up along with the word and choke it.
And I, the one who speaks God’s word, am no safer from these dangers than you who hear it.
I too must grieve over “an evil heart of unbelief.”
Whenever God allows persecution to come, even if it is only the small persecution of being insulted, I might be the first to stumble.

Or suppose I am given strength to bear that. If God let the worries of the world loose on me, or stopped guarding me against pleasures that do not lead to him, and against the desire for other things [than knowing and loving him], I would surely be overwhelmed. After preaching to others, I myself would be rejected.
So why do I speak this message at all?
Why? Because God has trusted me with the task of preaching the gospel. I do not know what I will do tomorrow, but today I will preach the gospel.
And about you, this is what my orders say: “Son of man, I am sending you to them. You must say to them, ‘This is what the Lord God says’ — whether they listen or refuse to listen.”
This is what the Lord God says: “Whoever you are, if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”
(To do this, “believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved.”)
“Do not stay away from meeting together, as some people usually do.”
Also, in private, “pray to your Father who sees in secret,” and “pour out your heart to him.”
Let my word be “a lantern for your feet and a light for your paths.”
Keep it “in your heart and on your lips, when you sit at home, when you walk along the road, when you lie down, and when you get up.”
“Turn to me with fasting” as well as prayer. Obey your dying Redeemer: eat that bread and drink that cup, and so “show the Lord’s death until he comes.”

You will receive power from heaven through these means. With that power, do everything the Law commands, and avoid everything it forbids. For you know that “if you break one point, you are guilty of breaking all of it.”
“And do not forget to do good and to share with others.” Yes, while you have time, do all the good you can to everyone.
Then “deny yourself and take up your cross every day.” And if you are called to it, “resist even to the point of shedding blood.”

And when each of you can say, “I have done all this,” let him go on to say to himself (words that could make not just someone like Felix tremble, but even the holiest person on earth): “Even if I give away everything I own to feed the poor, and even if I give my body to be burned, but I do not have love, it does me no good at all.”
So it is extremely important for all of us to know:
I. The full meaning of these words: “Even if I give away everything I own to feed the poor, and even if I give my body to be burned.”
II. The true meaning of the word love.
III. In what sense we can say that without love, all this does us no good.

I. First, notice that the word Paul uses really means to cut into small pieces and then hand out the pieces. So it does not just mean getting rid of all our worldly goods at once, perhaps because we suddenly dislike the world or feel a sudden burst of devotion. It means a deliberate choice, carried out calmly and steadily.
It may also mean that this is done not out of vanity, but partly for the right reason: we want to carry out God’s command, and we long to gain his kingdom.

Notice also that the word give means actually handing something over, as agreed. So, like the word before it, it does not mean a hasty, thoughtless act. It means an act done with open eyes and a firm heart, following a decision made beforehand.

So the full meaning of the words is this. Anyone with ears to hear should listen: “Suppose I gave away everything in my house to feed the poor. Suppose I did this after careful choice and thought. Suppose I spent my life handing it out to them with my own hands, and did it out of obedience. Suppose that, for the same reason, I suffered not only insults and shame, and not only chains and prison — all by my own continued choice, refusing to be set free — but even death itself, yes, death in the way that is most terrible to human nature. Even after all this, if I do not have love (love for God, and love for all people, ‘poured into my heart by the Holy Spirit given to me’), it does me no good at all.”
II. Let us ask what this love is. What is the true meaning of the word?

We can look at it in terms of its qualities or its effects. And so that we cannot possibly go wrong, we will ignore human opinions completely. We will go to our Lord himself to learn what love is. And to learn its effects, we will go to his inspired apostle.
The love our Lord requires of all his followers is love for God and love for people. We love God for his own sake, and we love people for God’s sake.

Now, what does it mean to love God? It means to delight in him, to rejoice in his will, to want to please him all the time, to look for our happiness in him and find it there, and to thirst day and night to enjoy him more fully.
As for how much we should love him, our Lord has told us clearly: “You must love the Lord your God with all your heart.”

This does not mean we may love or delight in no one but him. For he has commanded us to love our neighbor — that is, all people — as ourselves. We are to want and pursue their happiness as sincerely and steadily as our own. He has also commanded us to love many of his creatures in the fullest sense: to delight in them and enjoy them. But we must do this only in a way and to a degree that, as we know and feel, does not turn us away from enjoying him but prepares us for it.
So we are called to love God with all our heart.
In the chapter we are reading, the apostle describes the effects, or qualities, of this love.
Each of these is a sure sign by which anyone can judge whether he has this love or not. So they deserve our most careful attention.
“Love suffers long” — in other words, it is patient.

If you love your neighbor for God’s sake, you will be patient with his weaknesses for a long time. If he lacks wisdom, you will pity him, not look down on him. If he is wrong, you will gently try to win him back, without any harshness or blame. If he is caught in some fault, you will work to restore him with a gentle spirit. And if that cannot be done quickly, you will be patient with him, in case God may in the end bring him to know and love the truth.

Whenever people provoke you, whether out of weakness or out of malice, you will show yourself an example of gentleness and meekness. However often it happens, you will not be conquered by evil, but you will conquer evil with good.
Do not let anyone fool you with empty words: whoever is not patient like this does not have love.
Again: “Love is kind.”
Whoever feels the love of God and of people poured into his heart feels a burning, constant thirst for the happiness of all his fellow creatures.
His soul melts with the strong desire he always has to promote their happiness. And his mouth speaks from what fills his heart.
Kindness is the rule of his tongue.
The same kindness is stamped on everything he does.
The fire inside him keeps working its way out. It spreads further and further in every act of goodwill toward everyone he deals with.
So whether he thinks or speaks, or whatever he does, it all aims at the same goal: to increase in every possible way the happiness of all his fellow creatures.
So do not fool yourselves: whoever is not kind like this does not have love.
Next: “Love does not envy.”
In fact, this is already included when it says, “Love is kind.”
For kindness and envy cannot go together. They can no more live side by side than light and darkness.
If we truly wish every kind of happiness for everyone, we cannot be upset when anyone is happy.
When our wish comes true, it will be sweet to our soul. We will be far from feeling hurt by it.
If we are always doing what good we can for our neighbor, and wishing we could do more, we cannot possibly resent any good thing he receives. In fact, it will be the greatest joy of our heart.
So however much we may flatter ourselves or each other, whoever envies does not have love.
Next it says, “Love does not boast.” Or better: love is not rash or quick to judge. For this is really the true meaning of the word.
Everyone who loves his neighbor for God’s sake will not be quick to think badly of anyone. After all, he wishes them every good thing, spiritual as well as earthly.

Such people cannot condemn someone even in their heart without evidence. They will not do it on weak evidence either. In fact, they will not do it on any evidence without first, if possible, bringing him face to face with his accuser. Or at least they will tell him about the accusation and let him speak for himself.
Each of you feels that you could not act any other way toward someone you love dearly.
So then, whoever does not act like this does not have love.
I will mention just one more quality of this love: “Love is not puffed up.”
You cannot wrong someone you love. So if you love God with all your heart, you cannot wrong him by robbing him of his glory — by taking for yourself what belongs to him alone.

You will admit that all you are and all you have belongs to him. You will admit that without him you can do nothing, that he is your light and your life, your strength and your everything, and that before him you are nothing — even less than nothing.
And if you love your neighbor as yourself, you will not be able to put yourself above him.
In fact, you will no more be able to look down on anyone than to hate him.
[In fact, you will think everyone is better than you.]
Just as wax melts in front of a fire, pride melts away in front of love.
All arrogance, whether in the heart, in speech or in behavior, disappears where love rules.

Love brings down the proud looks of the person who boasted in his own strength. It makes him like a little child: unsure of himself, willing to listen, glad to learn, easily convinced, easily persuaded.
And anyone with a different attitude should give up all empty hope. He is puffed up, and so he does not have love.

III. We still need to ask in what sense we can say: “Even if I give away everything I own to feed the poor, yes, even if I give my body to be burned, but I do not have love, it does me no good at all.”

Without doubt, the main meaning of these words is this: whatever we do and whatever we suffer, if we are not made new in the spirit of our mind by “the love of God poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit given to us,” we cannot enter eternal life.
No one can enter there except on the basis of the covenant that God has given to people in the Son he loves.
But general truths tend to touch us less. So let us look at one or two specific areas where all we can do or suffer does us no good if we do not have love.
First, without love none of it helps to make life happy. Second, none of it helps to make death comfortable.
First, then: without love nothing can help us enough to make our lives happy.
By happiness I do not mean a small, trivial pleasure that may begin and end within the same hour. I mean a state of well-being that satisfies the soul and gives it steady, lasting contentment.

But one simple thought will show that nothing without love can help our present happiness: you cannot lack love in even one single case without pain. And the further you move away from it, the greater the pain.
Are you lacking in patience?
Then to the extent that you fall short of it, you fall short of happiness.
The more the opposite attitudes — anger, irritation, revenge — take control, the unhappier you are.
You know it; you feel it. The storm cannot be calmed, and peace can never return to your soul, unless meekness, gentleness, patience — in a word, love — takes hold of it.
Does anyone find in himself ill will, malice, envy or any other attitude that is the opposite of kindness?
Then misery is there. And the stronger that attitude, the more miserable he is.
If a lazy man can be said to eat his own flesh, this is even more true of the malicious or envious man.
His soul is a true picture of hell, full of torment as well as wickedness.
He already has the worm that never dies, and he is rushing toward the fire that can never be put out.
But for now the great gulf has not yet been fixed between him and heaven.

For now there is still a Spirit ready to help him in his weakness. The Spirit is still willing to purify his heart from evil desires, if he will stretch out his hands to heaven and grieve over his ignorance and misery. The Spirit is willing to renew his heart in the love of God, and so lead him through happiness now to eternal happiness.
Second: Without love, nothing can make death comfortable.
By comfortable I do not mean dull or unaware.

I would not say that someone died comfortably if he died of a stroke or was killed by a cannonball. Nor would I say it of someone whose conscience was seared and who died as carelessly as the animals that perish.
And I do not think you would envy anyone the comfort of dying completely insane.
By a comfortable death I mean a calm passage out of this life, full of steady, clear-minded peace and joy.
And all the doing and all the suffering in the world cannot give such a death without love.
To make this even clearer, I cannot appeal to your own experience. But I can appeal to what we have seen and to the experience of others.
I myself have seen two people leave this life in what I call a comfortable way, though not with the same amount of comfort.
One clearly had more comfort than the other, because he had more love.
I stayed with the first man during much of his final trial, and also when he gave up his soul to God.
He cried out, “God is disciplining me with severe pain. But I thank him for everything. I bless him for everything. I love him for everything!”
Not long before he was set free, someone asked him, “Do God’s comforts seem small to you?” He answered out loud, “No, no, no!”
He called everyone who was near him by name and said, “Think about heaven, talk about heaven. All the time we spend not thinking about heaven is lost.”
This was the voice of love. And as far as love was in control, everything was comfort, peace and joy.
But his love was not perfect, and so his comfort was not perfect either.
He had times of [anger or] irritation, and in those times, misery. Both of these proved beyond question that love can make both life and death sweet.
So when love is missing from the soul, or hidden in it, there is no peace or comfort there.
It was right here that I saw the other good soldier of Jesus Christ wrestling with his last enemy, death.
It truly was a sight worth seeing, for God, for angels and for people.
He used some of his last breath to sing a psalm of praise to the one who was then giving him the victory. Because he was sure of that victory, he began to celebrate it even in the heat of the battle.
When someone asked him, “Do you have the love of God in your heart?” he lifted up his eyes and his hands and answered, “Yes, yes!” with all the strength he had left.
Someone asked if he was afraid of the devil, since he had just said the devil was making his last attack on him. He replied, “No, no. My loving Savior has conquered every enemy. He is with me.
I am not afraid of anything.” Soon after, he said, “The way to our loving Savior is painful, but it is short.”
Not long after, he fell into a kind of sleep, and in it his soul gently returned to the God who gave it.
Notice that here there was no trace of any feeling or attitude opposed to love. So there was no misery. Perfect love drove out everything that could have caused torment.
And whoever you are, if you have the same amount of love, your end will be like his.

blocks.x: To the Reader

s: I am completely sure that what I say here is “the truth as it is in Jesus.” I am also sure that I have no choice: I must announce this truth to the whole world. Nothing less than this could have made me openly oppose the views of people I respect because of their work. May I be found at their feet on the day of the Lord Jesus!
If anyone thinks it is his duty to answer this, I have just one request. Whatever you do, do it from the heart, with love, and in a gentle spirit.

Let even the way you argue show that you have “put on, as God’s chosen people, a heart full of mercy, gentleness, and patience.” Then, even today, people may say, “Look how these Christians love one another!”
Someone has published a pamphlet called “Free Grace Indeed” against this sermon. I want its publisher to know that I cannot answer his booklet until he seems more serious.
For I do not dare to talk about “the deep things of God” like a prize-fighter or an actor on a stage.
“God did not hold back even his own Son, but gave him up for all of us. So won’t he also, together with him, freely give us everything?” Romans 8:32
1. How freely God loves the world!
While we were still sinners, “Christ died for ungodly people.”
While we were “dead in our sin,” God “did not hold back his own Son, but gave him up for all of us.”
And how freely, together with him, he “gives us everything”!
Truly, FREE GRACE is everything!
2. God’s grace, or love, is where our salvation comes from. It is FREE IN ALL, and FREE FOR ALL.
3. First, it is free in everyone who receives it.
It does not depend on any strength or worth in a person. Not at all—not in whole and not in part.
It does not depend in any way on the good deeds or the goodness of the one who receives it. It does not depend on anything he has done or anything he is.
It does not depend on how hard he tries.
It does not depend on his good character, his good desires, or his good plans and intentions. All of these come from God’s free grace. They are only the streams, not the spring they flow from.
They are the fruit of free grace, not its root.
They do not cause grace. Grace causes them.
Whatever good there is in a person, or whatever good a person does, God is the one who makes it and does it.

So God’s grace is free in all. That means it does not depend on any strength or worth in people. It depends on God alone, who freely gave us his own Son, and who “together with him freely gives us everything.”
4. But it is free for ALL, as well as IN ALL.
Some people have answered this by saying, “No. It is free only for those whom God has appointed to life. And they are only a small flock.
God has appointed most people to death. It is not free for them.
God hates them. So before they were even born, he decided that they would die forever.
And he decided this completely and without conditions, because it pleased him. It was his own supreme will.
So they are born for this one purpose: to be destroyed, body and soul, in hell.

And they grow up under God’s curse, which can never be taken back. There is no way for them to be rescued. Whatever grace God gives them, he gives only to make their punishment worse, not to stop it.”
5. This is that decree of predestination.
But I think I hear someone say, “That is not the predestination I believe in. I believe only in ‘the election of grace.’
All I believe is this: before the world was made, God chose a certain number of people. He chose them to be made right with him, made holy, and brought into glory.

All of these people will be saved, and nobody else. God leaves the rest of the human race to themselves. So they follow the ideas of their own hearts, which are always and only evil. They get worse and worse, and in the end they are fairly punished with a destruction that lasts forever.”
6. Is that all the predestination you believe in?
Think about it. Maybe it is not all.
Don’t you believe that God appointed those people to this very end? If you do, you believe the whole decree. You believe in predestination in the full sense I described above.
But maybe you think you don’t.
Then don’t you believe that God hardens the hearts of those who are lost? Don’t you believe that he (literally) hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and that he raised him up, or created him, for this purpose?
Well, that comes to exactly the same thing.
If you believe that Pharaoh, or any single person on earth, was created for this purpose—to be damned—then you believe everything I have said about predestination.

You do not even need to add anything more. You do not need to say that God backs up his decree (which is supposed to be unchangeable and impossible to resist) by hardening hearts. You do not need to say that he hardens the hearts of those “vessels of wrath” whom the decree had already made ready for destruction.

7. Well, maybe you do not even believe this. You do not believe in any decree of rejection. You do not think God decides that anyone will be damned. You do not think he hardens anyone, or makes anyone ready for damnation in a way that cannot be resisted. You only say this: “Before time began, God decided something. Since everyone was dead in sin, he would say to some of the dry bones, ‘Live,’ and to others he would not. So some would be made alive, and others would stay dead. The first group would bring glory to God by being saved, and the second group by being destroyed.”
8. Isn’t this what you mean by “the election of grace”?
If it is, I want to ask one or two questions. Is anyone who has not been chosen in this way ever saved? Has anyone ever been saved like that since the world began?
Is it possible for anyone to be saved unless he has been chosen in this way?

If you say “No,” you are right back where you started. You have not moved forward even the width of a hair. You still believe that most people stay dead, with no way to be rescued, because of a decree of God that cannot change and cannot be resisted. For only God can save them, and he will not.
You believe he has firmly decided not to save them. And what is that, if not deciding to damn them?

In effect, it is exactly the same—no more and no less. It comes to the same thing. Suppose you are dead and completely unable to make yourself alive. If God has firmly decided to make only other people alive, and not you, then he has firmly decided that you will die forever. You are completely handed over to damnation.

So even though you use softer words than some people, you mean exactly the same thing. As you describe it, God’s decree about “the election of grace” is exactly what others call God’s decree of rejection—no more and no less.
9. So call it whatever you like—election, being passed over, predestination, or rejection. In the end it all comes to the same thing.

What all of them plainly mean is this: God has made an eternal decree that cannot change and cannot be resisted. Because of it, one part of the human race will certainly be saved, and the rest will certainly be damned. None of the first group can possibly be damned, and none of the second group can possibly be saved.
10. But if this is true, then all preaching is useless.
Those who are chosen do not need it. With preaching or without it, they will certainly be saved.

So the purpose of preaching—to save souls—means nothing for them. And it is useless for those who are not chosen, because they cannot possibly be saved. With preaching or without it, they will certainly be damned.
So the purpose of preaching means nothing for them either. Either way, our preaching is useless, and your listening is useless too.
11. So this is a clear proof that the teaching of predestination does not come from God. It makes useless the very means God himself has set up. And God does not fight against himself.
A second proof is that it leads straight toward destroying holiness, which is the goal of everything God has set up.

I am not saying that no one who believes it is holy. (God is tenderly merciful to people who cannot help being tangled up in mistakes of any kind.) But I am saying that the teaching itself clearly tends to destroy holiness in general. This teaching says that from eternity every person is either chosen or not chosen, and that the first must be saved and the second must be damned. It completely takes away the first reasons for pursuing holiness, which Scripture gives so often: the hope of a future reward and the fear of punishment, the hope of heaven and the fear of hell.

Some will go away to punishment that lasts forever, and others to eternal life. But suppose a person believes his future is already fixed. Then this gives him no reason to struggle for life. If he thinks he has already been sentenced, to life or to death, and that this can never change, it makes no sense for him to try.
You will say, “But he doesn’t know whether it is life or death.”

So what? That does not help. Imagine a sick man who knows that he will either die for certain or get better for certain, but he does not know which. It would make no sense for him to take any medicine at all.

He could fairly say, “If I am meant to live, I will live. If I am meant to die, I will die. So I don’t need to worry about it.” (I have heard some people talk like this, both about sickness of the body and sickness of the soul.)
This teaching tends so directly to shut the very gate of holiness in general. It keeps unholy people from ever coming near it or trying to go in.
12. In the same direct way, this teaching tends to destroy several particular parts of holiness.
These include gentleness and love—I mean love for our enemies, for evil and ungrateful people.

I am not saying that no one who believes it is gentle and loving. (God’s mercy is as great as his power.) But I am saying that it naturally tends to create, or increase, a sharp and hot-tempered spirit. That is the very opposite of the gentleness of Christ. You can see this especially when people who hold this teaching are challenged about it.
In the same natural way, it creates scorn or coldness toward those whom we think God has thrown away.
“Oh, but,” you say,
“I don’t think that any particular person is rejected.”
You mean you would not think so if you could help it. But sometimes you cannot help applying your general teaching to particular people. The enemy of souls will apply it for you.
You know how often he has done this.
But you pushed the thought away in horror.

True—as soon as you could. But in the meantime, how it made your spirit sour and sharp! You know very well that it was not love you felt toward that poor sinner. Whether you wanted to or not, you imagined or suspected that God had hated him from eternity.
13. Third, this teaching tends to destroy the comfort of faith, the happiness of being a Christian.
This is obvious for all those who believe they are rejected, or who only suspect or fear it.
All of God’s great and precious promises are lost to them. They do not give them even a ray of comfort. After all, they are not God’s chosen people, so they have no share or part in those promises.
This truly blocks them from finding any comfort or happiness, even in the faith whose ways are meant to be “pleasant ways, with every path full of peace.”
14. And what about you who believe you are God’s chosen ones? What is your happiness?

I hope it is not just an idea, a theory, or a bare opinion of any kind. I hope it is having God in your heart in a way you can feel, which the Holy Spirit has brought about in you. In other words, it is God’s Spirit telling your spirit that you are a child of God.
This is also called “the full assurance of faith.” It is the true foundation of a Christian’s happiness.
It really does include being fully sure that all your past sins are forgiven and that you are now a child of God.
But it does not have to include being fully sure that we will keep going in faith in the future.
I am not saying the two never go together. But the one does not automatically include the other. Many people have the first without the second.

15. Now, experience shows that this teaching gets badly in the way of this witness of the Spirit. It does so in people who believe they are rejected, and who push that witness far away because of what they believe. But it also does so in people who have tasted that good gift. Yet they soon lost it again and fell back into doubts and fears and darkness—horrible darkness, so thick that it could be felt!
I appeal to any of you who believe this teaching. Tell me honestly, between God and your own heart: don’t your doubts and fears about being chosen, or about holding on to the end, often come back?
If you ask, “Who doesn’t have them?”

I answer: very few of those who believe this teaching. But many, very many, of those who do not believe it, all over the world. Many of these have enjoyed the witness of his Spirit without a break, the constant light of his face, from the moment they first believed. This has gone on for many months or years, right up to today.

16. The assurance of faith that these people enjoy shuts out all doubt and fear. It shuts out every kind of doubt and fear about whether they will hold on in the future. Yet, as I said before, it is not really an assurance about the future. It is only about what is true now.

This assurance does not need to be propped up by the theory that whoever is once appointed to life must live. It is created hour by hour by God’s mighty power, “by the Holy Spirit who has been given to them.”

So that teaching does not come from God. It tends to block, or even destroy, this great work of the Holy Spirit. And this work is where the main comfort of faith, the happiness of being a Christian, comes from.
17. Here is another point. What a painful thought it is that thousands and millions of people, without having done anything wrong first, were doomed to burn forever, and that this can never change!

How especially painful this must be for those who have put on Christ! Think of those who are filled with mercy, tenderness, and compassion—who could even “wish that they themselves were cursed for the sake of their brothers”!
18. Fourth, this cheerless teaching leads straight toward destroying our eagerness to do good works.
It does this, first, because it naturally tends (as I said before) to destroy our love for most people—that is, for evil and ungrateful people.
For whatever makes our love smaller is sure to make our desire to do them good much smaller too.

It does this, second, because it cuts off one of the strongest reasons for every kind of care for people’s bodies, like feeding the hungry, giving clothes to those who have none, and so on. That reason is the hope of saving their souls from death.
After all, what is the point of helping with the earthly needs of people who are just about to drop into eternal fire?
“Well, then, run and snatch them like burning sticks out of the fire.” No—you believe this is impossible.
You say they were appointed to it from eternity, before they had done anything good or bad. You believe it is God’s will that they should die.
And “who has ever resisted his will?”
But you say you do not know whether these people are chosen or not.
So what? If you know they are one or the other—either chosen or not chosen—then all your hard work is empty and useless.
Either way, your advice, your warnings, and your encouragement are just as unneeded and useless as our preaching.
Those who are chosen do not need it, for they will certainly be saved without it.
It is useless for those who are not chosen, for they will certainly be damned with it or without it. So if you stay true to your beliefs, you cannot make any effort to help them be saved.
So those beliefs lead straight toward destroying your eagerness for good works—for all good works, but especially for the greatest one of all: saving souls from death.
19. But, fifth, this teaching does not only tend to destroy Christian holiness, happiness, and good works. It also clearly and directly tends to overturn the whole Christian revelation.
The wisest unbelievers of our time work very hard to prove one point: that the Christian revelation is not necessary.
They know that if they could just show this, the conclusion would be too obvious to deny: “If it is not necessary, it is not true.” And you give up this basic point.

For if that eternal, unchangeable decree is true, then one part of the human race must be saved even if the Christian revelation did not exist. And the other part must be damned in spite of that revelation.
What more could an unbeliever want?
You give him everything he asks for.
By making the gospel unnecessary in this way for all kinds of people, you give up the whole Christian cause.
“Oh, don’t tell it in Gath, or the daughters of the uncircumcised will rejoice!” Don’t let the sons of unbelief celebrate their victory!
20. This teaching clearly and directly tends to overturn the whole Christian revelation. And it does the same thing, as a plain result, by making that revelation contradict itself.
For it is built on a way of explaining some Bible passages (how many does not matter) that flatly contradicts all the other passages—and in fact the whole message and direction of Scripture.
For example, those who defend this teaching take the verse “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau” to mean that God literally hated Esau, and all the rejected, from eternity.
Now what could contradict more flatly than this? It contradicts not only the whole message and direction of Scripture, but also all those particular verses that clearly say, “God is love.”

Again, they take the verse “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (Romans 4:15) to mean that God is love only to some people—that is, to the chosen—and that he has mercy only for them. But the whole direction of Scripture says the exact opposite. So does this clear statement in particular: “The Lord is loving to every person, and his mercy is over everything he has made.”

(Psalm 145:9) Again, look at that verse and others like it: “It is not up to the one who wills, or the one who runs, but up to God who shows mercy.” From these they conclude that he shows mercy only to those he had favoured from all eternity.
No—now who is talking back to God?
Now you are the one contradicting all of God’s word. Again and again it says, “God does not play favourites” (Acts 10:34), and “With him there is no favouritism.”

(Romans 2:11) Again, you take this verse: “The children were not born yet, and had done nothing good or evil. So that God’s purpose in choosing might stand, not because of deeds but because of the one who calls, it was said to her”—to Rebecca—“The elder shall serve the younger.” From this you conclude that our being predestined, or chosen, does not depend at all on what God knows beforehand.
But all the Scriptures say the exact opposite, especially these: “Chosen according to what God knew beforehand” (1 Peter 1:2), and “Those he knew beforehand, he also predestined” (Romans 8:29).
21. And “the same Lord over all is rich” in mercy “to all who call on him” (Romans 10:12). But you say, “No. He is like that only to those Christ died for.
And that is not everyone. It is only a few, whom God has chosen out of the world. For Christ did not die for everyone. He died only for those who were ‘chosen in him before the world was made.’”

(Ephesians 1:4) But your way of explaining these Scriptures is flatly contradicted by the whole direction of the New Testament. It is contradicted especially by these verses: “Do not bring ruin by your food on the one for whom Christ died” (Romans 14:15). This clearly proves that Christ died not only for those who are saved, but also for those who are lost. He is “the Saviour of the world” (John 4:42). He is “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). “He is the offering that makes peace with God for our sins, not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:2). “He,” the living God, “is the Saviour of everyone” (1 Timothy 4:10). “He gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6). “He tasted death for every person” (Hebrews 2:9).

22. You may ask, “Then why isn’t everyone saved?” The whole law and the testimony give the answer. First, it is not because of any decree of God. It is not because he is pleased that they should die. For “As I live,” says the Lord God, “I take no pleasure in the death of the one who dies.”

(Ezekiel 18:3, 32) Whatever the cause of their being lost, it cannot be his will—if God’s word is true. For it says, “It is not his will that any should be lost, but that all should turn from their sins” (2 Peter 3:9), and “His will is that everyone should be saved.”
And second, God’s word tells us why not everyone is saved: because they will not be saved. Our Lord says this clearly: “You won’t come to me, so that you might have life.”
(John 5:40) “The power of the Lord is there to heal” them, but they will not be healed.
“They turn down the advice,” the merciful advice, “of God, to their own harm,” just as their stubborn ancestors did.
So they have no excuse. God would save them, but they will not be saved. This is why they are condemned: “How often I would have gathered you together, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37)

23. So this teaching clearly tends to overturn the whole Christian revelation. It does this by making the Bible contradict itself. It explains some verses in a way that flatly contradicts all the other verses, and indeed the whole message and direction of Scripture. This is plenty of proof that it does not come from God.

But that is not all. Seventh, it is a teaching full of blasphemy. The blasphemy is so terrible that I would be afraid to mention it. But the honour of our gracious God and the cause of his truth will not let me stay silent.
So for God’s sake, and because I truly care about the glory of his great name, I will mention a few of the horrible blasphemies found in this horrible teaching.
But first I must warn every one of you who hears me—as you will answer for it on the great day. Do not accuse me of blasphemy (as some have done) just because I mention the blasphemy of others.

And the more upset you are with those who blaspheme like this, the more you should make sure you “confirm your love for them.” Let your heart’s desire, and your constant prayer to God, be: “Father, forgive them, for they have no idea what they are doing!”

24. With that said, notice that this teaching makes our blessed Lord—“Jesus Christ the righteous,” “the only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth”—look like a hypocrite, someone who fools people, a man without ordinary honesty.
For no one can deny that everywhere he speaks as if he wanted all people to be saved.
So to say he did not want all people to be saved is to make him out to be nothing but a hypocrite and a pretender.
No one can deny that the gracious words that came from his mouth are full of invitations to all sinners.
So to say he did not mean to save all sinners is to make him out to be someone who badly fools people.
You cannot deny that he says, “Come to me, all you who are worn out and weighed down.”
Now suppose you say he calls people who cannot come—people he knows are unable to come—people he could make able to come, but will not. How could anyone describe greater dishonesty than that?
You make him out to be mocking his helpless creatures by offering them what he never means to give.
You describe him as saying one thing and meaning another—as pretending to have a love he did not have.

He is the one “in whose mouth there was no deceit.” Yet you make him full of deceit, without ordinary honesty. You do this especially at the moment when he came near the city, wept over it, and said, “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I would have gathered your children together—and you would not!” (In Greek: ēthelēsa kai ouk ēthelēsate.)

Now, suppose you say that they were willing, but he was not. Then you make him out (who could bear to hear it?) to be crying fake “crocodile tears”—weeping over the prey that he himself had doomed to destruction!
25. Surely blasphemy like this should make a Christian’s ears ring with shock!
But there is still more. For this teaching honours the Father in just the same way as it honours the Son.
It destroys all of his qualities at once. It overturns his justice, his mercy, and his truth. Yes, it makes the most holy God look worse than the devil—more false, more cruel, and more unjust.

More false, because the devil, liar that he is, has never said, “He wants all people to be saved.” More unjust, because the devil could not, even if he wanted to, be guilty of the kind of injustice you blame on God. You say that God condemned millions of souls to everlasting fire, which was made ready for the devil and his angels. And you say he did this because they went on sinning—yet they cannot avoid that sin, because they lack the grace he will not give them. And more cruel, because that unhappy spirit “looks for rest and finds none.” So his own restless misery is a kind of temptation that pushes him to tempt others.

But God rests in his high and holy place. So imagine him, happy as he is, dooming his creatures to endless misery whether they want it or not—simply because he chose to, purely because he wanted to. That would be blaming him for a cruelty we cannot blame even on the great enemy of God and humanity.
It makes the high God (whoever has ears to hear, let him hear!) more cruel, more false, and more unjust than the devil!
26. This is the blasphemy clearly contained in the horrible decree of predestination!
And here I take my stand.
On this point I will argue it out with everyone who defends it.
You make God worse than the devil—more false, more cruel, more unjust.
But you say you will prove it from Scripture.
Stop! What will you prove from Scripture? That God is worse than the devil?
That cannot be. Whatever that Scripture proves, it can never prove this, whatever its true meaning may be.
This cannot be what it really means.
Do you ask, “Then what does it really mean?”
If I say, “I don’t know,” you have not won anything. For there are many Scriptures whose real meaning neither you nor I will know until death is swallowed up in victory.
But this I do know: it would be better to say it had no meaning at all than to say it meant something like this.
Whatever else it may mean, it cannot mean that the God of truth is a liar.
Let it mean whatever it means—it cannot mean that the Judge of all the world is unfair.
No Scripture can mean that God is not love, or that his mercy does not cover everything he has made. In other words, whatever else it proves, no Scripture can prove predestination.

27. This is the blasphemy that makes me hate the teaching of predestination (even though I love the people who hold it). Imagine it were true, even for a moment—call it election, rejection, or whatever you like, since it all comes to the same thing. Then someone might say to our enemy the devil, “You fool, why do you keep roaring around?
Your lying in wait to catch souls is as unneeded and useless as our preaching.
Haven’t you heard? God has taken your work out of your hands, and he does it much better than you!
You, with all your rulers and powers, can only attack us in a way that we can still resist. But He can destroy both body and soul in hell, and no one can resist him!
You can only tempt people to sin. But his unchangeable decree, which leaves thousands of souls in death, forces them to keep on sinning until they drop into the fire that burns forever.
You tempt us; He forces us to be damned, because we cannot resist his will.
You fool, why do you keep going around looking for someone to devour?

Haven’t you heard that God is the devouring lion, the destroyer of souls, the murderer of people? Moloch made only children pass through the fire. And that fire was soon put out; or, once the body that could decay was burned up, its pain was over. But you are told that God, by his eternal decree, fixed before they had done anything good or bad, makes not only tiny babies but their parents too pass through the fire of hell—‘the fire that will never be put out.’ And the body thrown into it can no longer decay or die, so it will always be burning and never burned up. But ‘the smoke of their torment,’ because it pleases God, ‘rises up for ever and ever.’”
28. Oh, how the enemy of God and humanity would celebrate to hear that these things were true!
How he would shout out loud and not hold back!
How he would raise his voice and say, “To your tents, O Israel!
Run away from this God, or you will be completely destroyed!
But where will you run?
Into heaven? He is there. Down to hell?
He is there too.
You cannot run away from a tyrant who is everywhere and all-powerful.
Whether you run or stay, I call heaven, his throne, and earth, his footstool, as witnesses against you: you will perish; you will die forever.
Sing, O hell, and rejoice, all you who are under the earth!
For God, the mighty God, has spoken. He has handed thousands of souls over to death, from where the sun rises to where it sets!
Here, O death, is your sting!
They will not, they cannot escape, for the Lord himself has said it.
Here, O grave, is your victory! Nations not yet born, before they have ever done anything good or bad, are doomed never to see the light of life. You will chew on them for ever and ever!
Let all those morning stars who fell with Lucifer, son of the morning, sing together!
Let all the sons of hell shout for joy!
For the decree has been made, and who can cancel it?”
29. Yes, the decree has been made, and it was made before the world began.
But what decree? This one: “I will set before the human race ‘life and death, blessing and curse.’
And the soul who chooses life will live, just as the soul who chooses death will die.”

This decree, by which “those God knew beforehand, he predestined,” truly was made from everlasting. By this decree, all who allow Christ to make them alive are “chosen according to what God knew beforehand.” It now stands firm, like the moon and like the faithful witnesses in heaven. And when heaven and earth pass away, this will not pass away. For it is as unchangeable and eternal as God himself, who made it.
This decree gives us the strongest encouragement to be full of good works and all holiness. It is also a spring of joy and happiness, bringing us great comfort that never ends.
This is worthy of God. It fits in every way with all the perfect qualities of his nature.
It gives us the noblest picture of his justice, mercy, and truth.
The whole message of the Christian revelation agrees with this, and so do all its parts.

Moses and all the Prophets bear witness to this, and so do our blessed Lord and all his Apostles. So Moses says, in the name of his Lord: “I call heaven and earth to testify against you this day: I have put life and death in front of you, blessing and cursing. So choose life, so that you and your offspring may live.”
So Ezekiel says (to quote one prophet for them all): “The soul that sins will die. The son will not bear” forever “the wrongdoing of the father.
The good person’s goodness will rest on him, and the wicked person’s wickedness will rest on him.”
(Ezekiel 18:20) So our blessed Lord says: “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink.”

(John 7:37) So his great Apostle, St. Paul, says (Acts 17:30): “God orders all people in every place to repent”—“all people in every place.” That means every person in every place, with no exception of place or person.
So St. James says: “If any of you is short of wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to everyone and does not scold, and it will be given to him.”
(James 1:5) So St. Peter says (2 Peter 3:9): “It is not the Lord’s will that any should be lost, but that all should turn from their sins.”

And so St. John says: “If anyone sins, we have someone who speaks for us to the Father. And he is the offering that makes peace with God for our sins—not only for ours, but for the sins of the whole world.”
30. Oh, listen to this, you who forget God!
You cannot blame him for your death! “‘Am I at all pleased when the wicked die?’ says the Lord God.”
(Ezekiel 18:23 and following) “Turn back, and turn away from all your wrongdoing. Then your sin will not destroy you.
Throw away all the wrong things you have done—for why would you choose to die, O house of Israel?
For the death of the one who dies gives me no pleasure, says the Lord God.
So turn yourselves around, and live!”
“As I live, says the Lord God, the death of the wicked gives me no pleasure.—Turn, turn from your evil ways! Why would you choose to die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11)
“You almost persuade me to be a Christian.” Acts 26:28.
Many people go this far. Ever since the Christian religion came into the world, there have been many people in every age and nation who were almost persuaded to be Christians.
But going only this far is worth nothing before God. So it is very important for us to consider the following:
First, what it means to be almost a Christian.
Second, what it means to be altogether a Christian.
I. (I.) 1. Being almost a Christian includes, first of all, heathen honesty.

I don’t think anyone will question this. That is especially so because by heathen honesty I do not mean only what their philosophers recommended in their writings. I mean the honesty that ordinary heathens expected from one another, and that many of them actually practised.

Its rules taught them that they must not be unjust. They must not take their neighbour’s goods, whether by robbery or by theft. They must not oppress the poor or use extortion against anyone. They must not cheat or take advantage of anyone, rich or poor, in any business they did with them. They must not rob anyone of what was rightfully his. And, if possible, they should owe no one anything.
2. The ordinary heathens also agreed that people should have some respect for truth, as well as for justice.
So they hated anyone who swore falsely and called God to witness to a lie. They also hated anyone known for slandering his neighbour and falsely accusing others.
In fact, they thought little better of deliberate liars of any kind. They saw them as a disgrace to the human race and a plague on society.
3. There was also a kind of love and help that they expected from one another.
They expected people to give each other whatever help they could, as long as it did not harm themselves.

This included the small acts of kindness that cost no money or effort. But it also included feeding the hungry, if they had food to spare, and clothing the naked with their own spare clothes. In general, it meant giving to anyone in need the things they did not need themselves.
That, at the very least, is how far heathen honesty went. It is the first thing included in being almost a Christian.

(II.) 4. The second thing included in being almost a Christian is having a form of godliness. This is the godliness that the gospel of Christ requires. It means having the outward look of a real Christian.

So the almost Christian does nothing that the gospel forbids. He does not take God’s name in vain. He blesses and does not curse. He does not swear at all, but his words are simply “Yes, yes” and “No, no.” He does not dishonour the Lord’s Day, and he does not let anyone else dishonour it, not even the stranger staying within his gates. He avoids all actual adultery, sexual immorality, and impurity. He also avoids every word or look that leads toward them, directly or indirectly. He even avoids all careless words. He keeps away from running people down, from backbiting, from gossip, and from speaking evil. He keeps away from “all foolish talk and joking”—eutrapelia, which the heathen moral teachers counted as a kind of virtue. In short, he keeps away from all talk that is not “good for building others up.” Such talk therefore “grieves the Holy Spirit of God, who has sealed us for the day of redemption.”
5. He keeps away from “wine that leads to excess.” He keeps away from wild parties and overeating.
As far as he can, he avoids all fighting and quarrelling. He always tries to live at peace with everyone.

If someone wrongs him, he does not take revenge or pay back evil for evil. He does not insult people or pick fights. He does not mock the faults or weaknesses of his neighbour. He does not willingly wrong, hurt, or upset anyone. In everything he does and says, he follows this plain rule: “Do not do to another what you would not want him to do to you.”
6. When he does good, he does not limit himself to cheap and easy acts of kindness. He works hard and suffers for the good of many, so that by all means he may help some.
In spite of hard work or pain, “whatever his hand finds to do, he does it with all his might.” He does this for his friends and for his enemies, for the evil and for the good.

He is “not lazy” in this or in any other “work.” Whenever he “has the opportunity,” he does “good”—every kind of good—“to everyone,” to their souls as well as their bodies. He corrects the wicked, teaches the ignorant, steadies those who waver, stirs the good to new life, and comforts those who suffer. He works to wake up those who are asleep. He works to lead those whom God has already awakened to the “fountain opened for sin and for impurity,” so that they may wash there and be clean. And he works to stir up those who are saved through faith to show the beauty of the gospel of Christ in everything.

7. The person who has the form of godliness also uses the means of grace—all of them, at every opportunity. He goes to the house of God regularly. But he does not go the way some people do. They come into the presence of the Most High loaded with gold and expensive clothes, or dressed in showy vanity. By their untimely politeness to each other, or by their out-of-place light-heartedness, they give up any claim to the form of godliness as well as to its power.

I wish to God that no one even among us deserved the same blame! Some come into this house perhaps staring around, or showing every sign of being bored, careless, and indifferent.
