Sometimes they may seem to pray for God’s blessing on what they are about to begin. But during that awe-inspiring service they are asleep, or leaning back in the most comfortable position for sleeping. Or they talk to one another or look around, as if they thought God were asleep, and as if they had nothing at all to do.
No one should accuse these people of having the form of godliness.
No. Anyone who has even this form behaves seriously and pays attention in every part of that solemn service.
This is especially true when he comes to the Lord’s Table. He does not come in a light or careless way. His manner, gestures, and bearing say only one thing: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”

8. Add to this the regular practice of family prayer by those who are heads of families. Add also setting aside times to pray to God in private, and behaving seriously every day. Anyone who consistently practises this outward religion has the form of godliness.
Only one more thing is needed for him to be almost a Christian. That is sincerity.
(III.) 9. By sincerity I mean a real, inner principle of religion, from which these outward actions come.
In fact, if we do not have this, we do not even have heathen honesty. We do not have enough of it to meet the demands of a heathen Epicurean poet.
Even this poor wretch, in his sober moments, could say:

blocks.x:
Oderunt peccare boni, virtutis amore;
Oderunt peccare mali, formidine poenae.

[Good men avoid sin because they love virtue;
Wicked men avoid sin because they fear punishment.]

s: So suppose a man keeps from doing evil only to avoid punishment. The pagan says to him, Non pasces in cruce corvos [You will not be hanged]. And there “you have your reward.”
But even the pagan will not allow such a harmless man to be called so much as a good heathen.

Suppose someone acts from the same motive—to avoid punishment, or to avoid losing his friends, his income, or his reputation. Suppose he not only keeps from doing evil, but also does a great deal of good, and even uses all the means of grace. Still, we could not rightly say that this person is even almost a Christian.
If he has no better principle in his heart, he is simply altogether a hypocrite.
10. So sincerity is necessarily included in being almost a Christian. Sincerity means a real purpose to serve God and a heartfelt desire to do his will.
It means that a person sincerely aims to please God in everything—in all his conduct, in all his actions, in all he does or leaves undone.
If anyone is almost a Christian, this purpose runs through his whole life.
It is what moves him when he does good, when he keeps away from evil, and when he uses the ordinances of God.
11. But someone will probably ask, “Is it possible for anyone to go this far and still be only almost a Christian?”
What more than this could being altogether a Christian include?
My first answer is this: it is possible to go this far and still be only almost a Christian. I know this not only from God’s own words, but also from the sure evidence of experience.
12. Brothers, “I am speaking to you with great boldness” about this.
“Forgive me this wrong” if I shout my own foolishness from the housetop for your sake and for the gospel’s sake. Let me speak freely about myself, as if I were speaking about someone else.
I am willing to be humbled so that you may be lifted up. I am willing to be thought even less of, for the glory of my Lord.

13. I did go this far for many years, as many people here can testify. I worked hard to avoid all evil and to keep a clear conscience. I made the most of my time. I took every opportunity to do all the good I could to everyone. I regularly and carefully used all the public and private means of grace. I tried to behave with steady seriousness at all times and in all places. And God is my witness, before whom I stand, that I did all this sincerely. I had a real purpose to serve God, and a heartfelt desire to do his will in everything. I wanted to please him who had called me to “fight the good fight” and to “take hold of eternal life.”
Yet my own conscience, in the Holy Spirit, tells me that all this time I was only almost a Christian.
II. Someone may ask, “What more than this does being altogether a Christian include?” I answer:
(I.) 1. First, the love of God.
For this is what his word says: “You must love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, all your mind, and all your strength.”

This kind of love fills the whole heart. It takes up all the feelings. It fills the soul completely and uses all its powers to the full. When someone loves the Lord his God like this, his spirit continually “rejoices in God his Saviour.” His delight is in the Lord, his Lord and his All. To him “he gives thanks in everything.
All his desire is for God and for the remembrance of his name.” His heart is always crying out, “Whom do I have in heaven but You? And there is no one on earth I desire besides You.”
In fact, what could he desire besides God?

Not the world or the things of the world. For he is “crucified to the world, and the world is crucified to him.” He is crucified to “the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life.”
Yes, he is dead to every kind of pride. For “love is not proud.” And the person who “lives in love lives in God, and God in him.” Such a person is less than nothing in his own eyes.
(II.) 2. The second thing included in being altogether a Christian is love for our neighbour.

For our Lord said in the words that follow, “You must love your neighbour as yourself.” If anyone asks, “Who is my neighbour?” we answer: every person in the world, every child of him who is the Father of the spirits of all people.
We may not leave out our enemies in any way, nor the enemies of God and of their own souls.
Every Christian loves these people too, as he loves himself—yes, “as Christ loved us.” If anyone wants to understand more fully what kind of love this is, he can look at St. Paul’s description of it.
It is “patient and kind.”
It “does not envy.” It is not rash or quick to judge.
It “is not proud.” Instead, it makes the one who loves become the least, the servant of all.
Love “does not behave improperly,” but becomes “all things to all people.”
She “does not seek her own interests,” but only the good of others, so that they may be saved.
“Love is not provoked.”
It drives out anger. Whoever has anger is lacking in love.
“It thinks no evil.
It does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices in the truth.
It covers all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.”

(III.) 3. There is one more thing included in being altogether a Christian. It can be considered on its own, though in reality it cannot be separated from what came before. It is the foundation of everything: faith.
Throughout God’s word, very excellent things are said about faith.
“Everyone who believes,” says the beloved disciple, “is born of God.”
“To all who received him, he gave power to become sons of God—to those who believe in his name.”
And “this is the victory that overcomes the world: our faith.”
Yes, our Lord himself declares, “Whoever believes in the Son has everlasting life. He does not come into condemnation, but has passed from death to life.”
4. But here no one should deceive his own soul.
“We must carefully note this: the faith that does not produce repentance, love, and all good works is not the right, living faith. It is a dead faith, the faith of devils.

For even the devils believe that Christ was born of a virgin. They believe that he did all kinds of miracles, showing that he was truly God. They believe that for our sake he suffered a most painful death, to rescue us from everlasting death. They believe that he rose again on the third day, that he went up into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, and that at the end of the world he will come again to judge both the living and the dead.
The devils believe these articles of our faith. They also believe everything written in the Old and New Testaments.
And yet, for all this faith, they are still only devils.
They still remain in their damned condition, because they lack the true Christian faith.”
[Homily on the Salvation of Man.]

5. To continue in the words of our own Church: “The right and true Christian faith is not only to believe that Holy Scripture and the Articles of our Faith are true. It is also to have a sure trust and confidence that we will be saved from everlasting damnation by Christ.

It is a sure trust and confidence that a person has in God, that through the merits of Christ his sins are forgiven, and he is brought back into God’s favour. From this comes a loving heart that obeys his commandments.”

6. Now think of this faith. It “purifies the heart” (by the power of God, who lives in it) from “pride, anger, and desire, from all unrighteousness,” from “all filthiness of flesh and spirit.” It fills the heart with love stronger than death, both for God and for all people. This love does the works of God. It delights to spend and be spent for everyone. It joyfully endures not only the disgrace of Christ—being mocked, despised, and hated by everyone—but whatever the wisdom of God allows the malice of men or devils to inflict. Whoever has this faith, working in this way through love, is not only almost a Christian, but altogether a Christian.
7. But who are the living witnesses of these things?
Brothers, I beg you, as in the presence of the God before whom “hell and destruction lie uncovered—how much more the hearts of human beings!”—let each of you ask his own heart, “Am I one of them?
Do I practise justice, mercy, and truth, at least as far as the rules of heathen honesty require?
If so, do I have even the outward look of a Christian—the form of godliness?
Do I keep away from evil—from everything that the written Word of God forbids?
Whatever good my hand finds to do, do I do it with all my might?
Do I seriously use all the ordinances of God at every opportunity?
And do I do all this with a sincere purpose and desire to please God in everything?”

8. Aren’t many of you aware that you have never come this far? You have not even been almost a Christian. You have not reached the standard of heathen honesty, or at least not the form of Christian godliness. Much less has God seen sincerity in you, a real purpose to please him in everything.
You never even intended to dedicate all your words and actions, your business, studies, and pastimes, to his glory.
You never even planned or wanted everything you did to be done “in the name of the Lord Jesus,” and so to be “a spiritual sacrifice, acceptable to God through Christ.”
9. But suppose you had. Do good plans and good desires make someone a Christian?
Not at all, unless they are carried out.
“Hell is paved,” someone has said, “with good intentions.”
So the greatest question of all still remains.
Has the love of God been poured out in your heart?
Can you cry out, “My God, and my All”?
Do you want nothing but him?
Are you happy in God?
Is he your glory, your delight, your crown of joy?
And is this command written in your heart: “Whoever loves God must love his brother also”?
Then do you love your neighbour as yourself?
Do you love every person—even your enemies, even the enemies of God—as your own soul? Do you love them as Christ loved you?
Yes, do you believe that Christ loved you and gave himself for you?
Do you have faith in his blood?

Do you believe that the Lamb of God has taken away your sins and thrown them like a stone into the depths of the sea? Do you believe that he has wiped out the written record that was against you, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross?
Do you really have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of your sins?
And does his Spirit testify with your spirit that you are a child of God?

10. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is standing among us right now. He knows that if anyone dies without this faith and this love, it would have been better for him never to have been born.
So wake up, you who are sleeping, and call on your God. Call on him while he may be found.

Do not let him rest until he makes his “goodness pass before you,” until he proclaims to you the name of the Lord: “The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient, and full of goodness and truth. He keeps mercy for thousands, and he forgives wrongdoing, rebellion, and sin.”
Do not let anyone use empty words to persuade you to stop short of this prize of your high calling.
But cry out day and night to him who, “while we were without strength, died for the ungodly.” Keep crying until you know whom you have believed, and can say, “My Lord and my God!”
Remember “always to pray and not to give up.” Keep on until you too can lift your hand to heaven and say to him who lives forever and ever, “Lord, You know everything. You know that I love You.”

11. May we all experience in this way what it is to be not only almost, but altogether Christians! May we be justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus. May we know that we have peace with God through Jesus Christ. May we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. And may we have the love of God poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us!
“Suppose someone does not work, but believes in the one who justifies ungodly people. That person’s faith is counted as righteousness.” Romans 4:5.
1. How can a sinner be justified before God, the Lord and Judge of all? For every human being, this is a question of great importance.
It holds the foundation of all our hope. For as long as we are enemies of God, we can have no true peace and no lasting joy, either in this life or in eternity.
What peace can we have while our own heart condemns us? And even more, while he who is “greater than our heart and knows everything” condemns us?
What lasting joy can we have, in this world or in the world to come, while “God’s anger remains on us”?
2. And yet people have understood this important question so poorly!
Many have had such confused ideas about it!

In fact, these ideas have been not only confused but often completely false. They are as opposite to the truth as light is to darkness. They do not fit at all with God’s own words or with the whole pattern of the faith.

So they went wrong about the very foundation, and they could not build on it. At least, they could not build with “gold, silver, or precious stones,” which would last when tested by fire. They could only build with “hay and straw,” which neither pleases God nor helps people.

3. This subject is hugely important, and I want to do it justice as far as I can. I want to save sincere seekers of the truth from “empty talk and arguments about words.” I want to clear up the confusion that so many have already been led into by these things. And I want to give them a true and right understanding of this great mystery of godliness. So I will try to show:
First, what the general basis is of this whole teaching about justification.
Second, what justification is.
Third, who the people are that are justified. And,
Fourth, on what terms they are justified.
I. First, then, I will show what the general basis is of this whole teaching about justification.
1. Man was made in the image of God. He was holy, just as his Creator is holy. He was merciful, just as the Maker of all things is merciful. He was perfect, just as his Father in heaven is perfect.
God is love. So man lived in love, and in this way he lived in God, and God lived in him.
God made him to be an “image of his own eternity,” a picture of the God of glory that could not decay.
So man was pure, just as God is pure, without any stain of sin.
He knew no evil of any kind or in any degree. Inside and outside, he was without sin and without stain.
He “loved the Lord his God with all his heart, and with all his mind, soul, and strength.”
2. Man was upright and perfect. So God gave him a perfect law, and he required full and perfect obedience to it.
God required full obedience in every point. And man had to obey without any break, from the moment he became a living soul until his time of testing was over.
No allowance was made for falling short in any way. In fact, none was needed. Man was fully able to do the task he was given, and he was completely equipped for every good word and deed.

3. The whole law of love was written in man’s heart. (Perhaps he could not sin against it directly.) But in his sovereign wisdom, God chose to add one specific command to it: “You must not eat the fruit of the tree that grows in the middle of the garden.” And God attached a penalty to it: “On the day you eat from it, you will surely die.”
4. So this was man’s condition in Paradise.
Through God’s free love, which man had not earned, he was holy and happy. He knew God, loved God, and enjoyed God. And that, in essence, is eternal life.
He would continue in this life of love forever, as long as he kept obeying God in everything. But if he disobeyed God in anything, he would lose it all.
God said, “On that day you will surely die.”
5. Man did disobey God.
He “ate from the tree that God had commanded him about, saying, You must not eat from it.”
And on that day God’s righteous judgment condemned him.
Then the sentence he had been warned about also began to take effect in him.
For the moment he tasted that fruit, he died.
His soul died. It was cut off from God. And a soul cut off from God has no more life than a body cut off from its soul.
His body also became subject to decay and death. So death took hold of his body too.
He was already dead in spirit: dead to God and dead in sin. And he was rushing on toward eternal death, toward the destruction of body and soul in the fire that never goes out.
6. So “sin entered the world through one man, and death came through sin.
And so death spread to all people,” because we were all contained in him. He was the common father and representative of us all.

So “through the offense of one man,” all are dead. They are dead to God and dead in sin. They live in a body that decays and dies and will soon fall apart. And they are under the sentence of eternal death.
For “by one man’s disobedience” all “were made sinners.” In the same way, through that one man’s offense, “judgment came on all people and condemned them.”
(Romans 5:12)
7. All of humanity was in this state when “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that we would not perish but have eternal life.”
At the right time, he became a man. He became another common head of humanity, a second parent and representative of the whole human race.
And in that role “he carried our sorrows,” as “the Lord laid on him the sins of us all.”
Then he was “wounded for our wrongdoing and bruised for our sins.”

“He made his soul an offering for sin.” He poured out his blood for those who broke God’s law. He “carried our sins in his own body on the cross,” so that by his wounds we might be healed. And by that one offering of himself, made once, he has redeemed me and all people. By doing this he “made a full, perfect, and sufficient sacrifice and payment for the sins of the whole world.”
8. The Son of God has “tasted death for everyone.” Because of this, God has now “brought the world back to himself, not counting their” past “sins against them.”
And so, “just as one man’s offense brought judgment and condemnation on all people, so one man’s righteousness brought the free gift to all people, so that they can be justified.”

So now, for the sake of his dearly loved Son and what he has done and suffered for us, God graciously offers to cancel the punishment our sins deserve. He offers to bring us back into his favor. And he offers to bring our dead souls back to spiritual life, as a down payment on eternal life. He does this on only one condition, and he himself also makes us able to meet it.
9. So this is the general basis of the whole teaching about justification.

Adam was not only the father of us all but also our representative. Through the sin of this first Adam, we all lost God’s favor. We all became children of wrath. Or, as the apostle puts it, “judgment came on all people and condemned them.”

In the same way, the Second Adam, as the representative of us all, made a sacrifice for sin. Because of it, God is reconciled to the whole world so far that he has given them a new covenant. Its condition is simple. Once it is met, “there is no more condemnation” for us. Instead, “we are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ.”
II. 1. But what does it mean to be “justified”?
What is “justification”? This was the second thing I planned to show.
From what we have already seen, it is clear that it does not mean actually being made just and righteous.
That is “sanctification.” In some degree, sanctification is the direct fruit of justification. But it is still a separate gift of God, and it is completely different in nature.
Justification is what God does for us through his Son. Sanctification is what he works in us by his Spirit.

In a few rare cases, the word “justified” or “justification” is used in such a broad sense that it includes “sanctification” too. But in general use, St. Paul and the other inspired writers keep the two clearly apart.
2. Some have a far-fetched idea that justification means clearing us from accusation, especially the accusation of Satan. But this is not easy to prove from any clear text of Holy Scripture.
In the whole account that Scripture gives of this matter, as I described it above, neither that accuser nor his accusation seems to play any part at all.
Of course, no one can deny that he is the “accuser” of human beings. That is the very name given to him.
But there is no sign at all that the great apostle refers to this in any way in everything he wrote about justification, either to the Romans or to the Galatians.

3. Some also claim that justification means clearing us from the accusation the law brings against us. This is much easier to assume than to prove from any clear statement of Scripture. At least, that is so if this forced, unnatural way of speaking means anything more or less than the following. We have broken God’s law and so deserve to be damned in hell. But God does not give those who are justified the punishment they deserved.

4. Least of all does justification mean that God is fooled about the people he justifies. It does not mean that he thinks they are something they really are not, or that he regards them as different from what they are.

It certainly does not mean that God judges us in a way that goes against the real facts. He does not think we are better than we really are. He does not believe we are righteous when we are unrighteous.
Surely not! The judgment of the all-wise God always agrees with the truth.
And his perfect wisdom could never think that I am innocent, or judge that I am righteous or holy, just because someone else is.
He can no more mix me up with Christ in this way than he could mix me up with David or Abraham.
Let anyone to whom God has given understanding weigh this without bias. He will surely see that this idea of justification fits neither with reason nor with Scripture.
5. The plain meaning of justification in Scripture is pardon, the forgiveness of sins.
It is the act of God the Father by which he “shows his righteousness (or mercy) by forgiving the sins of the past.” He does this for the sake of the atoning sacrifice made by the blood of his Son.
This is the simple, natural explanation St. Paul gives of it throughout this whole letter.
He explains it this way himself, especially in this chapter and the next.
So, two verses after our text, he says, “Blessed are those whose wrongs are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will not count against him.”
For the person who is justified or forgiven, God “will not count sin” against him to condemn him.
God will not condemn him for it, either in this world or in the world to come.
His sins, all his past sins in thought, word, and deed, are covered and wiped out. They will not be remembered or mentioned against him, just as if they had never been.
God will not make that sinner suffer what he deserved, because God’s beloved Son has suffered for him.
From the moment we are “accepted through the Beloved” and “reconciled to God through his blood,” God loves us, blesses us, and watches over us for our good, just as if we had never sinned.
It is true that in one place the apostle seems to stretch the meaning of the word much further. He says, “It is not those who hear the law, but those who do the law, who will be justified.”
Here he seems to connect our justification with the verdict of the great day.

Our Lord himself certainly does this when he says, “By your words you will be justified.” He shows by this that “people will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they speak.”
But perhaps we can hardly find another example of St. Paul using the word in that distant sense.

In his writings in general, he clearly does not. And least of all does he do so in the text we are looking at. It clearly speaks not of those who have already “finished their course,” but of those who are only now “setting out,” who are just beginning to “run the race set before them.”
III. 1. This brings us to the third thing we were to consider: Who are the people that are justified?
The apostle tells us plainly: the ungodly. “He (that is, God) justifies the ungodly.” He justifies ungodly people of every kind and degree, and no one but the ungodly.
“Those who are righteous need no repentance.” In the same way, they need no forgiveness.
Only sinners have any need of pardon. Only sin can be forgiven.
So forgiveness has to do directly with sin, and in this respect with nothing else.
It is our “unrighteousness” that the forgiving God is “merciful” to. It is our “wrongdoing” that he “remembers no more.”

2. Some people argue very strongly that a person must be sanctified, that is, holy, before he can be justified. Some of them even claim that complete holiness or obedience must come before justification. They do not seem to have considered this at all.
(Unless they mean justification at the last day, which is a completely different question.)

Far from it! The very idea is not only flatly impossible, but also grossly and deeply absurd, because it contradicts itself. (It is impossible because where there is no love for God, there is no holiness. And there is no love for God except from knowing that he loves us.)
For it is not a saint who is forgiven, but a sinner, and he is forgiven as a sinner.
God does not justify the godly but the ungodly. He does not justify those who are already holy, but those who are unholy.
We will soon look at the condition on which he does this. But whatever it is, it cannot be holiness.
To claim that it is holiness would be to say that the Lamb of God takes away only the sins that were already taken away.
3. Does the good Shepherd, then, search for and save only those who have already been found?
No! He searches for and saves what is lost.
He forgives those who need his forgiving mercy.

He saves sinners of every kind and every degree from the guilt of sin (and at the same time from its power). Until then, these people were completely ungodly. The Father’s love was not in them. So nothing good lived in them, no good or truly Christian attitude. Instead, all their attitudes were evil and hateful: pride, anger, love of the world. These are the true fruits of the “fleshly mind,” which is “at war with God.”
4. It is the sick who need a Doctor: those who find the burden of their sins unbearable. It is the guilty who need a pardon: those who groan under God’s anger.

Some people are “condemned already” for all their ungodliness in thought, word, and deed. They are condemned not only by God but also by their own conscience, which is like a thousand witnesses. These people cry out loudly for him who “justifies the ungodly” through the redemption that is in Jesus. He justifies the ungodly, and “the one who does not work.” Before he is justified, such a person does nothing good, nothing truly virtuous or holy. He only does evil all the time.
For his heart is necessarily and essentially evil until the love of God is poured into it.
And while the tree is rotten, so is its fruit. For “a bad tree cannot produce good fruit.”

5. Someone may object: “But a person who is not yet justified can feed the hungry or clothe the naked. And these are good works.” The answer is easy. Yes, he can do these things even before he is justified. And in one sense these are “good works.” They are “good and helpful to people.”
But that does not mean that, strictly speaking, they are good in themselves, or good in God’s eyes.
All truly “good works” (to use the words of our Church) “come after justification.” And they are good and “pleasing to God in Christ” for this reason: they “grow out of a true and living faith.”

By the same reasoning, all “works done before justification are not good” in the Christian sense, “because they do not grow out of faith in Jesus Christ.” (They may grow out of some kind of faith in God.) “In fact, because they are not done as God has willed and commanded them to be done, we have no doubt” (however strange this may seem to some) “that they have the nature of sin.”
6. Perhaps those who doubt this have not thought carefully enough about the weighty reason given here. It explains why no works done before justification can be truly and properly good.
The argument clearly goes like this:
No works are good unless they are done as God has willed and commanded them to be done.
But no works done before justification are done as God has willed and commanded them to be done.
So no works done before justification are good.

The first statement is obvious. The second is that no works done before justification are done as God has willed and commanded them to be done. This will seem just as plain and undeniable if we simply consider this: God has willed and commanded that “all our works” should “be done in charity” (en agape), that is, in love. That means in the love for God that produces love for all people.

But none of our works can be done in this love while the love of the Father (of God as our Father) is not in us. And this love cannot be in us until we receive the Spirit of adoption, who cries out in our hearts, Abba, Father.
So if God does not justify the ungodly, and the one who (in this sense) does not work, then Christ died for nothing. Then, in spite of his death, no living person could be justified.
IV. 1. On what terms, then, is a person justified who is completely “ungodly” and who until then “does not work”? On one term only, and that is faith. He “believes in him who justifies the ungodly.”
And “whoever believes is not condemned.” In fact, he “has passed from death to life.”

“For the righteousness (or mercy) of God comes by faith in Jesus Christ to all and upon all who believe. God set him forth as a sacrifice of atonement, through faith in his blood, so that he might be just and” (in keeping with his justice) “the one who justifies the person who believes in Jesus.” “So we conclude that a person is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.” That is, without first obeying the moral law, which in fact he could not do until now.
The words that follow clearly show that the moral law, and only the moral law, is meant here: “Do we then cancel the law through faith?
Of course not! In fact, we establish the law.
What law do we establish by faith?
Not the ritual law, not the ceremonial law of Moses.
Not at all. We establish the great, unchanging law of love: holy love for God and for our neighbor.”

2. Faith in general is a divine, supernatural “elegchos”: an “evidence” or “conviction” “of things not seen.” These are things our bodily senses cannot detect, because they are past, future, or spiritual.

Justifying faith includes a divine evidence or conviction that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” But it also includes a sure trust and confidence that Christ died for “my” sins, that he loved “me” and gave himself for “me.”

Whenever a sinner believes like this, whether as a young child, in the prime of life, or when old and gray, God justifies that ungodly person. For the sake of his Son, God pardons him and sets him free, though until then there was nothing good in him.
It is true that God had given him repentance before this. But that repentance was nothing more or less than a deep awareness that he lacked every good thing and that every evil was present in him.
And whatever good he has or does from the hour he first believes in God through Christ, faith does not “find” it there but “brings” it.
This is the fruit of faith.
First the tree is good, and then the fruit is good too.

3. I cannot describe the nature of this faith better than in the words of our own Church: “The only means of salvation” (and justification is one part of salvation) “is faith. That is, it is a sure trust and confidence that God has forgiven our sins and will forgive them, and that he has accepted us back into his favor, because of the merits of Christ’s death and suffering. But here we must be careful not to falter with God through a faith that is unsteady and wavering. Peter came to Christ on the water, but because his faith grew weak, he was in danger of drowning. In the same way, if we begin to waver or doubt, we must fear that we will sink as Peter did, not into the water, but into the bottomless pit of hell fire.” (“Second Sermon on the Passion”)

“So have a sure and steady faith, not only that the death of Christ is effective for the whole world, but that he has made a full and sufficient sacrifice for “you,” a perfect cleansing of “your” sins. Then you can say with the apostle that he loved “you” and gave himself for “you.”
For this is how you make Christ “your own” and apply his merits to “yourself.” (“Sermon on the Sacrament, First Part”)
4. I say that this faith is the term or “condition of justification.” By this I mean, first, that there is no justification without it.
“Whoever does not believe is condemned already.” As long as he does not believe, that condemnation cannot be taken away. Instead, “God’s anger remains on him.”

“There is no other name given under heaven” than the name of Jesus of Nazareth. There is no other merit by which a condemned sinner can ever be saved from the guilt of sin. In the same way, there is no other way to receive a share in his merit than “by faith in his name.”
So as long as we are without this faith, we are “strangers to the covenant of promise.” We are “outsiders to the community of Israel, and without God in the world.”

A person may have all kinds of so-called virtues. (I am speaking of those to whom the gospel is preached. For “what business is it of mine to judge those outside?”) He may do all kinds of works that are considered good. But it does him no good. He is still a “child of wrath” and still under the curse, until he believes in Jesus.
5. So faith is the “necessary” condition of justification. In fact, it is the “only necessary” condition.

This is the second point we must carefully note. The very moment God gives faith (for “it is the gift of God”) to the “ungodly” person who “does not work,” that “faith is counted to him as righteousness.”
Before this he has no righteousness at all. He does not even have negative righteousness, that is, innocence.
But “faith is credited to him as righteousness” the very moment he believes.
This does not mean (as I said before) that God thinks he is something he is not.

But “God made Christ to be sin for us.” That is, he treated him as a sinner and punished him for our sins. In the same way, God counts us righteous from the time we believe in him. That is, he does not punish us for our sins. In fact, he treats us as though we were innocent and righteous.
6. Some find it hard to agree that “faith is the only condition of justification.” Surely that difficulty must come from not understanding it.
What we mean is this: it is the only thing without which no one is justified. It is the only thing that is directly, absolutely required for pardon, the one thing that cannot be done without.

On the one hand, a person might have everything else, but without faith he cannot be justified. On the other hand, a person might lack everything else, but if he has faith, he cannot fail to be justified.

For imagine a sinner of any kind or degree. He fully knows how completely ungodly he is. He knows he is totally unable to think, speak, or do good, and that he fully deserves hell-fire. Now imagine that this sinner, helpless and hopeless, throws himself completely on God’s mercy in Christ (which in fact he can only do by the grace of God). Who can doubt that he is forgiven in that moment?
Who will claim that anything more is “absolutely required” before that sinner can be justified?

Now, suppose there has been even one such case since the beginning of the world. (And have there not been, and are there not still, ten thousand times ten thousand?) Then it clearly follows that faith, in the sense given above, is the only condition of justification.

7. We are poor, guilty, sinful worms. We receive every blessing we enjoy by grace, as pure favor, not because it is owed to us. This is true from the smallest drop of water that cools our tongue to the immense riches of glory in eternity. So it is not fitting for us to ask God the reasons for what he does.
It is not right for us to question him “who gives no account of any of his ways.” It is not right to demand, “Why did you make faith the condition, the only condition, of justification?
Why did you decide that ‘whoever believes,’ and only he, ‘will be saved’?”

This is the very point St. Paul insists on so strongly in the ninth chapter of this letter. The terms of pardon and acceptance must depend not on us but “on him who calls us.” There is no “unrighteousness with God” when he sets his own terms, not according to ours but according to his own good pleasure. He may rightly say, “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy,” that is, on the one who believes in Jesus.

“So then it does not depend on the one who wills, or on the one who runs,” to choose the condition on which he will be accepted, “but on God who shows mercy.” God accepts no one at all except out of his own free love, his undeserved goodness.

“So he has mercy on whom he wants to have mercy,” that is, on those who believe in the Son he loves. “And whom he wants,” that is, those who do not believe, “he hardens.” In the end he leaves them to the hardness of their hearts.
8. Still, we may humbly suggest one reason why God set this condition of justification: “If you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, you will be saved.” It was to “keep pride away from man.”
Pride had already destroyed even angels of God. It had thrown down “a third of the stars of heaven.”
Pride was also largely the reason Adam fell from his firm position and brought sin and death into the world. This happened when the tempter said, “You will be like gods.”
So it was an act of wisdom worthy of God to set a condition of reconciliation for Adam and all his descendants that would truly humble them and bring them down to the dust.
And faith is such a condition.

It is especially suited for this purpose. For whoever comes to God by this faith must fix his eyes only on his own wickedness, his guilt, and his helplessness. He must not pay the least attention to any good he supposes is in himself, to any virtue or righteousness of any kind.
He must come as a “mere sinner,” inside and out, ruined and condemned by himself. He brings nothing to God but ungodliness. He pleads nothing of his own but sin and misery.
Only in this way, when his “mouth is shut” and he stands completely “guilty before” God, can he “look to Jesus” as the whole and only “atoning sacrifice for his sins.”
Only in this way can he be “found in him” and receive the “righteousness that comes from God by faith.”
9. You ungodly one, who hear or read these words! You vile, helpless, miserable sinner!
Before God, the Judge of all, I solemnly charge you: go straight to him, with all your ungodliness.
Be careful not to destroy your own soul by pleading your own righteousness, whether much or little.
Go as someone completely ungodly, guilty, lost, and ruined, deserving hell and falling into it. Then you will find favor in his sight, and you will know that he justifies the ungodly.
As such a person you will be brought to the “sprinkled blood,” as a ruined, helpless, damned sinner.
So “look to Jesus!”
There is “the Lamb of God,” who “takes away your sins!”
Do not plead any works, any righteousness of your own! Do not plead humility, sorrow for sin, or sincerity!
Not at all. That would truly be denying the Lord who bought you.
No! Plead only the blood of the covenant, the ransom paid for your proud, stubborn, sinful soul.
Who are you, who now see and feel your ungodliness, both inside and out?
You are the man!
I want you for my Lord!
I claim “you” as a child of God by faith!
The Lord needs you.
You who feel that you are just fit for hell are just fit to advance his glory: the glory of his free grace, which justifies the ungodly and the one who does not work.
Oh, come quickly! Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you, yes you, are reconciled to God.
“Be careful not to do your good deeds for the poor in front of people just so they will see you. If you do, you will get no reward from your Father in heaven.
So when you give to the poor, don’t blow a trumpet to announce it, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets. They do it so that people will praise them.
I tell you the truth, they already have their reward.

But when you give to the poor, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand is doing. Then your giving will be in secret. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will himself reward you openly.
And when you pray, don’t be like the hypocrites. They love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners, so that people will see them.
I tell you the truth, they already have their reward.
But when you pray, go into your own room and shut the door. Pray to your Father, who is in secret. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you openly.
And when you pray, don’t keep repeating empty words, as the pagans do. They think they will be heard because they talk so much.
So don’t be like them. Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
This, then, is how you should pray: Our Father in heaven, may your name be honoured as holy.
Let your kingdom come. Let what you want be done on earth, just as it is done in heaven.
Give us today our bread for this day.
And forgive us our debts, just as we forgive those who owe us.
And don’t lead us into temptation, but rescue us from evil. For the kingdom, the power and the glory belong to you forever.

Amen. If you forgive people when they wrong you, your Father in heaven will forgive you too. But if you don’t forgive people when they wrong you, your Father won’t forgive the wrongs you do.” Matthew 6:1–15.
1. In the chapter before this, our Lord described the religion of the heart, in all its different parts.

He showed us the attitudes of the soul that make someone a real Christian. These are the inner qualities that make up the “holiness without which no one will see the Lord.” They are feelings and desires that come from the right source—a living faith in God through Christ Jesus. When they come from there, they are good in themselves, deep down, and God is pleased with them.

In this chapter he goes on to show how all our actions can also be made holy and good and pleasing to God. This is true even of actions that are neither good nor bad in themselves. What makes them holy is a pure and holy purpose.
He explains at length that anything done without this purpose is worth nothing to God.
But any outward work that is given to God in this way is very precious in his eyes.
2. He shows why this pure purpose is needed. First, he looks at the actions people usually call religious. And they really are religious when they are done with the right purpose.
Some of these are usually called works of devotion to God. The rest are called works of kindness or mercy.
Of the works of kindness, he names giving to the poor in particular. Of the works of devotion, he names prayer and fasting.
But the instructions he gives for these apply just as much to every work of kindness or mercy.
I. 1. First, let’s look at works of mercy.
He says, “Be careful not to do your good deeds for the poor in front of people just so they will see you. If you do, you will get no reward from your Father in heaven.”

“Not to do your good deeds for the poor”: only this one kind of good deed is named, but every act of kindness is included. That means everything we give, or say, or do, that helps our neighbour. It means anything by which another person may be helped in any way, in body or in soul.

It includes feeding the hungry and clothing those who have nothing to wear. It includes welcoming or helping strangers and visiting people who are sick or in prison. It includes comforting those who are suffering, teaching those who don’t know, warning those who do wrong, and cheering on and encouraging those who do right. And if there is any other work of mercy, this instruction covers it just the same.

2. “Be careful not to do your good deeds for the poor in front of people just so they will see you.” What is forbidden here is not simply doing good where people can see it. The fact that others see what we do does not make the action any worse or any better. What is forbidden is doing it in front of people “so they will see you”—when that is the aim, and the only aim.
I say the only aim, because in some cases this may be part of our aim. We may want some of our actions to be seen, and God may still be pleased with them.

We may want our light to shine in front of people. That is fine when our conscience, through the Holy Spirit, tells us that our final goal in wanting them to see our good works is “that they may give glory to our Father in heaven.”
But be careful not to do even the smallest thing to get glory for yourself. Be careful that wanting people’s praise has no place at all in your works of mercy.

If you are after your own glory, if you are trying in any way to win honour from people, then whatever you do with that aim is worth nothing. It is not done for the Lord. He does not accept it. For this “you get no reward from our Father in heaven.”

3. “So when you give to the poor, don’t blow a trumpet to announce it, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that people will praise them.” Here the word synagogue does not mean a place of worship. It means any public place where people gather, such as the market square or the place where merchants meet to trade.
Among the Jews, rich men often did this, especially the Pharisees. When they were about to give a large gift to the poor, they had a trumpet blown in front of them in the busiest parts of the city.
They said it was to call the poor together to receive the gift. But the real reason was so that people would praise them.
But don’t be like them.
Don’t have a trumpet blown in front of you.
Don’t show off when you do good.
Aim only for the honour that comes from God.
Those who look for people’s praise already have their reward. They will get no praise from God.

4. “But when you give to the poor, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” This is a common saying, and it means: do it as secretly as you can. Keep it as secret as you can while still doing it at all—for you must not leave it undone. Don’t miss any chance to do good, whether in secret or in the open. And keep it as secret as you can while still doing it in the most helpful way.

Here too there is an exception. Suppose you are fully convinced in your own mind that if you don’t hide the good you do, it will help you do more good, or it will stir others to do more good. Then you should not hide it. Then let your light be seen, and let it “shine on everyone in the house.”

But unless God’s glory and the good of people require something else, act as privately and quietly as the thing allows. Do this “so that your giving will be in secret. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you openly.” Perhaps he will do it in this present world—there are many examples of this written down from every age. But he will certainly do it in the world to come, before the great gathering of all people and angels.
II. 1. From works of kindness or mercy our Lord moves on to what are called works of devotion to God.
He says, “And when you pray, don’t be like the hypocrites. They love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners, so that people will see them.” “Don’t be like the hypocrites.”
So hypocrisy, or being fake, is the first thing we must guard against when we pray.
Be careful not to say what you don’t mean.
Prayer is lifting up the heart to God. Without this, all the words of a prayer are nothing but pretending.

So whenever you try to pray, make sure your one aim is to talk with God, to lift up your heart to him, to pour out your soul to him. Don’t be like the hypocrites. They love to, or they are used to, “stand and pray in the synagogues”—the trading places or market squares—“and on the street corners,” wherever the most people are, “so that people will see them.” That was the only aim, the only reason and goal, of the prayers they said there.
“I tell you the truth, they already have their reward.” They should not expect any reward from your Father in heaven.

2. But wanting people’s praise is not the only thing that cuts us off from any reward in heaven. It is not the only thing that leaves us no reason to expect God’s blessing on our works, whether works of devotion or of mercy.
A pure purpose is ruined just as much by aiming at any earthly reward at all.
We may say our prayers, go to church to worship God, or help the poor. But if we do it to gain money or some advantage, God is not one bit more pleased with it than if we did it to be praised.

Any earthly aim makes every action disgusting to the Lord, however good it may look to people. That includes any reason at all on this side of eternity—any aim except bringing glory to God and happiness to people for God’s sake.

3. “But when you pray, go into your own room and shut the door. Pray to your Father, who is in secret.” There is a time when you should give glory to God in public, praying to him and praising him in the large gathering of his people.
But sometimes you want to tell God your requests more fully and in more detail. It may be in the evening, or in the morning, or at noon. Then “go into your own room and shut the door.”
Be as private as you can.
(Only don’t skip prayer, whether you have a room and some privacy or not. If you can, pray to God where no one sees you but him. But if you can’t, pray to God anyway.)
In this way “pray to your Father, who is in secret.” Pour out your heart to him. “And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you openly.”
4. “And when you pray,” even in secret, “don’t keep repeating empty words, as the pagans do”—mē battalogēsēte.
Don’t use lots of words that mean nothing.
Don’t say the same thing over and over again. Don’t think your prayers will work better because they are long, as the pagans do. They think they will be heard because they talk so much.

What is corrected here is not simply long prayers, any more than short ones. First, it is length without meaning—saying a lot and meaning little or nothing. It is using empty repetitions. (Not all repetitions are wrong. Our Lord himself prayed three times, repeating the same words.) It means empty repetitions like those of the pagans, who recited the names of their gods over and over. People do the same among those who are called Christians—and not only among the Roman Catholics. They say the same string of prayers over and over without ever feeling what they are saying. Second, it is the idea that we will be heard because we say a lot. It is imagining that God measures prayers by how long they are, and that he likes best the ones with the most words, which sound longest in his ears.
These are examples of superstition and foolishness. Everyone who is called by the name of Christ should leave them to the pagans—to those on whom the glorious light of the gospel has never shone.
5. So don’t be like them. You have tasted God’s grace in Christ Jesus. You are fully convinced that your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

So the point of praying is not to tell God something, as if he didn’t already know what you need. It is more to remind yourselves. It fixes the feeling of those needs more deeply in your hearts. It also fixes the sense that you always depend on him, the only one who can supply everything you need.

Prayer is not so much to move God. He is always more ready to give than you are to ask. It is more to move you, so that you will be willing and ready to receive the good things he has prepared for you.

III. 1. Our Lord has taught what prayer really is and what it is for. Next he adds an example of it: that divine prayer which here seems mainly to be given as a pattern—the model and standard for all our prayers. “This, then, is how you should pray.”
But in another place he tells us to use these very words: “He said to them, When you pray, say...” (Luke 11:2.)
2. Speaking generally about this divine prayer, we can notice several things. First, it contains everything we can sensibly or rightly pray for.
There is nothing we need to ask God for, and nothing we can ask without offending him, that is not included in this prayer. It covers it all, either directly or indirectly.

Second, it contains everything we can sensibly or rightly want. It includes whatever brings glory to God, and whatever is needed or useful—not only for ourselves, but for every creature in heaven and on earth.
In fact, our prayers are the proper test of our desires. Nothing belongs in our desires that does not belong in our prayers. What we may not pray for, we should not want either.

Third, it contains all our duty to God and to people. Whatever is pure and holy, whatever God asks of human beings, whatever pleases him, whatever helps our neighbour—all of it is stated or hinted at in this prayer.
3. It has three parts: the opening, the requests, and the closing words of praise, called the doxology.
The opening, “Our Father in heaven,” lays a general foundation for prayer. It sums up what we must first know about God before we can pray, confident that he will hear us.
It also shows us all the attitudes of heart we need when we come to God. These are most necessary if we want God to accept our prayers or our lives.
4. “Our Father.” If he is a Father, then he is good. Then he loves his children.
And this is the first and greatest reason to pray.

God wants to bless us, so let’s ask for a blessing. “Our Father”—our Creator, the one who gave us our being. He raised us from the dust of the earth. He breathed the breath of life into us, and we became living souls.

And if he made us, let’s ask him. He will not hold back any good thing from what his own hands have made. “Our Father”—the one who keeps us alive. Day after day he keeps up the life he gave us. Because of his continuing love we receive life and breath and everything else, now and every moment.
So let’s come to him all the more boldly, and we will “receive mercy, and grace to help us when we need it.”

Above all, he is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of everyone who believes in him. He makes us right with himself “freely by his grace, through Jesus, who paid to set us free.” He has “wiped out all our sins, and healed all our weaknesses.” He has taken us in as his own children, by adoption and grace. And “because” we “are sons, he has sent the Spirit of his Son into” our “hearts, crying, Abba, Father.” He “has given us new birth from a seed that cannot decay,” and “created us new in Christ Jesus.”
That is why we know he always hears us. That is why we pray to him without stopping.
We pray because we love. And “we love him because he loved us first.”
5. “Our Father.” Not mine only, as I cry out to him now, but ours in the widest possible sense.
He is the God and “Father of the spirits of all people,” the Father of angels and humans. Even the pagans admitted that he was this: Pater te theōn te.
He is the Father of the whole universe, of all the families in heaven and on earth.
So he does not play favourites.
He loves everything he has made.
“He is loving to every person, and his mercy covers everything he has made.”
And the Lord delights in those who fear him and trust in his mercy. He delights in those who trust in him through the Son he loves, knowing that they are “accepted in his dearly loved Son.”

But “if God loved us so much, we should also love one another”—yes, all people. For “God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son,” even to die, so that they “would not perish but have everlasting life.”

6. “In heaven.” He is high and lifted up, God over all, blessed forever. He sits above the circle of the heavens and sees everything in heaven and on earth. His eye sees through the whole world of created things—yes, and even through the night that was never created. To him “all his works are known,” and all the works of every creature. They are known not only “from the beginning of the world”—a poor, weak translation—but ap’ aiōnos, from all eternity, from everlasting to everlasting. He makes the armies of heaven, as well as human beings, cry out in wonder and amazement: O the depth! How deep are the riches of both the wisdom and the knowledge of God!

In heaven: he is the Lord and Ruler of all, who watches over all things and arranges them. You are the King of kings and Lord of lords, the blessed and only Ruler. You are strong and wrapped in power, doing whatever you please. You are the Almighty, for whenever you want to do something, you are able to do it.
In heaven: he is there in a special way. Heaven is your throne, “the place where your glory” especially “lives.”
But you are not there only. You fill heaven and earth, the whole of space. “Heaven and earth are full of your glory.
Glory to you, O Lord Most High!”
That is why we should “serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice before him with awe.”
That is why we should think, speak, and act as if we are always under the eye of the Lord, the King, right in his presence.
7. “May your name be honoured as holy.” This is the first of the six requests that make up the prayer itself.
The name of God is God himself—God’s nature, as far as people can know it.

So it means his existence, together with all his qualities or perfections. It means his eternity. This is shown especially by his great name that belongs to no one else, JEHOVAH. The apostle John translates it as to A kai to Ō, archē kai telos, ho ōn kai ho ēn kai ho erchomenos—“the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end; the one who is, who was, and who is to come.” It means his fullness of being, shown by his other great name, I AM THAT I AM! It means that he is present everywhere. It means that he is all-powerful. He is in fact the only one who acts in the material world. All matter is dull and lifeless by nature. It moves only when the finger of God moves it. And he is the source of action in every creature, seen and unseen. Without the constant flow and working of his almighty power, no creature could act or even exist. It means his wisdom, which we clearly see from the things that are seen, from the beautiful order of the universe. It means his Trinity in Unity, and Unity in Trinity. This is shown to us in the very first line of his written word: bara Elohim, which literally means “the Gods created.” There a plural noun is joined to a singular verb. It is also shown in every later part of what he revealed through all his holy prophets and apostles. It means his perfect purity and holiness. And above all it means his love, which is the very brightness of his glory.

When we pray that God, or his name, may “be honoured as holy” or glorified, we are praying that he may be known as he really is. We pray that he may be known by all who are able to know him—by all beings who can think—and with feelings that match that knowledge. We pray that he may be properly honoured, feared, and loved by all in heaven above and on the earth below. We pray this for all angels and humans, whom he made able to know and love him forever for this very purpose.
8. “Let your kingdom come.” This is closely connected to the request before it.
We pray that his kingdom, the kingdom of Christ, may come, so that God’s name may be honoured as holy.
This kingdom comes to a person when he “turns from his sins and believes the gospel.” It comes when God teaches him to know himself, and also to know Jesus Christ and him crucified.

“This is eternal life: to know the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom he has sent.” In the same way, this is the kingdom of God begun here below, set up in the believer’s heart. “The Lord God Almighty” then “reigns,” when he is known through Christ Jesus.
He takes up his mighty power so that he can bring everything under his rule.
He keeps going in the soul, conquering and still conquering, until he has put everything under his feet. He goes on until “every thought is taken captive to obey Christ.”

One day God will “give his Son the nations as his inheritance, and the ends of the earth as his possession.” “All kingdoms will bow down before him, and all nations will serve him.” “The mountain of the Lord’s house”—the Church of Christ—“will be set up on the top of the mountains.” “The full number of the Gentiles will come in, and all Israel will be saved.” When that happens, everyone will see that “the Lord is King, and has clothed himself in glory.” He will appear to every human soul as King of kings and Lord of lords.

And it is right for all who love his appearing to pray that he will hurry that time along. They pray that his kingdom, the kingdom of grace, may come quickly and swallow up all the kingdoms of the earth. They pray that all people will receive him as their King and truly believe in his name. They pray that all will be filled with righteousness, peace, and joy, with holiness and happiness—until they are taken from here into his heavenly kingdom, to reign with him there forever and ever.

We also pray for this in the words “Let your kingdom come.” We pray for the coming of his everlasting kingdom, the kingdom of glory in heaven. That kingdom is the continuation and completion of the kingdom of grace on earth.

So this request, like the one before it, is offered for the whole creation of thinking beings. All of them have a stake in this great event: the final making new of all things. Then God will put an end to misery and sin, to weakness and death. He will take all things into his own hands and set up the kingdom that lasts through all ages.

The solemn words in the prayer at the burial of the dead match this exactly: “We ask you, if it pleases you, in your gracious goodness, soon to complete the number of your chosen ones, and to hurry the coming of your kingdom. Then we, with all those who have died in the true faith of your holy name, may have our perfect completion and joy, in both body and soul, in your everlasting glory.”

9. “Let what you want be done on earth, as it is in heaven.” This follows necessarily and immediately wherever the kingdom of God has come—wherever God lives in the soul by faith, and Christ reigns in the heart by love.

Many people, perhaps most, when they first look at these words, probably imagine they only express, or ask for, resignation. They think it is a prayer to be ready to accept God’s will, whatever it may be for us.
And this is without doubt a godly and excellent attitude, a most precious gift from God.
But this is not what we are praying for in this request—at least, not in its main and first meaning.
When we say, “Let what you want be done on earth, as it is in heaven,” we are not praying so much to accept God’s will passively. We are praying to do God’s will actively.
How do the angels of God in heaven do it—those who now circle his throne with joy?
They do it willingly. They love his commands, and they gladly listen to his words.
Doing his will is their food and drink. It is their highest glory and joy.
They do it all the time. Their willing service never stops.

They don’t rest day or night. They use every hour to carry out his commands, to accomplish his plans, and to do what he has decided. (I am speaking in human terms. Our ways of measuring time—days and nights and hours—have no place in eternity.)
And they do it perfectly.
Angels’ minds have no sin and no fault.
It is true that “the stars are not pure in his sight”—even the morning stars that sing together before him.
“In his sight” means compared with him. Compared with God, even the angels are not pure.
But this does not mean that they are not pure in themselves.
Of course they are. They are without spot and without blame.
They are completely devoted to his will, and they obey him perfectly in everything.
If we look at this from another angle, we can see that the angels of God in heaven do all of God’s will.
And they do nothing else—nothing except what they are completely sure is his will.
Also, they do all of God’s will in the way he wants it done, the way that pleases him, and no other way.
Yes, and they do it only because it is his will. That is their purpose, and they have no other reason.

10. So when we pray that God’s will may “be done on earth as it is in heaven,” this is what we mean. We pray that everyone who lives on earth, the whole human race, may do the will of their Father in heaven as willingly as the holy angels do. We pray that people may do it all the time, just as the angels do, with no break in their willing service. Yes, and we pray that they may do it perfectly—that “the God of peace, through the blood of the everlasting covenant, may make them perfect in every good work to do his will, and work in them all that pleases him.”
In other words, we pray that we and all people may do the whole will of God in everything. We pray that we may do nothing else—not the smallest thing—except what is God’s holy and pleasing will.

We pray that we may do the whole will of God in the way he wants, in the way that pleases him. And finally, we pray that we may do it because it is his will. We pray that this may be the only reason and basis, the whole and only motive, for everything we think, say, or do.
11. “Give us today our bread for this day.” In the first three requests we have been praying for all people.
Now we come more specifically to asking for what we ourselves need.
Even here, though, we are not told to keep our prayer only to ourselves. This request, and each of the ones after it, can be prayed for the whole Church of Christ on earth.

By “bread” we can understand everything we need, whether for our souls or our bodies—ta pros zōēn kai eusebeian, the things that belong to life and godliness. We don’t mean only ordinary bread, which our Lord calls the food that spoils. We mean much more the spiritual bread, the grace of God, the food that lasts to eternal life.

Many of the early church leaders believed that the bread of the Lord’s Supper is meant here too. In the beginning the whole Church of Christ received it every day. They valued it highly as the main channel through which the grace of his Spirit was brought to the souls of all God’s children—until the love of many grew cold.
“Our daily bread.” Different Bible scholars have explained the word we translate “daily” in different ways.
But its plainest and most natural meaning seems to be the one kept in almost all translations, old and new: what is enough for this day, and then for each day as it comes.
12. “Give us.” We don’t claim anything as our right. We ask only because of God’s free mercy.
We don’t deserve the air we breathe, the ground that holds us up, or the sun that shines on us.
We admit that all we deserve is hell. But God loves us freely. So we ask him to give us what we can’t get for ourselves, any more than we can earn it from him.
But God’s goodness and power are no reason for us to sit around doing nothing.

His will is that we work hard at everything and do our very best, as if our success came naturally from our own wisdom and strength. And then we are to depend on him as if we had done nothing, because he is the giver of every good and perfect gift.
“Today.” For we are not to worry about tomorrow.

This is the very reason our wise Creator divided life into these little pieces of time, so clearly separate from each other. He did it so we could see each day as a fresh gift from God, another life that we can give to his glory. And he did it so each evening could be like the end of life, with nothing beyond it for us to see but eternity.

13. “And forgive us the wrongs we have done, as we forgive those who have wronged us.” Only sin can keep God’s generous gifts from flowing out to every creature. So this request naturally comes after the one before it. Once every obstacle is taken away, we can trust the God of love more fully for every kind of good thing.
“The wrongs we have done.” The word really means our debts.
That is how Scripture often describes our sins. Every sin puts us in fresh debt to God. And we already owe him, so to speak, ten thousand talents.
So what can we answer when he says, “Pay me what you owe”?
We are completely bankrupt. We have nothing to pay with. We have wasted everything we had.
So if he deals with us by the strictness of his law, if he demands what he has every right to demand, he would have to order us to be “tied hand and foot, and handed over to the torturers.”
In fact, we are already tied hand and foot by the chains of our own sins.
Looked at from our side, these sins are chains of iron and shackles of brass.
They are wounds that the world, the flesh, and the devil have cut into us, until we are torn up all over.
They are diseases that drain our blood and our strength and bring us down to the grave.
But looked at as they are here, in relation to God, they are debts—huge and too many to count.
So, since we have nothing to pay with, we have every reason to cry out to him to “freely forgive” us all of it!
The word translated “forgive” can mean either to cancel a debt or to undo a chain.
And if we get the first, the second follows naturally. If our debts are cancelled, the chains fall off our hands.
Through the free grace of God in Christ, the moment we “receive forgiveness of sins,” we also receive “a place among those who are made holy by faith in him.”
Sin has lost its power. It has no control over those who “are under grace”—that is, those who have God’s favour.
“There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” In the same way, they are set free from sin as well as from guilt.
“What the law rightly demands is fulfilled in” them. They “live not by the flesh, but by the Spirit.”

14. “As we forgive those who have wronged us.” In these words our Lord clearly tells us two things: on what condition God will forgive us, and to what degree or in what way we can expect him to forgive us.
All our wrongs and sins are forgiven if we forgive others, and in the same way that we forgive others.
[First, God forgives us if we forgive others.]
This is extremely important.
Our blessed Lord cares so much that we never let this slip out of our minds that he doesn’t only put it in the middle of his prayer. Right afterward he repeats it twice.
He says, “If you forgive people when they wrong you, your Father in heaven will forgive you too. But if you don’t forgive people when they wrong you, your Father won’t forgive the wrongs you do.”
(Matthew 6:14–15.) Second, God forgives us in the same way that we forgive others.

So if any hatred or bitterness is left in us, if any trace of unkindness or anger remains, if we don’t forgive everyone clearly, fully, and from the heart, then we cut short our own forgiveness by that much. God cannot clearly and fully forgive us. He may show us some mercy. But we will not let him wipe out all our sins and forgive all our wrongdoing.
Meanwhile, if we don’t forgive our neighbour from our hearts, what kind of prayer are we offering to God every time we say these words?
We are actually defying God openly. We are daring him to do his worst.
“Forgive us the wrongs we have done, as we forgive those who have wronged us!”
In plain words, that means: “Don’t forgive us at all. We don’t want any kindness from you.
We ask you to keep remembering our sins, and to let your anger stay on us.”
But can you really pray a prayer like that to God?
And hasn’t he thrown you alive into hell yet? Oh, don’t test him any longer!
Now, right now, by his grace, forgive others as you want to be forgiven!
Right now, have compassion on your fellow servant, just as God has had pity on you and will have pity on you!
15. “And don’t lead us into temptation, but rescue us from evil.” “[And] don’t lead us into temptation.”
The word translated “temptation” means any kind of test.
In the same way, the English word temptation used to have a neutral meaning. But now people usually take it to mean being pulled toward sin.

St. James uses the word in both these ways—first in its general meaning, then in its narrower meaning. He uses the first meaning when he says, “Happy is the man who holds out under temptation. For when he has been tested,” or approved by God, “he will receive the crown of life.”
(James 1:12–13.) Right after this he uses the word in the second meaning: “No one who is tempted should say, I am being tempted by God. For evil cannot tempt God, and God himself tempts no one.
But each person is tempted when he is dragged away by his own lust,” or desire—exelkomenos, dragged out of God, the only place where he is safe—“and lured in,” caught like a fish with bait.
It is then, when he is “dragged away and lured in” like this, that he truly “enters into temptation.”
Then temptation covers him like a cloud. It spreads over his whole soul.
Then how hard it is for him to escape the trap!
So we ask God “not to lead us into temptation.” Since God tempts no one, this means we ask him not to let us be led into it.

“But rescue us from evil.” A better translation is “from the evil one”—apo tou ponērou. Ho ponēros is without any doubt the wicked one, the one who has that title above all others. He is the prince and god of this world, who works with great power in those who disobey God.
But everyone who is a child of God by faith has been rescued from his hands.
He may fight against them, and he will.
But he cannot win unless they betray their own souls.
He may torment them for a while, but he cannot destroy them. For God is on their side, and in the end he will surely “avenge his own chosen people, who cry out to him day and night.”
Lord, when we are tempted, don’t let us enter into temptation!
Make a way for us to escape, so that the wicked one cannot touch us!
16. The ending of this divine prayer, usually called the Doxology, is a solemn thanksgiving. It is a short summary that praises God for who he is and what he does.
“For yours is the kingdom”—the royal right over everything that exists or ever was created. Yes, your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your rule lasts through all ages.
“The power”—the power by which you carry out your rule and govern everything in your everlasting kingdom, by which you do whatever you please everywhere you rule.

“And the glory”—the praise that every creature owes you for your power, for the greatness of your kingdom, and for all the wonderful works you have done from everlasting and will do, world without end, “forever and ever!
Amen!” So may it be!

blocks.x: The Lord’s Prayer in Other Words

1 Father of everyone, your powerful voice
Called this whole universe into being.
Your mercies rejoice over all,
And they stay the same through endless ages.
You hold everything together by your word.
You show your generous love to all.
You hear the call of every creature you made,
And you fill every mouth with good things.

2 You rule in heaven, sitting on a throne of light.
All of nature is spread out beneath you.
Earth, air, and sea lie open before your eyes.
So does the deep darkness of hell.
Wisdom, strength, and love belong to you.
We bow down low before you.
We confess your divine qualities.
We praise you as the Sovereign Lord of all.

3 Sovereign Lord, let everything that moves
On the earth, in the air, or in the sky confess you.
Let them honor your power and praise your goodness.
Let them tremble before your eye that sees everything.
All of you who owe your life to Him,
Spend every hour of your day praising Him!
Jehovah reigns! Be glad, O earth!
Shout for joy, you morning stars!

4 Son, loved by your Father forever,
Take up your mighty power.
Let everyone on earth experience your mercy.
Let them all worship the grace you showed when you bled.
Show everyone how your love wins.
Be the only King in every heart.
Keep on until all your enemies admit that you rule.
Then glory will finish what grace began.

5 Spirit of grace, health, and power,
You are a fountain of light and love here below.
Pour out your healing power everywhere.
Let it flow over all the nations.
Set our hearts on fire with perfect love.
Finish the work of faith in us.
Then the armies of heaven will not move any faster
Than we on earth move to do your will.

6 Father, each day it is your work to give
Your children a fresh supply of what they need.
You dress the lilies in the field.
You hear the young ravens when they cry.
We throw all our worries on you. We live
Because of you, and you know everything we need.
Oh, feed us with your grace! Give
Our souls the bread of life today!

7 Eternal Lamb of God, without any stain,
You were killed before the world was made.
Sprinkle us with your blood always.
Oh, wash us clean and keep us clean forever.
Toward every person (all praise to you!)
Stir our hearts with deep compassion.
That way all people will be able to see
That God is in us, because God is love.

8 You give life, and you are the Lord of life. Your power
And your protecting care are free for everyone.
When temptation hits us hard,
Let us run to you, away from sin and Satan.
Lord, we belong to you, and you belong to us.
Show all your goodness in us.
Make our hearts new, make them bigger, and fill them
With peace and joy, with heaven, and with God.

9 Blessing and honor, praise and love
You Three, who are equal and eternal together:
On earth below and in heaven above,
Let all your works give them to you.
Three times Holy! The kingdom is yours.
All power belongs to you.
And when everything that was created dies,
Your glory will keep on shining forever.

s: “Jehu left that place and met Jehonadab son of Rechab, who was coming to meet him. Jehu greeted him and said to him, Is your heart right with me, as my heart is with you?
Jehonadab answered: It is.
If it is, give me your hand.”
2 Kings 10:15.

1. Even people who do not pay this great debt of love agree that we owe love to all people. The royal law says, “Love your neighbour as yourself,” and everyone who hears it can see that it is true.
