But it does not mean what the religious zealots of long ago made it mean. They turned it into “Love your neighbour”—your relatives, the people you know, your friends—“and hate your enemy.” Not so! Our Lord said, “I tell you, love your enemies. Bless those who curse you. Do good to those who hate you. Pray for those who treat you badly and persecute you. Then you will be the children”—and everyone will see that you are—“of your Father in heaven. He makes his sun rise on evil people and on good people, and he sends rain on those who do right and on those who do wrong.”
2. But there is certainly a special love that we owe to those who love God.
David put it this way: “All my delight is in God’s holy people on the earth, and in those who stand out in goodness.”
And someone greater than David said: “I am giving you a new commandment: love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also must love one another.
If you love one another, everyone will know by this that you are My disciples” (John 13:34, 35).
This is the love that the apostle John talks about so often and so strongly. He says, “From the very beginning, this is the message you heard: that we should love one another” (1 John 3:11).
“This is how we see the love of God: he laid down his life for us. And we ought,” if love calls us to do it, “to lay down our lives for our fellow believers” (verse 16).
And again: “Dear ones, let us love each other, for love has its source in God.
If someone does not love, he does not know God. For God is love” (4:7, 8).
“Love is not that we loved God. It is that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the sacrifice that pays for our sins.
Dear ones, if God loved us like this, then we too must love one another” (verses 10, 11).
3. Everyone agrees with this. But does everyone actually do it?
Everyday life shows that they do not.
Where are the Christians, even, who “love one another as he has commanded us”? So many things stand in the way!

There are two big, general obstacles. First, people cannot all think the same way. Second, because of this, they cannot all live the same way. In several smaller matters, what they do will differ just as much as what they believe differs.
4. A difference in opinions or in ways of worship may keep us from being fully united on the outside. But does it have to keep us from being united in love?
Even if we cannot think alike, can’t we love alike?
Can’t we be one in heart, even if we are not one in opinion?
Without any doubt, we can.
All of God’s children can unite in this, even with these smaller differences.
The differences can stay just as they are, and they can still help each other grow in love and in doing good.
5. In this matter, Jehu himself is a good example. He was a mixed character, but every serious Christian should pay close attention to his example and follow it.
“Jehu left that place and met Jehonadab son of Rechab, who was coming to meet him. Jehu greeted him and said to him, Is your heart right with me, as my heart is with you?
Jehonadab answered, It is.
If it is, give me your hand.”
The text falls naturally into two parts. First, Jehu asks Jehonadab a question: “Is your heart right with me, as my heart is with you?”
Second, when Jehonadab answers, “It is,” Jehu makes an offer: “If it is, give me your hand.”
I. 1. First, let’s think about the question Jehu asked Jehonadab: “Is your heart right with me, as my heart is with you?”
The very first thing we notice in these words is that Jehu does not ask about Jehonadab’s opinions.

And yet Jehonadab certainly held some very unusual opinions. Some of them were his alone. Some had a big effect on the way he lived. He thought these were so important that he made them binding on his children’s children, all the way down to his very last descendants.

We can see this from what Jeremiah wrote many years after Jehonadab died: “I took Jaazaniah and his brothers and all his sons—the whole family of the Rechabites. . . . I set bowls full of wine and cups in front of them, and I said to them, Drink some wine.

But they said, We will not drink wine. For Jonadab,” that is, Jehonadab, “the son of Rechab, our father” (it would be clearer if the words were put this way: “Jehonadab our father, the son of Rechab.” Out of love and respect for Rechab, Jehonadab probably wanted his descendants to be called by Rechab’s name), “gave us this command: You must never drink wine, not you and not your sons, ever.
You must not build a house, or sow seed, or plant a vineyard, or own one. All your lives you must live in tents....
And we have obeyed. We have done everything that Jonadab our father commanded us” (Jeremiah 35:3–10).

2. It seems that Jehu’s way was to “drive furiously” at everything, both in worldly matters and in religion. And yet he does not bother himself at all about any of these things. He leaves Jehonadab free to hold his own views.
And neither of them seems to have troubled the other in the least about the opinions he held.
3. It is quite possible that many good people today also hold unusual opinions. Some of them may be just as odd in this as Jehonadab was.
And as long as we know only in part, it is certain that people will not all see everything the same way.
In this life our understanding is weak and limited. Because of that, people will always have different opinions about religion, just as they do about everyday life. This cannot be avoided.
It has been this way since the world began, and it will stay this way “until everything is restored.”

4. And there is more. Everyone has to believe that each opinion he holds is true. (To believe that an opinion is not true is the same as not holding it.) Yet no one can be sure that all his opinions, taken together, are true.
In fact, every thinking person is sure that they are not. For humanum est errare et nescire: “Not knowing many things, and being wrong about some, is simply part of being human.”
So he realizes that this is true of him too.
He knows that, in general, he is wrong about some things. But he does not know—and perhaps cannot know—which things they are.

5. I say “perhaps he cannot know.” For who can tell how far invincible ignorance may reach—ignorance that cannot be overcome? Or (which comes to the same thing) invincible prejudice? Such prejudice is often planted so firmly in young minds that later it is impossible to pull out something that has put down such deep roots.

And who can say how much blame any mistake deserves, unless he knows every detail around it? For guilt always means that the will has gone along with something. And only the one who searches the heart can judge that.

6. So every wise person will give others the same freedom of thought that he wants them to give him. He will no more insist that they accept his opinions than he would want them to insist that he accept theirs.
He is patient with those who disagree with him. When he wants to unite in love with someone, he asks him only one question: “Is your heart right with me, as my heart is with you?”
7. Second, we notice that Jehu does not ask about Jehonadab’s way of worship either. Yet it is very likely that the two men were very different in this too.
For we can well believe that Jehonadab and all his descendants worshipped God at Jerusalem. Jehu did not. He cared more about politics than about religion.
So although he killed the worshippers of Baal and “wiped Baal out of Israel,” he “did not turn away” from the convenient sin of Jeroboam—the worship of the “golden calves” (2 Kings 10:29).

8. But even among people with honest hearts—people who want to “keep a conscience free from offence”—there will be different ways of worshipping God as long as there are different opinions. It has to be this way, because different opinions always lead to different practices.
In every age, people have disagreed about nothing more than about their ideas of the Supreme Being. In the same way, they have disagreed about nothing more than about how to worship him.
If this happened only among the heathen, it would not surprise us at all. For we know that “through” their “wisdom” they “did not know God.” So they could not know how to worship him either.

But isn’t it strange that the same thing happens even among Christians? They all agree on the general truth: “God is a Spirit, and those who worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” Yet the particular ways they worship God are almost as varied as among the heathen.
9. So how are we to choose among so many different ways?
No one can choose for another person or tell him what he must do.
Instead, everyone must follow his own conscience, simply and sincerely before God.
He must be fully convinced in his own mind, and then act by the best light he has.
And no one has the power to force another person to live by his rules.
God has not given anyone the right to boss around the consciences of his fellow believers. Each person must judge for himself, just as each person must give an account of himself to God.

10. Every follower of Christ must, by the very nature of Christianity, belong to some particular congregation—some Church, as people usually call it. (Belonging to a church means worshipping God in a particular way, because “two cannot walk together unless they agree.”) But no power on earth except his own conscience can force him to choose one congregation over another, or one way of worship over another.

I know people commonly think that the place where we are born decides which Church we should belong to. For example, they think someone born in England should be a member of what is called the Church of England, and should therefore worship God in the particular way that Church requires.
I once defended this idea very strongly. But I have found many reasons to cool down my zeal for it.
I am afraid it has problems that no reasonable person can get past.

One of the biggest is this: if people had followed this rule, there could never have been a Reformation that broke away from the Pope’s church. For this rule completely destroys each person’s right to judge for himself, and that right is the foundation of the whole Reformation.
11. So I dare not try to force my way of worship on anyone else.
I believe it is truly the way of the early church and the apostles. But what I believe is not a rule for anyone else.
So when I want to unite in love with someone, I do not ask him, Are you part of my church, my congregation?
Do you accept the same kind of church government as I do, and the same church leaders?
Do you use the same set prayers that I use to worship God?

I do not ask, Do you receive the Lord’s Supper in the same position and in the same way that I do? I do not ask whether you agree with me about baptism: whether there should be godparents for the one being baptized, how baptism should be done, or at what age people should be baptized.
In fact, I do not even ask you (though I am very clear in my own mind about it) whether you accept baptism and the Lord’s Supper at all.
Let all these things wait. If we need to, we will talk about them at a better time. For now, my only question is this: “Is your heart right with me, as my heart is with you?”
12. But what does this question really mean?
I don’t mean, What did Jehu mean by it?
I mean, What should a follower of Christ mean by it when he asks it of a fellow believer?
The first thing it means is this: Is your heart right with God?
Do you believe that God exists, and that he is perfect? Do you believe he is eternal, without limits, wise, and powerful? Do you believe he is just, merciful, and true?

Do you believe that he is now “holding all things together by his powerful word”? Do you believe he rules even the smallest things, and even the most harmful things, for his own glory and for the good of those who love him? Do you have proof from God himself—a certainty that comes from above—about the things of God?
Do you “live by faith, not by sight”? Do you look not at the things of this world that pass away, but at the things that last forever?
13. Do you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who is “God over all, blessed forever”?
Has he shown himself to your soul?
Do you know Jesus Christ, and him crucified?
Does he live in you, and you in him?

Is he formed in your heart by faith? Have you completely given up trusting in your own works and your own goodness? Have you “submitted yourself to the righteousness of God that comes by faith in Christ Jesus”?
Are you “found in him, not having your own righteousness, but the righteousness that comes by faith”?
And through him, are you “fighting the good fight of faith and taking hold of eternal life”?
14. Is your faith energoumene di agapes—filled with the energy of love?

Do you love God “with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your soul, and with all your strength”? (I do not say “above all things,” because that phrase is not found in Scripture and it is unclear.)
Do you look for all your happiness in him alone?
And do you find what you are looking for?

Does your soul always “praise the greatness of the Lord, and your spirit rejoice in God your Saviour”? Have you learned “to give thanks in everything”? And do you find that “it is a joyful and pleasant thing to be thankful”?
Is God the centre of your soul, the sum of everything you long for?
Because of this, are you storing up your treasure in heaven, and counting everything else as garbage and worthless trash? Has the love of God driven the love of the world out of your soul?
If so, you are “crucified to the world.” You are dead to everything down here. And your “life is hidden with Christ in God.”

15. Are you busy doing “not your own will, but the will of the one who sent you”? He sent you down here to stay for a little while—to spend a few days in a foreign land—until you have finished the work he gave you to do and you go back to your Father’s house.
Is it your food and drink “to do the will of your Father in heaven”?
Is your eye focused on one thing in everything you do? Is it always fixed on him? Are you always looking to Jesus?

Do you aim at him in whatever you do—in all your work, your business, your conduct? Are you aiming only at God’s glory in everything? Are you, “whatever you do, in word or deed, doing it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, and giving thanks to God the Father through him”?
16. Does the love of God move you to serve him with fear, to “be glad before him with deep respect”?
Are you more afraid of displeasing God than of death, or even of hell?
Is there nothing as terrible to you as the thought of offending God’s glorious eyes?

Because of this, do you “hate every evil way”—every breaking of his holy and perfect law? And do you work hard at this, “training yourself to keep a conscience free from offence toward God and toward people”?
17. Is your heart right toward your neighbour?
Do you love all people as you love yourself, with no exceptions?
“If you love only those who love you, why should anyone thank you for that?”
Do you “love your enemies”?
Is your soul full of kindness and tender love toward them?
Do you love even God’s enemies—the ungrateful and the ungodly?
Does your heart ache for them?
Could you even “wish yourself” “cursed” in this earthly life for their sake?
And do you show this by “blessing those who curse you, and praying for those who treat you badly and persecute you”?
18. Do you show your love by what you do?
While you have time, and whenever you have the chance, do you really “do good to everyone”—neighbours or strangers, friends or enemies, good or bad?

Do you do them all the good you can? Do you try to meet all their needs, and help them in body and soul as much as you possibly can? If this is how you think, every Christian may say to you: Yes, even if you only sincerely want this, and keep pressing on until you reach it, then “your heart is right with me, as my heart is with you.”
II. 1. “If it is, give me your hand.”
I don’t mean, “Agree with my opinions.”
You don’t have to. I don’t expect it, and I don’t want it.
And I don’t mean, “I will agree with your opinions.”
I can’t. It is not up to me. I can no more think whatever I choose than I can see or hear whatever I choose.
You keep your opinion, and I will keep mine—just as firmly as ever.
You don’t even need to try to come over to my side, or to bring me over to yours.
I don’t want you to argue about those points, or even to hear or say one word about them.
Let’s leave all opinions alone, on both sides. Just “give me your hand.”
2. I don’t mean, “Take up my ways of worship,” or, “I will take up yours.”
This is also something that is not up to you or to me.
Each of us must act as he is fully convinced in his own mind.
You hold on tightly to what you believe pleases God most, and I will do the same.
I believe that the Episcopal way of governing the church agrees with Scripture and goes back to the apostles.
If you think the Presbyterian or Independent way is better, go on thinking so, and act on it.
I believe babies should be baptized, and that this can be done either by dipping them or by sprinkling.
If you believe differently, go on believing it, and follow what you are convinced of.
I think written prayers are very useful, especially when a large congregation meets together.
If you think prayers made up on the spot are more useful, act on what you think.

I believe that I should not refuse water for people to be baptized, and that I should eat bread and drink wine in memory of my Master who died. But if you are not convinced of this, act according to the light you have.
I don’t want to argue with you for even a moment about any of these points.
Let’s set all these smaller matters aside.
Let’s never even bring them up. “If your heart is like my heart”—if you love God and all people—I ask nothing more. “Give me your hand.”

3. First, I mean: love me. And don’t love me only the way you love all people, or the way you love your enemies or God’s enemies—those who hate you, who “treat you badly and persecute you.” Don’t love me only as a stranger, someone you know nothing good or bad about. That is not enough for me. No! “If your heart is right with me, as mine is with you,” then love me with a very tender love. Love me as a friend who is closer than a brother. Love me as a brother in Christ, a fellow citizen of the New Jerusalem, a fellow soldier fighting in the same war under the same Captain of our salvation.
Love me as a companion in the kingdom of Jesus and in his patient endurance, and as someone who will share in his glory with you.

4. Love me more than you love most people. Love me with a love that is patient and kind. Be patient with me if I don’t know something or if I go the wrong way. Help carry my load instead of making it heavier. Keep on being tender, gentle, and full of compassion toward me. Love me with a love that is not jealous if God sometimes gives me even more success in his work than he gives you.
Love me with a love that does not get angry at my foolish mistakes or my weaknesses—or even when it looks to you (if it sometimes seems that way) as if I am not acting according to God’s will.
Love me in such a way that you don’t think evil of me. Put away all jealousy and all suspicion.

Love me with the love that covers all things—that never tells others about my faults or weaknesses. Love me with the love that believes all things—that is always ready to think the best, and to take everything I say and do in the kindest way. Love me with the love that hopes all things. Hope that the thing someone told you about me never happened. Or hope that it did not happen the way they said. Or at least hope that I meant well, or that I did it when a strong temptation suddenly came over me.
And keep hoping to the end that whatever is wrong in me will be corrected by God’s grace, and that whatever is missing will be supplied through the riches of his mercy in Christ Jesus.
5. Second, I mean: bring me before God in all your prayers. Wrestle with God for me. Ask him to quickly correct whatever he sees wrong in me, and to supply whatever is missing in me.

When you come closest to the throne of grace, ask him—for he is very near you then—to make my heart more like yours, more right toward God and toward people. Ask that I may be more deeply convinced of things that cannot be seen, and see the love of God in Christ Jesus more clearly. Ask that I may live by faith, not by sight, more steadily, and take hold of eternal life more eagerly.

Pray that the love of God and of all people will be poured into my heart more fully. Pray that I will be more eager and active in doing the will of my Father in heaven, more zealous to do good, and more careful to stay away from anything that even looks evil.
6. Third, I mean: stir me up to love and to good works.
Back up your prayers, whenever you have the chance, by speaking to me in love about whatever you think is good for my soul.
Urge me on in the work God has given me to do, and teach me how to do it better.
Yes, “correct me as a friend, and rebuke me,” whenever it looks to you as though I am doing my own will instead of the will of the one who sent me.

Oh, speak up and don’t hold back! Tell me whatever you think may help me: to fix my faults, to strengthen my weak spots, to build me up in love, or to make me more ready in any way for the Master to use.
7. Finally, I mean: love me not just in words, but in actions and in truth.
As far as your conscience allows (while you keep your own opinions and your own way of worshipping God), join with me in God’s work. Let’s go forward hand in hand.
And you can certainly go this far.
Wherever you are, speak with respect about the work of God, no matter whom he is working through. And speak kindly about his messengers.
And if you can, don’t just feel sorry for them when they are in trouble or distress. Give them cheerful and real help, so that they may praise God because of you.

8. Two things should be noticed about what I have said under this last point. First, whatever love I ask from the person whose heart is right with mine—whatever acts of love, whatever help for the soul or for daily life—I am ready to give him the same, by God’s grace, as far as I am able. Second, I have not asked this only for myself. I ask it for all whose hearts are right toward God and people, so that we may all love one another as Christ has loved us.
III. 1. From all this, we can draw one conclusion.
From this we can learn what a catholic (universal) spirit is.

Hardly any phrase has been so badly misunderstood, or so dangerously misused, as this one. But anyone who calmly thinks about what I have said can easily correct these misunderstandings and keep it from being misused.
First, we learn from this that a catholic spirit is not a loose, anything-goes attitude toward beliefs.
It is not being indifferent to all opinions. That attitude comes from hell, not from heaven.
This unsettled thinking—being “carried back and forth and thrown around by every wind of doctrine”—is a great curse, not a blessing. It is a bitter enemy, not a friend, of a truly catholic spirit.
A person with a truly catholic spirit is not still searching for his religion.
He is as fixed as the sun in his judgement about the main teachings of the Christian faith.

It is true that he is always ready to listen to and think about anything that can be said against what he believes. But this does not show that his mind is wavering, and it does not make it waver either.
He does not go back and forth between two opinions, or foolishly try to mix them into one.

Take note of this, you who don’t know what spirit you have! You call yourselves people with a catholic spirit only because your thinking is muddy, because your mind is all foggy, and because you have no settled, consistent beliefs, but want to mix all opinions together.
Be sure of this: you have completely lost your way. You don’t know where you are.
You think you have found the very spirit of Christ. In truth, you are closer to the spirit of Antichrist.
First go and learn the basics of the gospel of Christ. Then you will learn to have a truly catholic spirit.
2. Second, we learn from what has been said that a catholic spirit is not a loose, anything-goes attitude toward how we worship.
It is not being indifferent about public worship, or about the outward way it is done.
This, too, would be a curse and not a blessing.
Far from helping us worship God in spirit and in truth, it would, as long as it lasted, get in the way more than words can say.
But a person with a truly catholic spirit has weighed everything on God’s own scales. So he has no doubt and no hesitation at all about the particular way of worship he takes part in.
He is clearly convinced that this way of worshipping God agrees with Scripture and makes good sense.
He knows of no other way in the world that agrees more with Scripture, or makes more sense.
So he doesn’t wander here and there. He sticks closely to it, and he praises God for the chance to do so.
3. Third, we learn from this that a catholic spirit does not mean not caring which congregation you belong to.
This is another kind of looseness, and it is just as foolish and unscriptural as the one before.
A person with a truly catholic spirit is far from it.
He is settled in his congregation, just as he is settled in his beliefs.
He is joined to one congregation, not only in spirit but by all the outward ties of Christian fellowship.
There he takes part in all the practices God has given to his people.
There he receives the Lord’s Supper.
There he pours out his soul in prayer with others, and joins with them in praising and thanking God.
There he loves to hear the message of reconciliation, the good news of God’s grace.
On special occasions he seeks God by fasting together with these people, his closest and most dearly loved brothers.
He watches over these people in love in a special way, just as they watch over his soul. They warn, encourage, comfort, and correct one another, and in every way build each other up in the faith.
He sees them as his own family. So, as far as God has given him the ability, he naturally takes care of them and makes sure they have everything they need for life and godliness.

4. He stays firmly fixed in his beliefs, in what he believes is the truth as it is in Jesus. He holds tightly to the kind of worship he believes God accepts most. He is joined to one particular congregation by the tenderest and closest ties. But while all this is true, his heart is wide open toward all people, those he knows and those he doesn’t. He embraces with strong and warm love neighbours and strangers, friends and enemies.
This is catholic, or universal, love.
And whoever has this love has a catholic spirit.
For only love gives a person the right to this name: catholic love is a catholic spirit.

5. So, if we use this word in its strictest sense, a person with a catholic spirit is someone who, in the way I have described, gives his hand to everyone whose heart is right with his heart. He knows how to value all the blessings he has, and to praise God for them: his knowledge of the things of God, the true scriptural way of worshipping him, and above all his union with a congregation that fears God and does what is right. He guards these blessings with the greatest care, and keeps them as the apple of his eye. And at the same time he loves all who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, whatever their opinions, their way of worship, or their congregation. He loves all who love God and people, who are glad to please God and afraid to offend him, and so are careful to stay away from evil and eager to do good. He loves them as friends, as brothers in the Lord, as members of Christ and children of God, as people who share with him now in God’s present kingdom, and who will be heirs with him of God’s eternal kingdom.

The person with a truly catholic spirit carries all these people on his heart all the time. He has a tenderness for them that words cannot express, and he longs for their good. So he never stops bringing them before God in prayer, and he also speaks up for them before people. He speaks comforting words to them, and he works hard, with everything he says, to strengthen their hands in God.
He helps them as much as he possibly can in everything, both spiritual and practical.
He is ready “to spend and be spent for them”—yes, even to give his life for them.
6. You, O man of God, think about these things!
If you are already on this path, keep going.
If you have taken the wrong path until now, thank God, who has brought you back!
And now run the race set before you, on the royal road of universal love.

Be careful not to waver in what you believe, and not to let your heart grow narrow. Keep a steady pace. Stay rooted in the faith that was once given to the saints, and grounded in love—in true catholic love—until you are swallowed up in love forever and ever!

blocks.x:
Tired of all this war of words,
These ideas, forms, and ways, and names,
I come to you, the Way, the Truth, the Life,
Whose love sets my simple heart on fire;
Taught by God, at last I run
To live and die with you and yours.

I rest as one with the little flock,
The healthy members who hold on to the Head,
The chosen few, blessed with forgiveness,
And led by the Spirit who anoints
Into the mind that was in you,
Into the depths of God himself.

These are my brothers, friends, and family:
Those who do my heavenly Father’s will,
Who aim at perfect holiness,
And want to carry out all your plans,
Who long to be all that you are,
And love their God with all their heart.

For these, though we are apart in body,
Wherever they are scattered across the earth,
I find a sincere love that has no limits,
As constant as the life of God;
It sprang from him, the Fountain of life,
As pure, as steady, and as strong.

Joined to the hidden church the world does not know,
In this sure bond that makes us perfect,
Safe though unseen, I live alone
And glory in the grace that unites us,
Given to me and to every believer,
To all your saints on earth and in heaven.

s: “If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault. Do it just between the two of you. If he listens to you, you have won your brother back.
But if he will not listen, take one or two others with you. Then every word can be confirmed by two or three witnesses.
If he will not listen to them, tell it to the church.
And if he will not listen to the church, let him be to you like a pagan and a tax collector.” Matthew 18:15–17
1. The great apostle says, “Speak evil of no one.” This is as plain a command as “You must not commit murder.”
But who, even among Christians, pays attention to this command?
Indeed, how few people even understand it?
What is evil-speaking? Some people think it is the same as lying or slander. But it is not.
Everything a person says may be as true as the Bible. And yet saying it is still evil-speaking.
For evil-speaking is simply this: speaking evil about someone who is not there. It means telling something bad that a person really did or said, when that person is not present.
Suppose I see a man drunk, or hear him curse and swear. If I tell others about it when he is not there, that is evil-speaking.
In our language it also has a very fitting name: backbiting.
And there is no real difference between this and what we usually call telling tales.
Sometimes the story is told in a soft, quiet way. Perhaps the speaker says he wishes the person well, and hopes things are not quite so bad. Then we call it whispering.
But however it is done, it is the same thing. It is the same in substance, even if the details are different.
It is still evil-speaking. We still trample on the command “Speak evil of no one” whenever we tell someone the fault of a third person who is not there to answer for himself.
2. And how very common this sin is among people of every rank and class!
High and low, rich and poor, wise and foolish, educated and uneducated: how constantly they all fall into it!
People who disagree about everything else still agree in this.
How few can say before God, “I am innocent in this matter. I have always set a guard in front of my mouth and kept the door of my lips!”

What long conversation do you ever hear that does not include some evil-speaking? And this happens even among people who generally have the fear of God before their eyes. They truly want a clear conscience before God and before people.
3. The very fact that this sin is so common makes it hard to avoid.
It is all around us. So if we are not deeply aware of the danger, and always on guard against it, the flood can easily sweep us away.
Here almost the whole human race is, so to speak, plotting against us.
Their example creeps up on us, and we do not know how. So we slowly slide into copying it without noticing.
Besides, it is urged on us from inside as well as from outside.
There is hardly any wrong attitude in the human mind that it cannot satisfy at times. And so each of these attitudes pulls us toward it.
It feeds our pride to tell about faults in others that we think we do not have.

Speaking against people who displease us feeds our anger, our resentment, and every unkind feeling. And often, by telling the sins of their neighbors, people feed their own foolish and harmful desires.
4. Evil-speaking is even harder to avoid because it often attacks us in disguise.
We speak this way out of a noble, generous (maybe we even say holy) anger against these terrible people!
We commit sin just because we hate sin!
We serve the devil out of pure zeal for God!
We fall into this wickedness only to punish the wicked!
As someone has said, “This is how the passions all justify themselves.” They pass off sin to us under a cover of holiness!
5. But is there no way to avoid this trap?
Certainly there is. In the words quoted above, our blessed Lord has shown His followers a plain way.
No one who walks carefully and steadily on this path will ever fall into evil-speaking.
This rule either surely prevents it or surely cures it.

In the verses before this, our Lord had said, “How terrible for the world because of offenses!” Great misery will come into the world from this deadly source. (Offenses are anything that turns a person away from God’s ways or holds him back in them.) “For offenses are bound to come.” That is the nature of things. That is how wicked, foolish, and weak people are. “But how terrible for the man through whom the offense comes!” That man is truly miserable.

“So if your hand, your foot, or your eye makes you stumble…” It may be your dearest pleasure, or the person you love most and find most useful. If it turns you away from the way, or holds you back in it, “pluck it out.” Cut them off and throw them away from you.
But how can we avoid offending some people, and being offended by others?
Especially if they are clearly in the wrong, and we see it with our own eyes?
Here our Lord teaches us how. He gives a sure way to avoid both offenses and evil-speaking.
“If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, just between the two of you. If he listens to you, you have won your brother back.
But if he will not listen to you, take one or two others with you. Then every word can be confirmed by two or three witnesses.
If he will not listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he will not listen to the church, let him be to you like a pagan and a tax collector.”
I. 1. First: “If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, just between the two of you.”

Where it is possible, the best way to follow this first rule is the most literal way. Suppose you see with your own eyes a brother, a fellow Christian, commit a sin that cannot be denied. Or you hear it with your own ears, so that you cannot doubt it. Then what you must do is plain. Take the very first chance to go to him. And if you can get to see him, “tell him his fault, just between the two of you.”
Of course, you must take great care to do this in the right spirit and in the right way.
Whether a correction works depends very much on the spirit in which it is given.

So pray earnestly to God that you may give it in a humble spirit. Be deeply convinced that God alone makes you any different. And if anything good comes from what you say, God Himself is the one who does it.
Pray that He will guard your heart, give light to your mind, and lead your tongue to words that He will be pleased to bless.
Make sure you speak gently as well as humbly, “for man’s anger does not bring about God’s righteousness.”
If he has been “caught in a fault,” the only way to restore him is “in a spirit of gentleness.”
If he opposes the truth, he can still only be brought to know it through gentleness.
Keep speaking in a spirit of tender love, “which many waters cannot put out.”
If love is not defeated, it defeats everything.
Who can describe the power of love?

blocks.x:
Love can bend the stubborn neck,
And turn stone into flesh;
It can soften, melt, pierce, and break
A heart as hard as diamond.

s: So show him your love clearly. In this way you will “heap burning coals on his head.”
2. But also make sure that the way you speak agrees with the gospel of Christ.
Avoid anything in your look, gestures, words, or tone of voice that suggests pride or self-importance.
Carefully avoid anything bossy or dogmatic, anything that looks arrogant or presumptuous.
Stay far away from anything like disdain, domineering, or contempt.
Be just as careful to avoid any sign of anger. You may speak very plainly. But let there be no blame, no harsh accusations, no sign of any warmth except the warmth of love.
Above all, let there be no trace of hatred or ill will, and no bitter or sour words. Instead, use a sweet and gentle manner and gentle words, so that everything clearly comes from love in your heart.

Yet this sweetness does not have to stop you from speaking very seriously and solemnly. As far as possible, use the very words of God, for there are no words like them. And speak as one who is under the eye of Him who is coming to judge the living and the dead.

3. Perhaps you have no chance to speak to him in person, or you cannot get to see him. Then you may do it through a messenger: a friend you both know, whose good sense and honesty you can fully trust.
Such a person can speak for you, in the spirit and manner described above. This may serve the same purpose. It can largely make up for your not doing it yourself.
But be careful not to pretend you have no chance, just to avoid the cross. And do not simply assume you cannot see him, without ever trying.
Whenever you can speak to him yourself, that is far better.
But it is better to do it through someone else than not at all. This way is better than nothing.
4. But what if you cannot speak to him yourself, and cannot find a messenger you can trust?
If that is really the case, then all that is left is to write.
And in some situations this may be the wisest way to speak.
One such situation is when the person we are dealing with has a hot and hasty temper. Such a person does not take correction easily, especially from an equal or from someone below him.
But in writing, the correction can be introduced and softened so that it is much easier to accept.
Besides, many people will read the very same words that they could not stand to hear.
Reading does not shock their pride so badly, or hurt their sense of honor so much.
Even if it makes little impression at first, they may read it a second time. Then, after thinking it over, they may take to heart what they ignored before.
If you sign your name, this is almost the same as going to him and speaking in person.
And you should always do this, unless some very special reason makes it wrong to do so.
5. We should note this carefully. Our Lord does not only command us to take this step. He commands us to take this step first, before we try anything else.
No alternative is allowed. We have no choice of anything else. This is the way; walk in it.

It is true that He tells us to take two more steps if needed. But we must take them one after another, after this step, and neither of them before it. Much less may we take any other step, either before this one or alongside it.
So doing anything else, or not doing this, is equally inexcusable.
6. Do not try to excuse yourself for taking a completely different step by saying, “Well, I did not speak to anyone until I felt so burdened that I could not hold it in.”
You felt burdened! No wonder, unless your conscience had lost all feeling. For you were guilty of sin. You were disobeying a plain command of God!
You should have gone right away and told “your brother his fault, just between the two of you.”
If you did not, how could you not feel burdened (unless your heart was completely hard)? You were trampling on God’s command and “hating your brother in your heart.”
And what a way you found to relieve your burden!
God corrects you for a sin of omission: you did not tell your brother his fault. And you comfort yourself under His correction by a sin of commission: you tell your brother’s fault to someone else!
Relief bought with sin comes at a high price!
I trust in God that you will find no relief. I trust you will be burdened even more, until you “go to your brother and tell him,” and no one else.
7. I know of only one exception to this rule. There may be a special case where we must accuse a guilty person who is not present, in order to protect the innocent.
For example, you know that a man is planning something against his neighbor’s property or life.
The situation may be such that the only way to stop the plan is to tell it right away to the person it is aimed at.

In this case, then, this rule is set aside. So is the apostle’s rule, “Speak evil of no one.” It is right, and in fact it is our duty, to speak evil of someone who is absent. We do it to stop him from doing evil to others and to himself at the same time.
But remember that all evil-speaking is, by its very nature, deadly poison.
So if you are sometimes forced to use it as a medicine, use it with fear and trembling. It is such a dangerous medicine that only absolute necessity can excuse you for using it at all.
So use it as rarely as possible, and only when it is truly necessary. And even then, use as little of it as you can, only as much as you need for the purpose.
At all other times, “go and tell him his fault, just between the two of you.”
II. 1. But what “if he will not listen”?
What if he pays you back evil for good?
What if he becomes angry instead of convinced?
What if he hears you but it does no good, and he keeps on in his evil ways?
We must expect this to happen often. The mildest and kindest correction will have no effect. But the blessing we wished for the other person will come back to us.
What should we do then?
Our Lord has given us clear and complete directions.
Then “take one or two others with you.” This is the second step.
Take one or two people whom you know to have a loving spirit, people who love God and their neighbor.
Also make sure they have a humble spirit and are “clothed with humility.”
They should also be gentle and kind, patient and long-suffering. They should not be quick to “pay back evil for evil, or insult for insult, but instead give a blessing.”
They should be people of understanding, who have wisdom from above. They should be fair, not taking sides, and free from any kind of prejudice.
You should also make sure that he knows these people well, and knows their character. Choose people he accepts rather than anyone else.
2. Love will show them how to go about it, depending on the kind of case.
No single method can be laid down for every case.

But in general, perhaps this advice would help. Before they begin with the matter itself, let them tell him gently and warmly that they are not angry with him or prejudiced against him. They come only out of goodwill, and that is the only reason they are involved in his affairs at all.
To make this even clearer, they could then calmly listen as you repeat your earlier conversation with him, and what he said to defend himself. They should do this before they try to decide anything.

After this they will be better able to judge how to go on, “so that every word may be confirmed by two or three witnesses.” Then whatever you said will have its full force, with the added weight of their authority.
3. To do this, could they not (1)
Briefly repeat what you said, and what he answered?
(2) Explain more fully, make clear, and support the reasons you had given?
(3) Give weight to your correction, by showing how fair, how kind, and how timely it was?
And finally, press home the advice and appeals you had added to it?
And later, if necessary, these people can also be witnesses of what was said.
4. As with the first rule, we can see that our Lord gives us no choice here. He leaves us no alternative. He clearly commands us to do this, and nothing else instead.
He also tells us when to do this, not sooner and not later: after we have taken the first step, and before we take the third.
Only then are we allowed to tell the evil someone has done to those we want to join us in this great act of brotherly love.
But let us be careful not to tell it to anyone else until both these steps have been taken.
If we fail to take these steps, or take other ones, is it any wonder that we still feel burdened?
For we are sinning against God and against our neighbor. And however nicely we may dress it up, if we have any conscience, our sin will find us out and bring a burden on our soul.
III. 1. Our Lord wants us to be fully taught in this important matter. So He has given us one more direction: “If he will not listen to them,” then, and not before, “tell it to the church.”
This is the third step.
The only question is how we should understand the word “church” here.
But the very nature of the matter makes this clear beyond any reasonable doubt.
You cannot tell it to the national church, the whole body of people called “the Church of England.”
And even if you could, it would not serve any Christian purpose. So this is not what the word means.
Nor can you tell it to the whole body of people in England with whom you are more closely connected.
And this would not do any good either. So the word should not be understood in this way.
It would not serve any useful purpose to tell the faults of each member to the church (if you want to call it that), meaning the congregation or society joined together in London.

What remains is to tell it to the elder or elders of the church. These are the overseers of the flock of Christ to which you both belong. They watch over your soul and his, “as those who must give an account.”
If possible, this should be done with the person present. And it should be done plainly, but with all the tenderness and love that the matter allows.
It is properly their job to make decisions about the behavior of those in their care. It is also their job to rebuke “with all authority,” as the offense deserves.
So when you have done this, you have done everything God’s Word, or the law of love, requires of you. You no longer share in his sin. If he is lost, his blood is on his own head.

2. Here too, notice that this, and nothing else, is the third step we must take. We must take it in its proper order, after the other two. It must not come before the second step, much less before the first, except in some very special situation.
In fact, in one case the second step may be the same as this one. In a way, they may be one and the same.

The elder or elders of the church may be so closely connected with the brother who has sinned that the one or two witnesses are not needed. The elders can take their place. So it may be enough to tell it to them, after you have told it to your brother “just between the two of you.”
3. When you have done this, you have delivered your own soul.
“If he will not listen to the church,” if he keeps on in his sin, “let him be to you like a pagan and a tax collector.”
You no longer need to think about him, except when you commit him to God in prayer.
You do not need to talk about him any more. Leave him to his own Master.
Of course, you still owe him sincere and tender goodwill, as you owe it to all other pagans.
You owe him politeness. And when the chance comes, you owe him every kindness that one human being owes another.
But have no friendship or close relationship with him. Have no more to do with him than with an open pagan.
4. But if this is the rule Christians live by, where is the land where Christians live?
You may perhaps find a few people here and there who make it a matter of conscience to keep it.
But how very few!
How thinly scattered across the earth!
And where is there any group of people who all live by it?
Can we find them in Europe?
Or, without going further, in Great Britain or Ireland?
I am afraid not. I fear we could search every part of these kingdoms and still search in vain.
How sad for the Christian world!
How sad for Protestants, for Reformed Christians!
Oh, “who will stand up with me against the wicked?”
“Who will take God’s side” against those who speak evil?
Are you the one?
By the grace of God, will you be one who is not swept away by the flood?
Are you fully determined, with God as your helper, from this very hour to set a guard, a constant “guard in front of your mouth,” and to “keep the door of your lips”?
From now on, will you live by this rule: “Speak evil of no one”?
If you see your brother do wrong, will you “tell him his fault, just between the two of you”?
And after that, “take one or two witnesses,” and only then “tell it to the church”?
If this is truly what your heart intends, then learn one lesson well: “Hear evil of no one.”
If there were no one to listen to evil, there would be no one to speak it.
And as the common saying goes, isn’t the one who receives stolen goods as bad as the thief?
So if anyone starts to speak evil where you can hear, stop him right away.

Refuse to listen to the charmer’s voice, no matter how sweetly he charms. He may use a very soft manner and a very mild tone. He may say again and again that he wishes well to the person he is stabbing in the dark, the one he strikes under the fifth rib!
Firmly refuse to listen, even if the whisperer complains that he is “burdened until he speaks.”
Burdened! You fool! Are you in labor with your cursed secret, like a woman giving birth to a child?
Then go, and be set free from your burden in the way the Lord has appointed!

First, “go and tell your brother his fault, just between the two of you.” Next, “take one or two” friends you both know, and tell him while they are there. If neither of these steps works, then “tell it to the church.”
But, at the risk of your soul, tell it to no one else, before or after! The only exception is that one case, when it is absolutely necessary to protect the innocent.
Why should you burden someone else as well as yourself, by making him share in your sin?
5. Oh, that all of you who bear the shame of Christ, who are mockingly called Methodists, would set an example to the so-called Christian world, at least in this one thing!
Put away evil-speaking, telling tales, and whispering. Do not let any of them come out of your mouth!
Make sure you “speak evil of no one.” Say nothing but good about those who are absent.
If you must be marked out as different, whether you want it or not, let this be the mark of a Methodist: “He criticizes no one behind his back. By this fruit you may know him.”
What a blessed effect of this self-denial we would soon feel in our hearts!
How our “peace would flow like a river,” when we “pursued peace with everyone” in this way!
How God’s love would overflow in our own souls, as we proved our love for our brothers in this way!
And what an effect it would have on all who were united in the name of the Lord Jesus!
How brotherly love would keep growing, once this great obstacle to it was removed!
Then all the members of Christ’s mystical body would naturally care for one another.
“If one member suffered, all would suffer with it. If one was honored, all would rejoice with it.” And everyone would love his brother “with a pure heart, fervently.”
And that is not all. What an effect this might have even on the wild, thoughtless world!

How soon they would see in us what they could not find among all the thousands of their brothers! And they would cry out (as Julian the Apostate did to his pagan courtiers), “See how these Christians love one another!”

This above all is how God would convince the world and also prepare them for His kingdom. We can easily learn this from the remarkable words of our Lord’s last, solemn prayer: “I pray for those who will believe in Me, that they may all be one, just as You, Father, are in Me and I am in You, so that the world may believe that You sent Me!”
[John 17:21] May the Lord bring that time soon!
May the Lord help us to love one another like this, not only “with words and talk, but with actions and in truth,” just as Christ has loved us.
“Let me die like a person who is right with God. Let the end of my life be like his!” Numbers 23:10.
1. “Let the end of my life be like his!”
How many of you share this wish?
Even in this huge crowd, there are probably very few of you who do not!

Oh, I pray that this wish will stay in your minds! I pray that it will not fade away until your souls are also safe in the place “where the wicked stop causing trouble, and where the tired are at rest!”
2. No one will expect me to explain this Bible text in detail today.

That would keep you too long from thinking about your beloved brother, friend, and pastor. That thought is sad, and yet it is also sweet. Yes, he was your father too. So many people here were brought to new life “in the Lord” through him!

So wouldn’t it suit your feelings, and this serious occasion, better if I spoke directly about this man of God? You have heard him speak in this very place so many times. And you know the outcome of his whole way of life: “Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever.”
So shouldn’t we do these three things?
I. Look at a few facts about his life and death.
II. Take a look at his character. And,
III. Ask how we can gain something good from this solemn event, when God took him from us so suddenly.
1. First, let’s look at a few facts about his life and death.
He was born in Gloucester in December 1714. When he was about twelve years old, he was sent to a grammar school there.
When he was seventeen, he began to take his faith seriously. He served God as well as he knew how.

At about eighteen he went to university. He was accepted at Pembroke College in Oxford. About a year later he got to know the people called “Methodists.” From then on he loved them as much as his own soul.
2. They convinced him that we “must be born again.” Without that, religion on the outside does us no good at all.

He joined them in fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays. He visited the sick and the prisoners with them. Like them, he used even the smallest scraps of time, so that not one moment was wasted. He also changed what he studied. He read mostly books that went to the heart of faith, books that led straight to knowing Jesus Christ, and Him crucified, by personal experience.
3. Soon his faith was tested, as if by fire.
He lost his good name, and some of his closest friends turned their backs on him. But he also suffered troubles on the inside, and they were the hardest kind.
Many nights he lay awake in his bed. Many days he lay face down on the ground.

For several months he groaned under “the spirit of being a slave.” But then God kindly took the heavy load away. He gave him “the Spirit of adoption.” Through a living faith, God helped him take hold of “the Son of His love.”
4. His health had become very poor. So people thought he needed to go to the countryside to get better.
So he went to Gloucester. There God used him to wake up several young people to faith.
They soon formed a small group of their own. They were some of the first fruit of his work.
Soon after that, he began reading to some poor people in the town two or three times a week. Every day he also read to the prisoners in the county jail and prayed with them.
5. He was now about twenty-one years old. People urged him to become an ordained minister.
He was very afraid of this, because he felt deeply that he was not good enough for it.

But the Bishop himself sent for him. He told him, “I had planned not to ordain anyone under twenty-three. But I will ordain you whenever you come.” Several other things that God arranged also pointed the same way. So he gave in, and he was ordained on Trinity Sunday, 1736.
The next Sunday he preached to a packed church, in the same church where he had been baptized.
The week after that, he went back to Oxford and got his Bachelor’s degree. Now he was fully busy, because caring for the prisoners and the poor rested mostly on him.
6. But before long he was invited to London. A friend who was going away to the countryside needed someone to take over his church work.

He stayed there two months and lived in the Tower. Twice a week he read prayers in the chapel, and once a week he taught the catechism and preached. He also visited the soldiers in the barracks and in the hospital.
He also read prayers every evening at the Wapping chapel, and he preached at Ludgate prison every Tuesday.

While he was there, letters came from his friends in Georgia. They made him long to go and help them. But he did not yet see clearly that God was calling him. So at the planned time he went back to his small flock at Oxford. There several young men met in his room every day to build each other up in their most holy faith.
7. But he was soon called away again, this time to fill in for the minister at Dummer, in Hampshire.
There he read prayers twice a day: early in the morning, and in the evening after the people came home from work.
Every day he also taught the children the catechism and visited people from house to house.
He now split his day into three parts. He gave eight hours to sleep and meals, eight to study and quiet time alone, and eight to reading prayers, teaching the catechism, and visiting the people.
Is there any better way for a servant of Christ and His Church to live?
If not, who will “go and do the same”?

8. But he still kept thinking about going overseas. Now he was fully convinced that God was calling him to do it. So he put everything in order, and in January 1737 he went to Gloucester to say goodbye to his friends.
It was on this journey that God began to bless his preaching in an unusual way.

Wherever he preached, huge crowds came flocking to hear him—in Gloucester, in Stonehouse, in Bath, in Bristol. The churches got so hot that people could hardly stand it. And the effect on the minds of many people was just as extraordinary.
Then he returned to London. General Oglethorpe kept him waiting there week after week and month after month. During that time God blessed his preaching even more.

He never seemed to get tired of working. On Sundays he usually preached four times to very large crowds. On top of that, he read prayers two or three times, and he often walked ten or twelve miles back and forth.
9. He left London on December 28.
On the 29th he preached without notes for the first time.
On December 30 he boarded the ship. But it was more than a month before they got away from the coast.
The next April he wrote about one happy result of their very slow trip: “Praise God, we now live very happily together in the big cabin.
We talk about almost nothing except God and Christ. When we are together, you hardly hear a word that is not about how we fell in the first Adam and how we are born again in the Second Adam.”

It also seems to have been a special act of God that he spent a little time at Gibraltar. There citizens and soldiers, important people and ordinary people, young and old, all recognized that God had come to visit them.

10. From Sunday, May 7, 1738, until late in the following August, he “fully carried out his ministry” in Georgia, especially at Savannah. Twice a day he read prayers and explained the Bible, and every day he visited the sick.

On Sundays he explained the Bible at five in the morning. At ten he read prayers and preached, and he did the same again at three in the afternoon. At seven in the evening he explained the Church Catechism.
How much easier it is for our fellow ministers in England, Scotland, or Ireland to criticize a worker like this in our Lord’s vineyard than to follow in his footsteps!

11. At this time he saw how terrible life was for many children there. And God put into his heart the first idea of starting an orphanage. He decided to raise money for it in England, if God brought him back there safely.
The following December he did return to London. On Sunday, January 14, 1739, he was ordained a priest at Christ Church, Oxford.
The next day he came back to London. On Sunday the 21st he preached twice.
The churches were large and extremely crowded. Even so, many hundreds of people stood outside in the churchyard, and hundreds more went home.
This first gave him the idea of preaching outdoors.
But when he told some of his friends about it, they thought it was simply crazy. So he did not actually do it until after he had left London.

On Wednesday, February 21, he found that all the church doors in Bristol were shut. Besides, no church could hold even half the crowd. So at three in the afternoon he went to Kingswood and preached outdoors to nearly two thousand people.
On Friday he preached there to four or five thousand people. On Sunday he preached to what people thought was ten thousand!
The crowds kept growing the whole time he stayed at Bristol. A fire of holy love was lit that will not easily be put out.
Later the same fire was lit in many parts of Wales, Gloucestershire, and Worcestershire.
In fact, wherever he went, God strongly confirmed the message of the one He had sent.
12. On Sunday, April 29, he preached for the first time in Moorfields and on Kennington Common. Thousands of people listened, and they were as quiet as they would have been in a church.
Once again he was kept in England month after month. So he made short trips into several counties, and large crowds gladly gave money for an orphanage in Georgia.
At this time ships were banned from sailing. That gave him time for more journeys through different parts of England. Many people will thank God for those journeys forever.
Finally, on August 14, he set sail. But he did not land in Pennsylvania until October 30.

After that he traveled through Pennsylvania, the Jerseys, New York, Maryland, Virginia, and North and South Carolina. All along the way he preached to enormous crowds, with just as great an effect as in England.
On January 10, 1740, he arrived in Savannah.
13. On January 29 he took in three orphans who had no one to care for them. He already had nearly twenty in his house.
The next day he marked out the land for the orphanage building, about ten miles from Savannah.
On February 11 he took in four more orphans. Then he set out for Frederica to bring back the orphans who lived in the southern parts of the colony.
On the way back he started a school at Darien, for both children and adults, and he took four orphans from there.
On March 25 he laid the first stone of the orphanage. He gave it the very fitting name Bethesda. Children who are not even born yet will praise the Lord for this work.
He now had about forty orphans, so there were nearly a hundred mouths to feed every day.
But he did not “worry about anything.” He handed his worries over to the One who feeds the young ravens when they call to Him.
14. In April he made another trip through Pennsylvania, the Jerseys, and New York.
Unbelievably large crowds came to hear him, and among them were a great many Black people.
Everywhere, most of the listeners were moved to an amazing degree.
Many became deeply aware that they were lost. Many truly turned to God.

In some places thousands cried out loud. Many seemed to be in the pain of dying. Most were in floods of tears. Some turned as pale as death. Others were wringing their hands. Others were lying on the ground. Others were collapsing into their friends’ arms. Almost all of them were looking up and crying out for mercy.
15. He returned to Savannah on June 5.

The next evening, during the church service, the whole congregation, young and old, broke down in tears. After the service several members of the church, and his whole household, especially the little children, walked home crying along the street. Some could not help praying out loud.
The children kept groaning and crying all night and for much of the next day.
16. In August he set out again. He traveled through several colonies and came to Boston.

While he was there and in the nearby towns, his body was extremely weak. Yet the crowds were so huge, and the effects on them so astonishing, that even the oldest men in town had never seen anything like it.
The same power was present when he preached in New York, especially on Sunday, November 2. Almost as soon as he started, you could hear crying, weeping, and wailing on every side.
Many people sank to the ground, cut to the heart. And many were filled with comfort from God.

Near the end of this journey he wrote: “Today is the seventy-fifth day since I arrived at Rhode Island, very weak in body. Yet God has helped me preach in public one hundred and seventy-five times, besides often encouraging people in private!
God has never given me greater comfort. I have never made my journeys with less tiredness. And I have never seen God’s presence stay so constantly with the people I preached to.”
In December he went back to Savannah, and the next March he arrived in England.
17. You can easily tell that most of this account comes from his own journals. They are written so simply and honestly that they can match any writings of that kind.

And this is a true sample of his work in Europe and America during the next thirty years, all done for the honor of his beloved Master. It also shows the steady shower of blessings that God was pleased to pour on his work!
Isn’t it a great pity that something stopped him from continuing this account, at least until close to the time when his Lord called him to enjoy the fruit of his work?
If he has left any papers like this, and his friends think I am worthy of the honor, it would be my glory and joy to organize them, copy them out, and get them ready to be published.
18. A gentleman from Boston gives this detailed account of the last part of his life: —

“He spent about a month with us in Boston and the area around it, preaching every day. Then he went to Old York and preached there on Thursday, September 27. He went on to Portsmouth and preached there on Friday.
On Saturday morning he set out for Boston. He had promised to preach at Newbury the next morning. But before he got there, people begged him to preach along the way.
The house was not big enough for all the people, so he preached in an open field.
He had been sick for several weeks, and this wore him out so much that when he reached Newbury, he could not get out of the ferry boat without two men helping him.
But in the evening he felt better again and was as cheerful as usual.
At nine o’clock he went to his room. That was his fixed bedtime, and no company could ever keep him from it. He slept better than he had for several weeks.
He got up at four in the morning on September 30 and went into his small private room. His companion noticed that he stayed alone there unusually long.
He came out of the room, went back to his companion, threw himself on the bed, and lay there about ten minutes.
Then he fell on his knees and prayed very earnestly to God. He asked that, if it was God’s will, he might finish his Master’s work that very day.
Then he asked his servant to call Mr. Parsons, the minister whose house he was staying in. But within a minute, before Mr. Parsons could get to him, he died, without a sigh or a groan.
When the news of his death came, six gentlemen set out for Newbury to bring his body back here. But his body could not be moved, so his precious remains have to stay at Newbury.
Hundreds of people would have gone from this town to his funeral, if they had not expected him to be buried here....
May God use this blow for good in His Church everywhere, and especially in this colony!”
II. 1. Second, we will take a look at his character.

Soon after his death, a short description of it was printed in the Boston Gazette. Here is part of it: — [“There is little to say about him that every friend of living Christianity who has sat under his preaching would not confirm.”]
“For many years his public work amazed the world with its eloquence and devotion.
With what heavenly feeling he urged unrepentant sinners to take up a life of godliness and goodness!

[Filled with the spirit of grace, he] spoke from the heart. His zeal was so passionate that perhaps no one has equaled it since the days of the Apostles. [He decorated the truths he preached with the most graceful beauty of fine speaking.]
In the pulpit no one could match the way he held the attention of his always-packed audience.
He was just as pleasant and helpful to talk with in private. He was wonderfully easy to approach, glad to share what he knew, and eager to build people up.
May the next generation catch a spark of that flame! It shone so brightly in the spirit and life of this faithful servant of the Most High God!”
2. One of the English newspapers has printed a fuller description of his character, and it is just as fair.
You may like it if I add the main points of this one too: —
“Every friend of true, living religion must have the character of this truly godly man [deeply] printed on their heart.

His body was weak [and delicate]. Even so, right up to the last day of his life, he kept preaching so often and so passionately that it seemed to be more than even the strongest person could naturally do.
He was called to do the work of a minister at an age when most young men are only starting to train for it. So he did not have time to get very far in learning the ancient languages.
But he more than made up for this with a lively and creative mind, with burning zeal, and with a powerful and very persuasive way of speaking.
In the pulpit he often found he had to “persuade people” by speaking of “the terror of the Lord.” Yet there was nothing gloomy about him. He was unusually cheerful, and also generous and kindhearted.
He was just as ready to help with people’s physical needs as with their spiritual needs when they came to him.
It should also be noted that he always urged his listeners to do every moral duty. He especially urged them to work hard at their jobs and to obey those in charge of them.

He worked incredibly hard at preaching in many different places, even in open fields. He did this to wake up the poorer people from the deepest carelessness and ignorance, so that they would begin to take religion seriously.
Because of this, and his other work, the name of GEORGE WHITEFIELD will be remembered with respect and honor for a long time.”
3. Everyone will readily agree that both of these accounts are true and fair—as far as they go.
But they hardly go beyond the outside of his character.
They show you the preacher. But they do not show you the man, the Christian, the saint of God.
May I add a little about this? I knew him personally for nearly forty years.
I know very well how hard it is to speak about such a delicate subject. It takes great wisdom to avoid both extremes and to say neither too little nor too much!
In fact, I know it is impossible to say anything at all—whether less or more—without some people blaming me for saying too little, and others for saying too much.
Some will honestly think I have said too little, and others that I have said too much.
But I will not let that worry me. I will say just what I know, in the presence of the One to whom we all must give an account.

4. We have already mentioned his zeal, which no one could match. We have mentioned how he never tired of working, how tender he was toward people who were suffering, and how generous he was to the poor.
But shouldn’t we also mention how deeply thankful he was to everyone God had used to do him good? He never stopped speaking about them with the greatest respect, right up to the day he died.
Shouldn’t we mention that his heart was open to the most generous and tender friendship?
I have often thought that this, more than anything else, was what made his character stand out.
How few people we have known with such a kind nature, with such big and overflowing love!
Wasn’t this the main reason why other people’s hearts were so wonderfully drawn to him and joined to his?
Can anything except love produce love?
This love shone in his very face. It breathed through all his words all the time, whether in public or in private.
Wasn’t it this love that flew from heart to heart, as fast and piercing as lightning? Wasn’t it this that gave such life to his sermons, his conversations, and his letters?
You yourselves are witnesses!
5. But away with the ugly twisting of this by people with dirty minds, who know no love except the earthly, physical kind!
At the same time, remember that he had the purest and most spotless modesty.
His work as a minister meant that he often had long talks with women as well as men, of every age and situation in life.
But the way he acted toward them was a living example of St. Paul’s advice to Timothy: “Appeal to the older women as mothers, and to the younger women as sisters, in all purity.”
6. His friendly spirit also fit well with how open and honest he was when he talked with people! And yet he was never rude on the one hand, and never sneaky [or pretending] on the other.
Wasn’t this openness both a result of his courage and fearlessness, and a proof of it?

With these as his armor, he was not afraid of anyone. He “spoke very plainly” to people of every rank and situation, high and low, rich and poor. His only goal was, “by making the truth clear, to win a place in every person’s conscience in the sight of God.”
7. He was not afraid of hard work or pain, any more than he was afraid of “what people [could] do to him.” He was just as

blocks.x: Patient in putting up with trouble as in doing good.

s: You could see this in how steadily he kept at whatever he took on for his Master’s sake.
Take just one example: the orphanage in Georgia. He started it and finished it, even though everything seemed to be against him.
In things that only concerned himself, he was easygoing and flexible.
In those cases he was “easy to reason with.” It was easy to convince him or to persuade him.
But in the things of God, or wherever his conscience was involved, no one could move him.
No one could talk him into changing even the smallest point, and no one could scare him into it either. His integrity was part of his whole character, and it guided everything he said and did.
In this he truly did

blocks.x:
Stand like a strong iron pillar,
And firm as a wall of bronze.

s: 8. Someone may ask what the foundation was for this integrity, or for his sincerity, courage, patience, and all his other good and lovely qualities. The answer is easy.

It was not that he was born with a good nature. It was not his great intelligence. It was not the power of his education. No, and it was not the advice of his friends. It was nothing else but faith in a Lord who bled for him, “faith that God Himself works in us.”
It was “a living hope of an inheritance that will never rot, never be stained, and never fade.”
It was “the love of God spread through his heart by the Holy Spirit, who was given to him.” That love filled his soul with tender, unselfish love for every human being.

This was the source of that flood of eloquence that often swept away everything in its path. This was the source of that amazing power to persuade, which even the most hardened sinners could not resist.
This was what often made him weep as if his “head were full of water, and his eyes a fountain of tears.”
This was what helped him pour out his soul in prayer in his own special way. His prayers were full and flowing at the same time, with such strength and variety in both thoughts and words.

9. I will finish this point by showing the great honor God gave His faithful servant. God let him announce His everlasting good news in so many different countries, to so many people, and with such a great effect on so many of their precious souls!
Since the time of the Apostles, have we ever read or heard of anyone who spread the good news of God’s grace over such a wide area, through so much of the inhabited world?
Have we ever read or heard of anyone who called so many thousands, even tens of thousands, of sinners to repent?
Above all, have we read or heard of anyone God has used so wonderfully to bring so many sinners “from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God”?
It is true that if we talked this way to people who live for pleasure, they would think we were speaking a foreign language.
But you understand the language of the country you are traveling to, where our dear friend has gone a little ahead of us.
III. But how can we gain something good from this solemn event that God has sent?
This is the third thing we need to think about.
The answer to this important question is easy. (May God write it in all our hearts!)
We do it by holding tightly to the great teachings he preached, and by soaking up his spirit.
1. So first, let us hold tightly to the great Bible teachings that he preached everywhere.
There are many teachings that are less essential. On these, even sincere children of God have disagreed for many centuries, and they still do. That is how weak human understanding is right now.
On these points we can think for ourselves and let others think for themselves. We can “agree to disagree.”

But at the same time, let us hold on firmly to the essentials of “the faith that was once handed down to the saints.” This champion of God insisted so strongly on these, at all times and in all places!
2. His most basic point was: “Give God all the credit for whatever is good in people.” And: “When it comes to salvation, lift Christ up as high as possible, and put people as low as possible.”
He and his friends at Oxford, the first people called Methodists, started out with this point.
Their great principle was this: by nature people have no power of their own, and nothing in them earns God’s favor.

They insisted that all the power to think, speak, or act rightly is in the Spirit of Christ and comes from Him. And everything that earns God’s favor is found only in the blood of Christ—not in people, no matter how far they have grown in grace.
That is what he and they taught. People have no power, until it is given to them from above, to do one good deed, to speak one good word, or even to have one good desire.
It is not enough to say that everyone is sick with sin. No, we are all “dead in our wrongdoing and sins.”
So it follows that all human beings are “by nature children under God’s anger.”
We are all “guilty before God,” and we deserve to die, both in this life and forever.
3. And we are all helpless, both against the power of sin and against its guilt.
“For who can make something clean out of something unclean?”
No one but the Almighty.
Who can raise people who are dead—spiritually dead in sin?
No one but the One who raised us up from the dust of the earth.
But why would He do this?
“Not on account of any right things we have done.”
