“The dead cannot praise You, O Lord.” And they cannot do anything to earn being brought back to life.
So whatever God does, He does only for the sake of His dearly loved Son. “He was wounded because of our rebellion. He was bruised because of our evil.”
He Himself “bore” all “our sins in His own body on the wooden cross.”
He “was given up for our wrongs, and was raised again so that we could be declared right with God.”
So here is the only thing that earns every blessing we have or ever can have. This is especially true of our forgiveness, of God accepting us, and of our being fully and freely made right with Him.
But how do we come to have a share in what Christ has done and suffered?
“Not by our own deeds, so that nobody can brag.” We receive it by faith alone.
“We conclude,” says the Apostle, “that a person is made right with God by faith, without doing the works the law requires.”
And “to all who” in this way “receive Him, He gives the power to become sons of God—to those who believe in His name. They are born, not because a human being wanted it, but because of God.”
4. And “unless a person is” born again in this way, “he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
But everyone who is “born of the Spirit” in this way has “the kingdom of God inside them.”
Christ sets up His kingdom in their hearts: “right living, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.”
They have in them “the same mind that was in Christ Jesus.” This makes them able to “walk just as Christ walked.”
His Spirit, living in them, makes them holy in their hearts and also “holy in every part of their lives.”
But all of this is still a free gift, given because of Christ’s goodness and His blood. So there is always the same reason to remember: “Anyone who brags should brag about the Lord.”
5. You know very well that these are the basic teachings he insisted on everywhere.
And can’t they be summed up in two phrases: the new birth, and being made right with God by faith?
Let us insist on these teachings boldly, at all times and in all places. Those of us who are called to it should do so in public, and we should all do so in private whenever we get the chance.
Hold on tight to these good, old, unfashionable teachings, no matter how many people argue against them and insult them.
Keep going, my brothers and sisters, “in the name of the Lord, and in the power of His strength.”
Carefully and faithfully “keep safe what has been put in your care.” Know that “heaven and earth will pass away, but this truth will never pass away.”
6. But is it enough to hold tightly to his teachings, however pure they are?
Isn’t there something even more important than this? Isn’t it to soak up his spirit—to follow him in this, just as he followed Christ?
Without this, pure teaching would only make our judgment worse.
So this is the main thing: to copy his spirit.
We have to admit that in some ways we can only admire what we cannot copy. But in many other ways we can share in the same blessing, through the same free grace.

So remember how much you lack and how generous His love is. He “gives freely and does not scold.” Cry out to Him, the One who does everything in everyone, for some of the same precious faith, the same zeal and energy, the same tender heart, generosity, and deep, heartfelt mercy.
Wrestle with God in prayer for some of the same thankful, friendly, loving nature, the same openness, simplicity, and godly sincerity, and “love that does not pretend.”
Keep wrestling until the power from on high produces in you the same steady courage and patience. And above all, ask for the same unchanging integrity, because that is the crown of everything!
7. Was there any other fruit of God’s grace that he had in a special way? Was there something that he often and passionately grieved to see missing among God’s children?

Yes, there is one: catholic love. That is the sincere and tender love we owe to everyone we have reason to believe is a child of God by faith. In other words, it is love for everyone, in every church group, who “fears God and does right.”
He longed to see everyone who had “had a taste of God’s good word” have a truly catholic spirit. Many people often say that word, but few understand it, and even fewer have experienced it.
Who fits this description?
Who is the person with a catholic spirit?

It is someone who loves all who believe in the Lord Jesus, no matter what their opinions, their way of worship, or their church. He loves them as friends, as brothers and sisters in the Lord, as people who share with him in the kingdom of heaven now, and as fellow heirs of God’s eternal kingdom. He loves all who love God and people, who are glad to please God and afraid to offend Him, who are careful to stay away from evil, and who are eager to do good.

A person with a truly catholic spirit keeps all these people on his heart all the time. He cares for them more tenderly than words can say, and he truly wants what is best for them. So he never stops praying to God for them, and he also stands up for them in front of others. He speaks words of comfort to them, and with everything he says he works to make them stronger in God.
He helps them as much as he possibly can in everything, both spiritual and practical. He is ready to “spend and be spent” for them. Yes, he is ready “to lay down his life for his brothers.”
8. What a lovely character this is!
Every child of God should long for it!
So why is it so rarely found?
Why are there so few examples of it?
If we really have tasted God’s love, how can any of us rest until we have this love too?
Well, Satan has a clever trick. With it he convinces thousands of people that they can stop short of this love and still not be guilty.
I fear that many people here may be caught in this “snare of the devil,” where he has trapped them to do as he pleases.
“Oh yes,” someone says, “I have all this love for the people I believe are God’s children. But I will never believe that anyone who belongs to that awful church is a child of God!
Do you really think someone who holds such terrible opinions could be a child of God? Or someone who joins in such foolish and superstitious worship—maybe even idol worship?”
So we try to excuse one sin by adding a second one to it!
We excuse our own lack of love by blaming other people!
To cover up our own devilish attitude, we declare that our brothers and sisters are children of the devil!
Oh, watch out for this! And if you are already caught in this trap, get out of it as fast as you can!

Go and learn that truly catholic love that “is not reckless” or quick to judge. It is the love that “does not think evil,” that “believes and hopes all things.” It is the love that makes all the allowances for others that we want others to make for us!

Then we will recognize the grace of God in every person, whatever their opinion or way of worship. Then everyone who fears God will be close and dear to us, “with the deep, heartfelt love of Jesus Christ.”
9. Wasn’t this the spirit of our dear friend?
So why shouldn’t it be ours too?
O God of love, how long will Your people be a joke among unbelievers?
How long will they laugh at us and say, “Look how these Christians love one another!”
When will You take away our shame?
Will the sword go on destroying forever?
How long will it be before You tell Your people to turn back from “chasing after each other”?
Now, at least, “let all the people stop, and chase their brothers no more!”
But whatever other people do, my brothers and sisters, let all of us listen to the voice of this man who, though he is dead, still speaks!
Imagine that you hear him say, “Now, at least, follow my example, as I followed Christ!
Let brother “never again raise a sword against brother, and never learn war anymore!”
Instead, as God’s chosen people, put on hearts full of mercy, humble minds, brotherly kindness, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another in love.
You have spent enough time already on fighting, jealousy, and arguing, and on biting and tearing each other apart.
Praise God that you have not destroyed each other long ago!
From now on, hold on to the oneness that the Spirit gives, tied together with peace.”
10. O God, nothing is impossible for You!
You do whatever You please!
Oh, how we wish You would make the cloak of Your prophet, whom You have taken up to Yourself, fall on us who are left behind!
“Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?”
Let his spirit rest on these servants of Yours!
Show that You are the God who answers by sending fire!
Let the fire of Your love fall on every heart!
And because we love You, help us love one another with a “love that is stronger than death!”
Take away from us “all anger, rage, and bitterness, all shouting and hurtful talk!”
Let Your Spirit rest on us so that from this moment on we may be “kind to one another, gentle-hearted, forgiving each other, in the same way that God has forgiven us for Christ’s sake!”

blocks.x: A Hymn

1 Well done, servant of God!
Your great fight is over now;
The battle is fought, the race is won,
And you are crowned at last.
Everything your heart longed for
Is yours now in triumph;
The ministering choir has placed you
Close to your Redeemer’s heart.

2 In love that stooped down low,
He heard your constant prayer;
He called you to leave suddenly
For your full reward.
Your beautiful feet had shoes on,
Ready to bring the news of peace,
When mercy signed your soul’s release
And took you up to God.

3 With saints on thrones up high,
You now praise your Lord,
And still you cry, “Salvation to God!
Salvation to the Lamb!”
O happy, happy soul!
Filled with the joy of praise,
As long as endless ages roll,
You see your Savior’s face!

4 Set free from earth and pain,
Oh, when will we rise up
And all reign where Jesus is
With our friend who was taken up?
Come, Lord, come quickly!
And when we are made complete in You,
Bring Your longing servants home
To celebrate in triumph at Your feet!

s: “If I speak in the languages of people and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like a booming piece of brass or a jingling cymbal.
And if I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I can move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing.
And if I give away everything I own to feed the poor, and give my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it does me no good at all.”
1 Corinthians 13:1–3.
We know that “all Scripture is given by God’s inspiration.” So it is true and right about everything.
But we also know that some parts of Scripture speak more directly to everyone’s conscience.
The passage in front of us belongs to this group. Hardly anyone objects to it.
In fact, most people are very quick to appeal to it.
It is very common to find people who deny the authority of the Holy Scriptures, but still say, “This is my religion: what is described in the thirteenth chapter of Corinthians.”
Even a Jewish man, Dr. Nunes, a Spanish doctor who had settled at Savannah in Georgia, used to say very earnestly, “Paul of Tarsus was one of the finest writers I have ever read.
I wish the thirteenth chapter of his first letter to the Corinthians were written in letters of gold.
And I wish every Jew would carry it with him wherever he went.”
He believed that this one chapter contained the whole of true religion. And he was certainly right about that.
It contains “whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely. If there is any virtue, if there is anything worth praising,” it is all contained in this.
To see this as clearly as possible, we can consider the following:
I. What the charity spoken of here is.
II. What things people usually put in its place.
Then we can,
III. Show that none of these things, not even all of them together, can make up for not having it.
I. 1. First, we need to consider what this charity is.
What is it like, and what are its qualities?
The word Paul uses is agape. It means exactly the same as the plain English word love.
That is why all the old translations of the Bible used the word love.
This is how it read in William Tyndale’s Bible. I believe that was the first English translation of the whole Bible.
It was the same in the Bible published by the authority of King Henry VIII.

It was also the same in all the editions of the Bible published in England, one after another, during the reigns of King Edward VI, Queen Elizabeth, and King James I. In fact, you can find it in the Bibles printed while King Charles I reigned. I believe this was so right up to the end of his reign.

The first Bibles I have seen where the word was changed were printed in 1649 by Roger Daniel and John Field, the printers for Parliament. So it seems likely that the change was made while the Long Parliament was meeting. That is probably when the Latin word charity replaced the English word love.

It was a sad day when this change was made. Its bad effects are still with us today. You can see them among poor people and people who cannot read: thousands of ordinary men and women understand the word charity no better than they understand the original Greek. But the same terrible mistake has also spread among educated and learned people.

Thousands of them are misled by it. They imagine that the charity this chapter talks about is mainly, or even only, about outward actions. They think it means little more than giving money to the poor!
I have heard many sermons preached on this chapter, especially before the University of Oxford.
And I only ever heard one in which its meaning was not completely misrepresented.
But if the old and proper word love had been kept, no one could have misrepresented it.
2. But what kind of love is the apostle talking about all through this chapter?
Many people who are very learned and godly believe it is love for God.
But I have read the whole chapter countless times and looked at it from every angle. And I am fully convinced that Paul is speaking here directly about love for our neighbour.
I believe anyone who carefully considers the whole flow of what he says will be fully convinced of this.
But we must admit that it is a kind of love for our neighbour that can only come from love for God.

And where does this love for God come from? It comes only from the faith that is God’s own work. Whoever has this faith has direct evidence that God was in Christ, bringing the world back into friendship with himself.

Suppose this is applied personally to his heart, so that he can say with humble boldness: The life I now live, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. Then, and not until then, the love of God is poured out in his heart.

And this love sweetly compels him to love every human being with the love spoken of here. This is not a love of admiration or of approval. That kind of love has no place toward those who are enemies of God and of their own souls, even if they are not his personal enemies. No, it is a love of goodwill—a tender goodwill toward every soul that God has made.

3. But someone may ask: “Suppose there is no true love for our neighbour except the love that comes from loving God. And suppose love for God comes from no other source than faith in the Son of God. Doesn’t that mean the whole heathen world has no possible way to be saved?
After all, they are cut off from faith. For faith comes by hearing, and how can they hear without a preacher?”
I answer that Paul’s words, spoken about a different matter, apply here too: “What the law says, it says to those who are under the law.”

In the same way, the sentence “Whoever does not believe will be damned” is spoken about those who have had the Gospel preached to them. It does not concern anyone else. And we are not asked to decide anything about their final state.
We can leave it to God himself to decide how he, the Judge of all, will deal with them.

But this much we know. He is not only the God of Christians; he is also the God of the heathen. He is “rich in mercy to all who call on him,” according to the light they have. And “in every nation, whoever fears God and does what is right is accepted by him.”
4. But let’s get back to the subject.
This is the nature of the love the apostle is talking about here.
But what are its qualities? What fruits always go together with it?
The apostle lists many of them. But these are the main ones.
First: “Love is not puffed up.”
However much love we have, that is how much humility we have.

Nothing humbles the soul as deeply as love does. It drives out all “high opinions of ourselves that breed pride.” It drives out all arrogance and conceit. It makes us small and poor and lowly and worthless in our own eyes.

It humbles us before God and before people. It makes us willing to be the least of all and the servant of all. And it teaches us to say, “A speck of dust in a sunbeam is small, but in the presence of God I am infinitely smaller.”
5. Second: “Love is not provoked.” Our present English translation says, “is not easily provoked.”
But where did the word easily come from?
There is not a trace of it in the text. The apostle’s words are simply these: ou paraxynetai.
Isn’t it likely that the translators added it to excuse Paul? Perhaps they were afraid that what he did would seem to contradict what he taught.

For we read in Acts 15:36 and the verses after it: “Some days later Paul said to Barnabas, Let’s go back and visit our brothers in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they are doing.
Barnabas decided to take John, who was also called Mark, with them.
But Paul did not think it was a good idea to take someone who had left the work.
The quarrel between them was so sharp that they parted from each other. Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus. Paul chose Silas and left, and the brothers entrusted him to the grace of God.
And he traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.”
6. When you read these words, wouldn’t you think they were both equally sharp?
Wouldn’t you think Paul was just as heated as Barnabas, and just as lacking in love?
But the text says no such thing. This becomes clear if we first look at what led to it.
When Paul suggested that they should “go back and visit the brothers in every city where they had preached the word,” they were in agreement so far.
“Barnabas decided to take John with them,” because John was his sister’s son. He did this without asking for Paul’s advice or getting it.
“But Paul did not think it was right to take him along, since he had left them in Pamphylia”—whether out of laziness or cowardice—“and had not gone on with them to the work.”
And Paul was surely right. Reason was on his side.
The next words are egento oun paroxysmos. Literally they mean, “and there was a fit of anger.”
It does not say that this anger was in Paul. Probably it was in Barnabas alone. He made up for his lack of reason with passion, “so that they separated from each other.”
Barnabas was determined to have his own way. So he did what his nephew had done before: he “left the work,” “took Mark with him, and sailed to Cyprus.”
But Paul carried on with his work, “entrusted by the brothers to the grace of God.” Barnabas does not seem to have waited for that.
“And he traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.”
From the whole story, it does not seem that Paul did anything wrong. He did not have any feeling, or say any word, that went against the law of love.
So since he did nothing wrong, he does not need any excuse.
7. Certainly, someone who is full of love is “gentle toward everyone.”

He “gently teaches those who oppose him.” They oppose what he loves most—the truth of God, or the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. For who knows? “Perhaps God will bring them to know the truth.”
No matter how much he is provoked, he does “not pay back evil for evil, or insult for insult.”
Yes, he “blesses those who curse him, and does good to those who treat him cruelly and persecute him.”
He “is not overcome by evil, but” always “overcomes evil with good.”
8. Third: “Love suffers long.”
It puts up with more than a few insults, criticisms, and wrongs. It puts up with everything that God allows people or devils to do to it.

It arms the soul with a patience that cannot be broken. This is not the hard patience of the Stoics. It is a patience that gives way like the air. The air does not resist a blow, so it is not harmed by it.
The person who loves all people remembers the One who suffered for us, “leaving us an example, so that we might walk in his steps.”
So, “if his enemy is hungry, he feeds him; if he is thirsty, he gives him something to drink.” By doing this, he “heaps burning coals” of melting love on his head.
“Many waters cannot put out this love, and the floods” of ingratitude “cannot drown it.”
II. 1. Second, we need to ask what things people commonly think can take the place of love.
The first of these is eloquence. This is the ability to speak well, especially about religious subjects.
People usually tend to think well of someone who speaks well.
If he speaks about God and the things of God properly and fluently, who could doubt that God is pleased with him?
And it is very natural for him to think well of himself too, and to have as high an opinion of himself as others have.

2. But thoughtful people are not satisfied with this. A flood of words is not enough for them. They value thinking more than talking. They believe that someone who knows a lot is far better than someone who talks a lot.
And knowledge certainly is an excellent gift from God. This is especially true of knowing the Holy Scriptures, which contain all the depths of divine knowledge and wisdom.
So people generally think that a person with a lot of knowledge, especially knowledge of Scripture, must not only have God’s favour but must have a large share of it.
3. But people who think even more deeply often say, “I don’t put any weight on any knowledge except knowing God by faith.
Faith is the only knowledge that is of great value in God’s sight.
‘We are saved by faith’—by faith alone. This is the one thing we need.
Whoever believes, and only that person, will be saved forever.”
There is a lot of truth in this. It is certainly true that “we are saved by faith.” So it is also true that “whoever believes will be saved, and whoever does not believe will be damned.”
4. But some people will say with the apostle James, “Show me your faith without your works” (if you can—but really it is impossible), “and I will show you my faith by my works.”
And many are led to think that good works—works of devotion and of mercy—matter far more than faith itself. They think good works will make up for anything else a person lacks to be ready for heaven.

In fact, this seems to be what most people believe. Not only members of the Church of Rome think this, but Protestants too. And not just careless, thoughtless people, but serious members of our own Church.
5. And no one can deny this. Our Lord himself said, “You will know them by their fruits.” By their works you can tell those who believe from those who do not.

But we may still ask whether there is a surer proof that our faith is sincere than even our works. That proof is being willing to suffer for doing what is right. This is especially true if a person suffers insults and pain and the loss of friends and possessions, and then gives up life itself. He might even die a shameful and painful death, giving his body to be burned, rather than give up his faith and a good conscience by neglecting a duty he knows he has.

6. At this point we should notice, first, what a beautiful ladder this is, with each step rising above the last. It is the list of things that various people called Christians—and usually thought of as Christians—really believe can make up for not having love.
Paul begins at the lowest point, speaking well. Then he moves up step by step, each one higher than the one before, until he reaches the highest of all.
One step above eloquence is knowledge. Faith is one step above that.
Good works are one step above that faith. And even above good works is suffering for doing what is right.
Nothing is higher than this except Christian love—love for our neighbour that flows from love for God.

7. Second, we should notice something else. Whatever passes for religion anywhere in the Christian world can very easily be placed under one or another of these headings. That is true whether it really is part of religion or no part of it at all—just foolishness, superstition, or wickedness.
Protestants and Roman Catholics may think something is religion when it is not. Every such thing fits under one or another of these five points.
Test this as often as you like with anything that is wrongly called religion. You will find that the rule holds with no exceptions.

III. 1. Now, third, I want to prove something to everyone who has ears to hear and who does not harden himself against being convinced. None of these five things, and not even all of them together, will be worth anything before God without the love described above.
To do this as clearly as possible, we can look at them one at a time.

First: “If I speak in the languages of people and of angels.” Suppose I speak about the nature, qualities, and works of God, in creation or in providence, with an eloquence that no human has ever had. Suppose I am not the least bit behind the greatest apostles, preaching like Peter and praying like John. Even so, unless humble, gentle, patient love rules my soul, I am no better in God’s judgment “than a booming piece of brass or a rumbling cymbal.”

So the greatest eloquence, whether in private conversation or in public ministry—the most brilliant gifts for preaching or prayer—might sink me deeper into hell if they were not joined with a humble, gentle, and patient acceptance of God’s will. But they will not bring me one step closer to heaven.
2. A simple example may show this.

Between fifty and sixty years ago I knew a young man who, for several years, never tried to convince anyone of a religious truth without that person being convinced. And he never tried to persuade anyone to take up a religious practice without that person being persuaded. So what?

All that power to convince, all that force of persuasion, would not make him any more fit to enjoy God than a clear voice or a good complexion would—if it was not joined with gentleness and humility, with acceptance of God’s will and patient love.
In fact, it would rather earn him a hotter place in the everlasting flames!

3. Second: “If I have the gift of prophecy”—the gift of foretelling future events that no creature can foresee—and “if I understand all” the “mysteries” of nature, of providence, and of God’s word, and “have all knowledge” of things divine or human that any human being has ever reached. Suppose I can explain the most mysterious passages of Daniel, Ezekiel, and Revelation. Even so, if I do not have humility, gentleness, and acceptance of God’s will, “I am nothing” in God’s sight.
A little before the end of the recent war in Flanders, someone who came from there told us a very strange story.
I did not know what to make of it. So I waited until John Haime came back. I could no more doubt his honesty than his good sense.
This is what he told us: “Jonathan Pyrah was a member of our Society in Flanders.
I knew him for several years, and I knew that no one could find fault with his character.
One day he was ordered to appear before the Board of General Officers.
One of them said, ‘What is this we are hearing about you?
We hear that you have become a prophet. We hear you are predicting the fall of the bloody house of Bourbon and the proud house of Austria.
We would be glad if you were a real prophet and your prophecies came true.
But what sign will you give us to convince us that you are a prophet and that your predictions will happen?’
He answered at once, ‘Gentlemen, I will give you a sign. Tomorrow at twelve o’clock you will have a storm with more thunder and lightning than you have ever had since you came to Flanders.
I will give you a second sign. None of you expects anything like this, and there is no sign of it now. But within three days you will fight a full battle with the French.
I will give you a third sign. I will be ordered to advance in the front line.
If I am a false prophet, I will be shot dead in the first volley. But if I am a true prophet, I will only be hit by a musket ball in the calf of my left leg.’
At twelve o’clock the next day there was thunder and lightning like nothing they had ever had before in Flanders.
On the third day, against everyone’s expectations, the great battle of Fontenoy took place.
He was ordered to advance in the front line. And in the very first volley, he was indeed hit by a musket ball in the calf of his left leg.”
4. And yet none of this did him any good, either for happiness in this life or for eternal happiness.

When the war was over, he came back to England. But the story had got there before him. Because of this, the Countess of St—s and several other people of high rank sent for him. They wanted to hear such an amazing story from his own mouth.
He could not handle so much honour.
It completely turned his head.
Before long he went completely mad.
And he is still like that today. As far as I know, he is still living at Wibsey Moorside, a few miles from Leeds.
[This was so when this sermon was written.
He has since died.]
5. And what good would it do a person to “have all knowledge”—even the knowledge that is infinitely better than all other knowledge, the knowledge of the Holy Scripture?

About twenty years ago I knew a young man who knew the Bible extremely well. If someone asked him about any Hebrew word in the Old Testament or any Greek word in the New Testament, he would pause a moment. Then he would tell not only how often that word appeared in the Bible, but also what it meant in each place.
His name was Thomas Walsh.
[His journal, which he wrote himself, still exists.]
I had never seen such a master of Bible knowledge before, and I never expect to see one again.

But suppose that, with all his knowledge, he had no love. Suppose he had been proud, hot-tempered, or impatient. Then he and all his knowledge would have perished together, as surely as he was ever born.

6. “And if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains.” Faith that can do this cannot come from empty imagination. It is not just a madman’s dream or a set of opinions. It must be a real work of God. Otherwise it could not have such an effect.
But if this faith does not work through love—if it does not produce holiness in every part of life, if it does not bring humility, gentleness, and acceptance of God’s will—it will do me no good.
This is as certain as any truth in all of God’s word.

Any faith that now exists, ever existed, or ever can exist, is not Christian faith if it is separated from tender goodwill toward every human being—friend or enemy, Christian, Jew, heretic, or pagan. It is not Christian faith if it is separated from gentleness toward all people, from acceptance of whatever happens, and from contentment in every situation. Such faith will be of no use to us when we stand before God.
7. Listen to this, all of you who are called Methodists!
This concerns you more than anyone else alive.
You always talk about salvation by faith. And you are right to do so.
All of you, every one, hold that a person is justified by faith, without the works of the law.
And you cannot do anything else without giving up the Bible and betraying your own souls.
You insist that we are saved by faith. And we certainly are.

But at the same time, remember this. No matter how much faith we have, and no matter how strong it is, it will never save us from hell unless it saves us now from every unholy attitude. It must save us from pride, hot temper, and impatience; from all arrogance, all haughtiness and bossiness; from rage, anger, and bitterness; from discontent, grumbling, fretting, and irritability.

We have been warned so often against that powerful delusion. So we would have less excuse than anyone if we still give in to any of these attitudes, and at the same time congratulate ourselves and dream that we are on the way to heaven!

8. Fourth: “If I give all my goods to the poor.” Suppose I divide all my land and all my belongings into small portions (that is what the original word properly means). Suppose I carefully give them to the people I have good reason to believe most deserve them. Even so, if I am proud, hot-tempered, or discontented—if I give in to any of these attitudes—then whatever good I may do for others, I do none for my own soul.
Oh, how sad this is!
Who would not grieve that these generous people should lose all their work!
It is true that many of them get a reward in this world—if not before their death, then after it.
They have expensive and grand funerals.
They have marble monuments made with the finest craftsmanship.
They have epitaphs written in the most elegant style, praising their virtues to the skies.
Perhaps speeches are given over them every year, to pass their memory on to every generation.
Many founders of religious houses, colleges, almshouses, and most charitable institutions have all this too.
And it is an accepted rule that no one can praise the founder of his house, college, or hospital too much.
But even so, what a poor reward this is!
Suppose they are in the hands of the devil and his angels—which must be the case if they did not die in faith. Will all this add to their comfort or to their misery?
What insults, what cutting scorn, it would bring them from their companions in hell!

Oh, if only they were wise! If only all who are eager to do good works would put those works in their proper place! They should not imagine that good works can make up for a lack of holy attitudes. Instead they should make sure that their works grow out of those attitudes.
9. How very strange this must sound to most of the people whom English politeness calls Christians!
But even stranger is the apostle’s last statement: “If I give my body to be burned, and do not have love, it does me no good.”

Suppose I willingly accept a cruel death—“hand over my body to be burned”—rather than deny the faith, commit a known sin, or neglect a known duty. Even so, if pride or anger or fretfulness has power over me, “it does me no good.”
10. Perhaps an example will help show this.
There is a remarkable story in the writings of Dr. Geddes. He was an expert in civil law and served as Queen Anne’s envoy to the Court of Portugal near the end of her reign.
He was present at one of those Autos de Fé, or “Acts of Faith,” where the Roman Inquisitors burned heretics alive.
One of the people brought out to be executed had been locked in the dungeons of the Inquisition. He had not seen the sun for many years.
It turned out to be a bright, sunny day.
He looked up and cried out in surprise, “Oh, how can anyone who sees that glorious light worship anyone but the God who made it!”
A friar standing nearby ordered them to push an iron gag through his lips so that he could not speak any more.
Now, what did that poor man feel inside when this order was carried out?

He could not say anything with his lips. But suppose he said in his heart, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.” Then the angels of God were certainly ready to carry his soul to Abraham’s side.
But suppose instead he held on to resentment in his heart that he could not express with his tongue. Then, even though his body was burned up in the flames, I will not say his soul went to paradise.

11. Here is the sum of all we have seen. Whatever I say, whatever I know, whatever I believe, whatever I do, whatever I suffer—if I do not have the faith that works through love, the faith that produces love for God and for all people, then I am not on the narrow road that leads to life. I am on the broad road that leads to destruction.

In other words: whatever eloquence I have; whatever natural or supernatural knowledge; whatever faith I have received from God; whatever works I do, whether of devotion or of mercy; whatever I suffer for conscience’ sake, even if I resist to the point of shedding blood—all these things together, however much people praise them, will be worth nothing before God. They are worth nothing unless I am gentle and humble in heart, and can say in everything, “Not what I want, but what you want!”
12. From all this we conclude—and this can never be stressed too much, because the whole world votes the other way—that true religion, at its very heart, is nothing less than holy attitudes.
So all other religion, whatever name it has—pagan, Muslim, Jewish, or Christian; Roman Catholic or Protestant; Lutheran or Reformed—is lighter than emptiness itself without these.
13. So everyone who has a soul to be saved must make sure of this one thing.
Along with all his eloquence, knowledge, faith, works, and sufferings, he must hold on to this “one thing that is needed.”

Whoever, through the power of faith, endures to the end in humble, gentle, patient love—that person, and that person alone, will, through the merits of Christ, “inherit the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world.”
“You adulterers, both men and women! Don’t you know that friendship with this world is hostility toward God?
So whoever wants to be a friend of the world is an enemy of God.” James 4:4.

1. In Paul’s letter to the Romans there is a passage that people have often thought means the same as this one: “Do not shape yourselves to fit this world” (Romans 12:2). But it has little or nothing to do with it. It speaks about something quite different.
In fact, people only think the two are alike because the word “world” is used in both places.

This naturally makes us think that Paul means by “fitting in with the world” the same thing James means by “friendship with the world.” But they are completely different things. In the original text the words are quite different too: Paul’s word is aion, and James’s word is kosmos.
Still, Paul’s words give God’s children an important direction.
It is as if he had said, “Do not shape yourselves to fit the wisdom, the spirit, or the fashions of your age. Do not copy either the unconverted Jews or the pagans you live among.

You are called to show by the whole direction of your life and conduct that you are ‘made new in the spirit of your mind,’ in the image of the One who created you. Show that your rule is not what people do or want, but ‘the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God.’”
2. But it is not surprising that James’s warning against friendship with the world is so poorly understood, even among Christians.
For as far as I can find, no writer, old or new, has written about this subject. No, not in sixteen or seventeen hundred years (as far as I have ever noticed).

Even that excellent writer Mr. Law, who has dealt so well with many other subjects, has not written one chapter on it in all his practical books. No, as far as I remember, he has not said one word about it or given one warning against it.
I have never heard one sermon preached on it, either before the University or anywhere else.
I have never been with any group of people where the conversation turned directly to this subject, even for one hour.

3. Yet there are very few subjects so deeply important. Few subjects touch so closely on the very heart of religion: the life of God in the soul. They concern whether that life continues and grows, or decays and even dies out.
Because people have not been taught about this, very sad results have followed.
These results have not affected people who were still dead in their wrongdoings and sins. But they have fallen heavily on many who were truly alive to God.
In particular, they have affected many of the people called Methodists—perhaps more than any other group.

Many of them did not understand the apostle’s advice (I hope that was the reason, rather than that they looked down on it). So many among them are sick—spiritually sick. And many who were once fully awake are now asleep.
It will be good if they ever wake up again before God demands their souls from them.

I have found it hard to explain something I have often seen. Many people were once very much alive to God. Their way of life was in heaven. Their hearts were set on things above, not on earthly things. They faithfully used all the ordinances of God. They were still full of good works. They stayed away from every known sin, and even from anything that looked like evil. And yet they slowly wasted away without noticing it, like Jonah’s plant when the worm ate its root. So now they are less alive to God than they were ten, twenty, or thirty years ago.
But it is easy to explain if we notice this: as they gained more possessions, they also grew in friendship with the world. And this must always happen, unless God’s mighty power steps in.
But as much as they grew in this friendship, the life of God in their souls shrank by the same amount.

4. Is it surprising that it shrank, if these words really are found in the very words of God: “You adulterers, both men and women! Don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?”
What do these words mean?
Let us think about it seriously.
And may God open the eyes of our understanding! In spite of all the fog that the wisdom of the world would wrap around us, may we see clearly what God’s good and acceptable will is!
5. First, let us think about what the apostle means here by “the world.”
He is not talking here about the outward frame of things, which the Bible calls heaven and earth. He means the people who live on the earth—the children of men—or at least the larger part of them.
But which part? Our Lord himself and his beloved disciple both answer this fully.
First, our Lord himself.
He says, “If the world hates you, you know that it hated me before it hated you.
If you belonged to the world, the world would love you as its own. But you do not belong to the world. I have chosen you out of the world. That is why the world hates you.
If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you too.
They will do all these things to you because they do not know the One who sent me.”
(John 15:18.) You see that here “the world” is placed on one side. On the other side are those who “are not of the world.”
Some people God has “chosen out of the world,” namely by “the Spirit making them holy and by their believing the truth.” These are set directly against those whom he has not chosen in this way.
And again, our Lord says that those “who do not know the One who sent me”—those who do not know God—are “the world.”
6. The words of the beloved disciple are just as clear: “Do not be surprised, my brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers.”
It is as if he said, “You must not expect anyone to love you except those who have ‘passed from death to life.’”
So it follows that those who have not passed from death to life, who are not alive to God, are “the world.”
We can learn the same thing from the words in the fifth chapter, verse 19: “We know that we belong to God, and the whole world lies in the evil one.”
[1 John 5:19] Here “the world” clearly means those who do not belong to God, and who therefore “lie in the evil one.”
7. On the other hand, those who love God belong to God. So do those who at least “fear him and keep his commandments.”

This is the lowest level of those who “belong to God.” They are not really sons, but servants. They turn away from evil and work hard to do good. They faithfully use all his ordinances. They do this because they have the fear of God in their heart and sincerely want to please him.
Fix this plain meaning of the words “the world” firmly in your heart: it means those who do not fear God in this way.
Do not let anyone fool you with empty words. It means no more and no less than this.
8. If we understand the word in this way, what kind of friendship may we have with the world?

We may, and we should, love them as we love ourselves, for they too are included in the word “neighbour.” We should truly wish them well. We should want them to be happy as sincerely as we want our own souls to be happy. Yes, in a sense we should even honour them (since the apostle tells us to “honour all people”). We honour them as creatures God has made. More than that, we honour them as spirits that will never die, who are able to know God, love him, and enjoy him forever.
We should honour them because they were redeemed by the blood of the One who “tasted death for every person.”
We should feel tender pity for them when we see them turning away from the mercies offered to them, wandering off the path of life, and rushing toward everlasting destruction.

We should never willingly hurt their feelings or cause them any pain. Instead, we should give them all the pleasure we can, as long as it is innocent. For we are told to “please all people for their good.”
We should never make their faults look worse than they are. Instead we should gladly recognise all the good that is in them.
9. We may, and should, always speak to them in the kindest and most courteous way we can.

We should not speak evil of them when they are not there, unless it is absolutely necessary—unless it is the only way we know to stop them from doing harm. Otherwise we should speak about them with all the respect we can, without going beyond the truth.
When we are with them, we should treat them with every courtesy. We should show them all the respect we can, without supporting them in their sin.

We should do them all the good we can—all the good they are willing to receive from us. In this we follow the example of the Friend of all, our Father in heaven. Until they are willing to receive greater blessings, he gives them the ones they are willing to accept. He “makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends” his “rain on the just and on the unjust.”
10. “But then what kind of friendship may we not have with the world?
May we not spend time with ungodly people at all?
Should we avoid their company completely?”
Not at all. We have already said the opposite.
If we were not to mix with them at all, “we would have to leave the world.”
Then we could not show them the acts of kindness we have already mentioned.

We certainly may spend time with them. First, in business—in the many tasks of this life, according to the place in life where God’s providence has put us. Second, when politeness requires it—only we must be very careful not to carry it too far. Third, when we have a reasonable hope of doing them good.
But here too we especially need to be careful and pray a great deal. Otherwise we may easily burn ourselves while trying to pull other burning sticks out of the fire.
11. We can easily harm our own souls by slipping into a close attachment to any of those who do not know God.

This is the friendship that is “hostility toward God.” We cannot watch ourselves too carefully, so that we do not fall into this deadly trap. We must be careful that we do not, before we realise it, begin to take pleasure and delight in them.
We are only on safe ground when we can say with the psalmist, “All my delight is in the holy people on the earth, and in those who stand out in goodness.”
We should not have unnecessary conversations with them.
It is our duty, and it is wise, to be with them no more often and no longer than we strictly need to.
And the whole time we need to remember and follow the example of the one who said, “I kept my mouth as if with a bridle while the ungodly person was in front of me.”
We should not form any kind of tie with them beyond what is absolutely necessary.
When Jehoshaphat forgot this and formed an alliance with Ahab, what happened?
First he lost his wealth: “The ships” they sent out “were wrecked at Ezion-geber.”
He was not satisfied with this warning or with the warning of the prophet Micaiah. He insisted on going up with Ahab to Ramoth-gilead. And there he almost lost his life.
12. Most of all, we should tremble at the very thought of making a marriage covenant with anyone who does not love God, or at least fear him. Marriage is the closest bond of all.

This is the most horrible foolishness, the most tragic madness, that a child of God could ever fall into. For it involves every kind of tie with the ungodly that a Christian’s conscience requires him to avoid.
No wonder, then, that God forbids it so plainly, and that the command is so absolute and firm: “Do not be unequally yoked with an unbeliever.”
Nothing could be clearer.

This is especially true if by the word “unbeliever” we mean someone who is far from being a believer in the gospel sense. He cannot say, “The life I now live, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” In fact, he does not even have the faith of a servant. He does not “fear God and do what is right.”
13. But why is friendship with the world so completely forbidden?
Why are we so strictly required to keep away from it?
There are two general reasons. First, it is a sin in itself. Second, it brings the most dreadful results.
First, it is a sin in itself—and not an ordinary sin, either.
According to God’s own words, friendship with the world is nothing less than spiritual adultery.
The Holy Spirit speaks to all who are guilty of it in these words: “You adulterers, both men and women.”
It clearly breaks our marriage covenant with God, because we love what God made more than God who made it. It flatly goes against that kind command: “My son, give me your heart.”
14. It is a sin of the most wicked kind. It shows not only that we do not know God, forget him, or pay no attention to him. It shows actual “hostility against God.”
It is openly and obviously hostility.
“Don’t you know,” says the apostle—can you really be unaware of this truth, so plain and so undeniable?—“that friendship with the world is hostility against God?”
And how terrible is the conclusion he draws from this!

“So whoever will be a friend of the world”—(if we translate the words correctly, they say, “Whoever wants to be a friend of the world”)—a friend of people who do not know God, whether he succeeds or not—by that very fact becomes an enemy of God.
This desire alone, whether it succeeds or not, gives him the right to that name.
15. And just as it is a sin in itself—a very wicked sin—it also brings the most dreadful results.
It often traps people again in the very sins they had “fully escaped.”
It usually makes them “share in other people’s sins,” even sins they do not commit themselves.
Little by little it weakens their hatred and fear of sin in general. In this way it makes them an easy victim for any strong temptation.
It leaves them open to all the sins of neglect that their worldly friends are guilty of.
Without their noticing it, it makes them less careful about private prayer, family worship, fasting, going to public worship, and taking the Lord’s Supper.

The people close to them do not care about any of these things, and that attitude will slowly influence them. Even if those people never say a word to recommend their own way of living (which is hardly likely), their example still speaks. And many times it is more powerful than any words.

Through this example they are drawn, without being able to help it and almost all the time, into useless talk—yes, even unloving talk. In the end they no longer “set a guard over their mouth and keep watch over the door of their lips.” They can join in gossip, tale-telling, and speaking evil of others without their conscience stopping them. They have grieved God’s Holy Spirit so often that he no longer corrects them for it. So their talk is no longer, as it once was, “seasoned with salt, and fit to give grace to those who hear.”
16. But these are not all the deadly results that come from close friendship with unholy people.
It not only keeps them from living rightly. It also directly tends to corrupt the heart.
It tends to create or increase in us all the pride and self-satisfaction, all the touchy readiness to take offence—yes, every disordered passion and wrong attitude—that their companions give in to.

Gently it leads them into the habit of pleasing themselves and not wanting to deny themselves. It makes them unwilling to bear or take up any cross. It makes them soft and delicate. It leads them into the wrong kind of shame and into the fear of people, which brings countless traps.
It pulls them back into the love of the world, into foolish and harmful desires, into the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life, until these swallow them up.
So in the end these people are far worse off than they were at first.

17. Suppose the children of God join themselves to the people of the world. The worldly people may not try to make them like themselves (though we should never assume that). They may not even plan or want to. Yet they will actually do it, whether they plan it or try to or not. I do not know how to explain it, but it is a real fact: their very spirit is catching.

While you are near them, you tend to catch their spirit, whether they mean it or not. Many doctors have noticed that not only the plague and putrid or dangerous fevers, but almost every disease people can get, is more or less catching.
And no doubt all spiritual diseases are catching too, though in many different ways.
Some pass on the infection more quickly than others.
Either way, the person who already has the disease does not want or plan to infect anyone else.
The man who has the plague does not want or intend to pass his disease on to you.
But that does not make you safe. So keep your distance, or you will surely be infected.
Doesn’t experience show that it is the same with diseases of the mind?
Suppose proud people, vain people, hot-tempered people, and lustful people do not want or plan to infect you with their own diseases. Even so, it is best to keep your distance from them.
You are not safe if you come too close to them.
You will find (and it will be good if it is not too late) that their very breath is catching.
It has recently been discovered that every human body has an atmosphere around it. This naturally affects everyone who comes within its limits.
Isn’t there something like this with a human spirit?
If you stay long in their atmosphere, so to speak, you can hardly avoid being infected.
The infection spreads from soul to soul, just as it does from body to body, even when the sick people do not intend or want it to.
But is that a reasonable thing to suppose?

Isn’t it well known that people of the world (with very few exceptions) are eager to make their companions like themselves? Yes, and they use every means, with all their skill and effort, to get what they want.
So run for your life!
Do not play with fire. Escape before the flames catch hold of you.
18. But how many arguments people give for friendship with the world!
And how strong the temptations to it are!
We will look at the ones that are the most dangerous and also the most common.
Let us begin with the most dangerous one of all, which is also by no means rare.
Someone says, “I admit that the person I am about to marry is not a religious person.
She does not claim to be.
She does not think much about it.
But she is a beautiful creature.
She is very pleasant, and I think she will be a lovely companion for me.”
This is a trap indeed!
Perhaps it is one of the greatest traps human nature can fall into.
No human power can overcome a temptation like this.
Only the mighty power of God can make a way for you to escape from it.
And his power can set you completely free: his grace is enough for you.
But only if you work together with him—only if you deny yourself and take up your cross.
And whatever you do, you must do it at once!
Nothing can be done little by little.
Whatever you do in this important matter must be done in one stroke.
If it is to be done at all, you must cut off your right hand at once and throw it away!
This is no time to ask advice from flesh and blood!
Win at once, or perish!
19. Now let us turn it around.
Suppose a woman who loves God is courted by a pleasant man. He is refined, lively, and good company, and he suits her in every other way, though he is not religious. What should she do?
If she believes the Bible, it is clear enough what she should do.
But what can she do?
Isn’t this

blocks.x: A test too hard for human weakness?

s: Who can stand firm in such a trial?
Who can resist such a temptation?
No one except someone who holds tightly to the shield of faith and cries out earnestly to the Strong One for strength.
No one except a woman who gives herself to watching and prayer and keeps on at it with all perseverance.
If she does this, she will be a happy witness in the middle of an unbelieving world. She will show that just as “all things are possible with God,” so “all things are possible for her who believes.”
20. But a man or a woman may ask, “What if the person who wants to know me has a strong natural mind, trained by many kinds of learning?
Couldn’t I gain a lot of useful knowledge by spending time closely with him?
Couldn’t I learn many things from him and greatly improve my own mind?”
Of course you may improve your own mind, and you may gain a lot of knowledge.
But still, if he does not have at least the fear of God, you will lose far more than you gain.
For you can hardly avoid losing as much in holiness as you gain in knowledge.
And if you lose even one degree of holiness, inside or outside, all the knowledge you gain will not make up for it.
21. “But his fine, strong mind, improved by education, is not the main thing in his favour.
He has qualities worth more than these. He is remarkably good-natured. He has a kind and caring spirit, and he is very generous by nature.”
For these very reasons, if he does not fear God, he is infinitely more dangerous.
If you spend close time with a person like this, you will surely soak up his spirit.
You will hardly be able to avoid stopping exactly where he stops.
Nothing in all my life has been as hard for me as spending time with men like this (“good sort of men,” as people usually call them) without being harmed by them.
Oh, beware of them!

Spend time with them only as much as business requires, and no more. Otherwise, even if you do not feel any harm right now, they will slowly and without your noticing tie you to earthly things again. They will dampen the life of God in your soul.
22. It may be that the people who want to know you are not experienced in religion, yet they understand it well. So you often gain something from talking with them.

If that is really so (and I have known a few cases like this), it seems you may spend time with them—but only very rarely and very carefully. Otherwise you will lose more of your spiritual life than all the knowledge you gain is worth.
23. “But these people are useful to me in running my business in this world.
In fact, they are often necessary to me. I could hardly carry on my business without them.”
Cases like this often happen.
And this is certainly a good enough reason to have some dealings with people who do not fear God, perhaps even often.
But even this is no reason at all for you to form a close friendship with them.
And here you must take the greatest care. “Otherwise, even through the contact with them that is necessary, the grace of God may decrease in your soul while your fortune in the world increases.”
24. There may be one more reason that sounds convincing for being close to an unholy man.
You may say, “I have helped him.
I helped him when he was in trouble.
And he remembers it with thankfulness.
He respects and loves me, though he does not love God.
So shouldn’t I love him?
Shouldn’t I return love for love?
Don’t even pagans and tax collectors do that?”
My answer is: you should certainly return love for love. But that does not mean you should be close friends with him.
That would put your soul in danger.
Let your love pour itself out in constant and fervent prayer. Wrestle with God for him.
But do not let your love for him carry you so far that it weakens your own soul, or even destroys it.
25. “But must I not be close to my relatives, whether they fear God or not?
Hasn’t God in his providence entrusted them to me?”
Of course he has. But some relatives are nearer and some are more distant.
The nearest relatives are husbands and wives.

They have taken each other for better or for worse, so they must make the best of each other. For since God has joined them together, no one can separate them—except in the case of adultery, or when the life of one of them is in immediate danger.
Parents are almost as closely tied to their children.
You cannot leave them while they are young, because it is your duty to “train them up” with all care “in the way they should go.”
How often you should spend time with them when they are grown up is something Christian wisdom must decide.
Christian wisdom will also decide how long it is wise for children to stay with their parents, if it is their own choice.
In general, if they do not fear God, you should leave them as soon as it is convenient.
But wherever you are, make sure (if you can) that they do not lack what they need or what makes life comfortable.
As for all other relatives, even brothers or sisters, if they belong to the world you are not obliged to be close to them. You may be polite and friendly from a distance.

26. Let us grant that “friendship with the world is hostility against God.” Then it follows that the most excellent way to heaven—indeed the only way—is to avoid all close friendship with worldly people. But who has the determination to walk in this way? Who does, even among those who love or fear God? For only these people are concerned in this question.

I have known a few who were lights in a dark land, even in this matter. They did not and would not either start or keep up any friendship with people of the most refined and cultivated minds and the most attractive personalities. They refused simply because those people belonged to the world and were not alive to God. They refused even though those people could have increased their knowledge or helped them in business. They refused even though those people admired and respected them for the very religion that they themselves did not experience. You would hardly think this possible, but there are many examples of it today.
For conscience’ sake they steadily and firmly keep away from close friendship even with people like these.
27. Whoever you are, if you are a child of God by faith, go and do the same!
Whatever it costs, run from spiritual adultery.
Have no friendship with the world.
However much profit or pleasure tempts you, do not become close friends with worldly-minded people.
And if you already have such a friendship, break it off right away.

Yes, even if your ungodly friend is as dear to you as your right eye, or as useful as your right hand, do not ask advice from flesh and blood. Pluck out the right eye, cut off the right hand, and throw them away!
This is not a small matter.
Your life is at stake: eternal life or eternal death.
And isn’t it better to enter life with one eye or one hand than to have both and be thrown into the fire of hell?
When you did not know any better, God overlooked those times of ignorance.
But now your eyes are opened. Now the light has come. Walk in the light!
Do not touch tar, or you will be made dirty.
Whatever happens, “keep yourself pure!”
28. But whatever others do, whether they listen or refuse to listen, hear this, all of you who are called Methodists!
No matter how much you are pressed or tempted, have no friendship with the world.
Look around you, and see the sad results it has produced among your brothers!
How many of the mighty have fallen!
How many have fallen through this very thing!
They would not take any warning. They insisted on spending time, and close time, with earthly-minded people, until they “walked their steps back to earth again!”
Oh, “come out from among them!”—from all unholy people, however harmless they may seem—“and be separate.” At least be separate enough to have no close friendship with them.
Your “fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.” So let your fellowship be with those, and only those, who at least sincerely seek the Lord Jesus Christ.
Then “you will be,” in a special way, “my sons and my daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”
“Do not hate your brother in your heart. Be sure to rebuke your neighbour, and do not let sin remain on him.” Leviticus 19:17.

A large part of the book of Exodus, and almost all of the book of Leviticus, deals with the ritual or ceremonial law of Moses. This law was given especially to the people of Israel. But the apostle Peter says it was “a yoke” that “neither our fathers nor we were able to carry.”
So we have been set free from it. This is one part of “the freedom with which Christ has set us free.”
Still, it is easy to see that many excellent moral commands are scattered among these ceremonial laws.
We find several of them in this very chapter. For example: “Do not gather every grape from your vineyard. Leave them for the poor and the stranger.
I am the Lord your God.”
(Leviticus 19:10.) Do not steal, and do not lie to one another.
(Leviticus 19:11.) “Do not cheat your neighbour or rob him. Do not keep a hired worker’s wages with you until the morning.”
(Leviticus 19:13.) “Do not curse the deaf, and do not put something in front of the blind to make them stumble. Fear your God instead. I am the Lord.”
(Leviticus 19:14.) It is as if he said: I am the one whose eyes watch over the whole earth, and whose ears are open to their cry.
“Do not be unjust when you judge. Do not favour the poor”—kind-hearted people may be tempted to do that—“and do not honour the powerful”—there are a thousand temptations to do that.
(Leviticus 19:15.) “Do not go around spreading gossip among your people.” (Leviticus 19:16.) Yet this is a sin that human laws have never been able to stop.
Then come these words: “Do not hate your brother in your heart. Be sure to rebuke your neighbour, and do not let sin remain on him.” (Leviticus 19:17.)
This is an important instruction. To understand it rightly, and to apply it to our own souls in a helpful way, let us look at these questions:
I. What is it that we must rebuke or correct?
What exactly is being commanded here?
II. Who are the people we are commanded to correct? And,
III. How should we correct them?
I. 1. First, let us ask: What is the duty that is commanded here?
What is it that we must rebuke or correct?
And what does it mean to correct someone?
What does it mean to correct?
It means telling a person about his faults. This is clear from the words that follow: “Do not let sin remain on him.”
So sin is the thing we are called to correct—or rather, the person who commits the sin.
We must do everything we can to convince him of his fault and lead him into the right way.
2. Love does require us to warn him about sin, and mainly about sin. But love also requires us to warn him about any error that would naturally lead to sin if he kept holding on to it.
If we do not “hate him in our heart,” and if we love our neighbour as ourselves, we will always try to do this. We will warn him about every evil way, and about every mistake that leads toward evil.
3. But if we do not want to waste our effort, we should seldom correct anyone about something that can be argued—something where much can be said on both sides.
Something may seem wrong to me, so I have doubts about doing it. And if I did it while I still had those doubts, I would be sinning before God.
But another person is not to be judged by my conscience. He stands or falls before his own master.
So I would not correct him except for what is clearly and undeniably wrong.
One example is cursing and swearing that dishonours God. Even people who do it most will seldom dare to defend it, if someone gently reasons with them.
Drunkenness is another. Even a habitual drunkard will condemn it when he is sober.
And most people would say the same about dishonouring the Lord’s day.
Some who are guilty of these sins may try to defend them for a while. But very few will keep it up if you look them steadily in the face and appeal to their own conscience before God.
II. 1. Second, let us ask: Who are the people we are called to correct?
This is all the more important to think about, because many serious people claim that there are some sinners whom the Bible itself forbids us to correct.

They take this meaning from our Lord’s solemn warning in his Sermon on the Mount: “Do not throw your pearls in front of pigs. If you do, they will trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you apart.”

But the plain meaning of these words is this: Do not offer the pearls—the great teachings or mysteries of the gospel—to men you know are like beasts. They are sunk in sin and have no fear of God before their eyes.
That would expose those precious jewels to scorn, and it would expose you to harm.

But think of people whom we know to be dogs and pigs in our Lord’s sense. If we see them do, or hear them say, something they themselves know is wrong, we must still correct them. Otherwise we “hate our brother in our heart.”
2. “Our neighbour” means every human being—everyone who breathes the air of life, everyone who has a soul to be saved.
Suppose we hold back from doing this loving service for some people because they are worse sinners than others. They may go on in their sin, but God will require their blood from our hands.
3. How striking are Mr. Baxter’s thoughts about this in his book “The Saints’ Everlasting Rest”!
“Suppose you met someone in the world below whom you had refused this loving service while you both lived under the sun. What answer could you give when he blamed you?
‘At such a time and place, while we lived under the sun, God put me into your hands.
Back then I did not know the way of salvation. I was chasing death, lost in the error of my life. And you left me like that, without even once trying to wake me out of my sleep!
If you had shared your knowledge with me, and warned me to flee from the coming wrath, neither of us would ever have had to come to this place of torment.’”
4. So everyone who has a soul to be saved has a right to this loving service from you.
But this does not mean that it must be given to everyone to the same degree.
No one can deny that it is owed especially to some people.
First of all, it is owed to our parents, if we have parents who need it—unless we put our husbands or wives and our children on the same level as them.
Next come our brothers and sisters. After them come our relatives, whether they are close or distant to us, by blood or by marriage.
Right after these come our servants, whether they are bound to us for a number of years or for a shorter time.

Last of all, each to their own degree, come the people of our country, our fellow citizens, and the members of the same society, whether civil or religious. Religious societies have a special claim on our service. They are formed for this very purpose: to watch over each other, so that we do not let sin remain on our brother.
If we fail to correct any of these people when a good chance comes, we certainly belong among those who “hate their brother in their heart.”
And how severe is the apostle’s sentence on those who come under this condemnation!
“Anyone who hates his brother”—even if the hatred never comes out in words or actions—“is a murderer. And you know,” the apostle goes on, “that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.”
That seed which grows up into eternal life has not been planted in his soul. In other words, he is in such a state that if he dies in it, he cannot see life.
So it clearly follows that neglecting this is no small thing. It puts our final salvation in great danger.
III. We have seen what it means to correct our brother, and who we should correct.
But the most important thing still has to be considered.
How, in what way, should we correct them?
1. We must admit that it is quite hard to do this in the right way. At the same time, it is much less hard for some people than for others.
Some people are especially fitted for it, whether by nature, by practice, or by grace.
They are not held back by wrong shame, or by that heavy burden, the fear of people. They are both ready to take on this work of love and skilful at doing it.
So for them it is little or no cross to bear. In fact, they rather enjoy it. They find satisfaction in it, beyond the satisfaction of knowing they have done their duty.
But whether it is a big cross or a small one for us, we know that we are called to this.
And no matter how hard it is for us, we know whom we have trusted. We know he will surely keep his word: “As your day is, so your strength will be.”
2. So how should we correct our brother, so that our correction will do the most good?

First of all, let us make sure that whatever we do is done in “the spirit of love.” That means tender goodwill toward our neighbour. We should treat him as a son of our common Father, and as someone Christ died for, so that he might share in salvation.
Then, by the grace of God, love will produce love.
The warm feeling of the speaker will spread to the heart of the listener. And in time you will find that your work has not been in vain in the Lord.
3. Meanwhile, take the greatest care to speak in a spirit of humility.
Be careful not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think.
If you think too highly of yourself, you will hardly be able to avoid looking down on your brother.
And if you show, or even feel, the smallest contempt for the people you correct, it will ruin your whole work. It will make you lose all your effort.

To prevent even the appearance of pride, you will often need to say this openly. Make it clear that you do not put yourself above him. And at the very moment you correct what is wrong, acknowledge what is good in him and thank God for it.
4. Third, take great care to speak in a spirit of gentleness as well as humility.
The apostle assures us that “the anger of men does not bring about the righteousness of God.”
Anger produces anger, even when it is dressed up with the name of zeal. It does not produce love or holiness.
So we should avoid even the appearance of anger, with all possible care.
Let there be no trace of it in your eyes, your gestures, or your tone of voice. Instead, let all of these together show a loving, humble, and calm spirit.
5. But all the while, make sure you do not trust in yourself.
Do not rely on your own wisdom, or skill, or any other ability.
For the success of everything you say or do, do not trust in yourself. Trust in the great Author of every good and perfect gift.
So while you are speaking, keep lifting up your heart to him who works all in all.
Whatever is said in the spirit of prayer will not fall to the ground.
6. That is enough about the spirit in which you should speak when you correct your neighbour.
Now I will move on to the outward way of doing it.
People have often found that beginning a correction with an honest statement of goodwill makes the words sink deep into the heart.
This will usually work far better than that great fashionable tool—flattery. Worldly people have often done surprising things by means of flattery.
But the very same things, and far greater ones, have been done much more often by a plain and simple declaration of unselfish love.
When you feel that God has lit this flame in your heart, do not hide it. Let it out fully!
It will strike like lightning.
Stubborn and hard-hearted people will melt before you. They will know that God is truly with you.

7. It is certain that the main thing in correcting is to do it with the right spirit. Still, we must admit that several small details about the outward manner are useful, so they should not be looked down on.
One of these is this: whenever you correct someone, do it very seriously. You really are in earnest, so you should look like it too.
A joking correction makes little impression, and it is soon forgotten. Besides that, it is often taken badly, as if you were making fun of the person you are correcting.
And people who are not used to making jokes do not like being joked about.
One way to give a serious tone to what you say is to use the very words of Scripture as often as you can.
We often find that God’s word has a special power, even in a private conversation. When the sinner least expects it, he feels it is “sharper than a two-edged sword.”
8. Still, there are some exceptions to this general rule of correcting seriously.
There are some special cases where, as a wise observer of human nature says,

blocks.x: Ridiculum acri fortius—

s: a little well-placed teasing will pierce deeper than solid argument.
But this applies mainly when we are dealing with people who are strangers to religion.

Sometimes we may stoop to correct such a person in a light-hearted way. When we do, it seems that Solomon’s advice gives us the right to do so: “Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes.”
9. In other ways too, the manner of correcting can change to fit the occasion.
Sometimes it may be right to use many words and explain your view fully.

At other times it may be wiser to use few words, maybe just one sentence. At still other times it may be best to use no words at all—just a gesture, a sigh, or a look. This is especially true when the person you want to correct is far above you in rank.
Often this silent kind of correction will come with the power of God. So it will have a far better effect than a long, laboured speech.
10. One more thing: remember what Solomon said: “A word spoken at the right time—how good it is!”

It is true that if God in his providence calls you to correct someone you will probably never see again, you must take the chance right then. You must speak “in season” or “out of season.” But with people you often have the chance to see, you may wait for a good moment.
Here the poet’s advice applies.
You may speak

blocks.x: Si validus, si laetus erit, si denique poscet:

s: when he is in a good mood, or when he asks you to.
Here you may catch the

blocks.x: Mollia tempora fandi,—

s: the time when his mind is soft and gentle. Then God will both teach you how to speak and bless what is said.
11. But here let me warn you against one mistake.
People treat this as a rule that cannot be questioned: “Never try to correct a man when he is drunk.”
They say that correction is wasted then, and can do no good.
I dare not say that.
I have seen quite a few clear examples of the opposite.
Here is one. Many years ago I was passing a man in Moorfields. He was so drunk he could hardly stand. I put a paper into his hand.
He looked at it and said, “A Word—A Word to a Drunkard—that is me—Sir, Sir!
I am wrong—I know I am wrong—please let me talk with you a little.”
He held my hand for a full half-hour. And I believe he never got drunk again.
12. I beg you, brothers, by the mercies of God, do not look down on poor drunkards!
Have compassion on them!
Keep at it with them, whether the time seems right or not!
Do not let shame or the fear of people stop you from pulling these burning sticks out of the fire. Many of them already condemn themselves:

blocks.x:
They do see the evil plight
That they are in;

s: but they despair. They have no hope of escaping from it. And they sink deeper and deeper into it, because no one else has any hope for them!
“I have often known sinners of every other kind converted to God,” said a respected old clergyman.
“But I have never known a habitual drunkard to be converted.”
But I have known five hundred, perhaps five thousand.
Listen! Are you one who is reading these words?
Then hear the words of the Lord!
I have a message from God for you, sinner!
This is what the Lord says: Do not throw away your hope.
I have not forgotten you.
Whoever tells you there is no help is a liar from the beginning.
Look up! See the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
Today salvation has come to your soul. Only make sure you do not despise the one who is speaking!
Right now he is saying to you: “Son, take heart!
Your sins are forgiven!”
13. Finally: you who work hard at this labour of love, do not be discouraged, even if you see no fruit right now after doing your best.
You need patience. Then, “after you have done the will of God” in this, the harvest will come.
Never grow “weary of doing good; at the right time you will reap, if you do not lose heart.”
Follow the example of Abraham, who “against hope, still believed in hope.”
“Throw your bread on the waters, for you will find it after many days.”
14. Now I have just a few words to add for you, my brothers, who are commonly called “Methodists.”
I have never heard or read of any large revival of religion that did not come with a spirit of correcting sin.
I believe it cannot be any other way. For what is faith, unless it works by love?

That is how it was in every part of England when the present revival of religion began about fifty years ago. All who were touched by that revival—all the so-called Methodists everywhere—corrected outward sin.
And indeed, so do all who, “being justified by faith, have peace with God through Jesus Christ.”
That is how they are at the start. And if they use that precious gift, it will never be taken away.
Come, brothers, in the name of God, let us begin again!
Rich or poor, let us all rise up as one man. And let every man be sure to “rebuke his neighbour, and not let sin remain on him!”
Then all Great Britain and Ireland will know that we do not “go to war at our own cost.” Yes, “God will bless us, and all the ends of the world will fear him.”
Manchester, July 28, 1787
